<term>Crucifixion</term>: The central image depicts the execution of Jesus on the cross, a standard motif in Christian art.
<term>Lamb of God</term>: <note>original: "Agnus Dei"</note> A title for Jesus used in the liturgy and scripture to emphasize his role in the redemption of humanity.
<term>INRI</term>: The "titulus" or label placed above Jesus' head during the crucifixion.
<term>Blind-stamping</term>: A decorative technique where patterns are pressed into leather using hot metal tools without the use of gold leaf or ink, creating a subtle, recessed relief.
<term>Leather binding</term>: The protective outer cover of the book, often made from calf or pigskin during the 16th and 17th centuries.
<term>Latin</term>: The scholarly and liturgical language of Western Europe at the time this book was bound.

<meta>This is the title page of a 1602 edition of Johannes Nider’s "Formicarius," originally written in the 15th century. It establishes the author’s credentials and the pedagogical intent of the work.</meta>

# THE ANTHILL OF THE GOOD. <note>The title "Myrmecia" is derived from the Greek word for anthill, symbolizing a community of the faithful.</note>
## Or
# THE ANT-BOOK <note>Original Latin: "Formicarius." This is Nider’s most famous work, using the industrious ant as a metaphor for Christian living.</note>
## BY JOHANNES NIDER
### DOCTOR OF SACRED THEOLOGY AND MOST DISTINGUISHED PREACHER, DIVIDED INTO FIVE BOOKS.

*By which any Christian is most effectively instructed, both by the wonderful example of the Ants and by stories suited to the subject, both to obtain wisdom for themselves and to establish a life of honor and piety.*

**A unique work, filled with the most famous miracles and examples.**

<insert>From the library of the College of the Society of Jesus <note>The Jesuits</note> at Innsbruck. June 14, 1602.</insert> <note>Innsbruck is referred to here by its Latin name, Oenipons.</note>

<image-desc>An ornate woodcut printer's device featuring a circular frame with decorative scrollwork. Inside the circle, a unicorn stands at the edge of a stream, dipping its horn into the water to purify it. <note>The unicorn dipping its horn was a popular legendary motif; the horn was believed to neutralize toxins.</note> Above the unicorn, a banner scroll reads "I DRIVE AWAY POISONS" <note>original: "VENENA PELLO"</note>. At the bottom of the frame is a small shield with the monogram of the printer, Balthazar Bellère. To the right of the woodcut is a later ink stamp consisting of a crown above a cross; the cross contains abbreviations and text, including "IN ROME".</image-desc>

# DOUAI, <note>Douai (Latin: Duaci) was a major center for Catholic printing and education in the Spanish Netherlands during the Counter-Reformation.</note>

**From the Printing Office of BALTHAZAR BELLÈRE, At the Sign of the Golden Compass, In the Year 1602.**

<summary>This is the title page for a 1602 edition of Johannes Nider's "Formicarius," a 15th-century treatise that uses the behavior of ants as an allegorical framework for moral and religious instruction. This specific copy belonged to a Jesuit college in Innsbruck and was printed in Douai, a hub for Catholic scholarship.</summary>

# THE PROLOGUE BEGINS
## OF THE ANT-HILL ACCORDING TO THE EDI-
### FICATION OF BROTHER JOHN
### NIDER, OF SACRED THEOLOGY
An eminent Professor, who lived his life during the time of the Councils of Constance and Basel <note>These were major 15th-century church councils; Nider was a prominent reformer and diplomat during these events.</note>, fortunately.

Traveling frequently through certain regions, especially Germany, I have sometimes heard the complaints of men who are lazy in their faith: Why does God now no longer strengthen His Church among Christians with any miracles, or illuminate it with revelations for the protection of the faith and virtues for living well, as He once did?
<margin>Psalm 73</margin>
For they cry out with the faithless <term>Jews: "We have not seen our signs, there is no longer a prophet, and he will know us no more."</term> <note>original: "Signa noſtra non vidimus, iam non eſt propheta, & nos non cognoſcet amplius." This is a reference to Psalm 74:9 in modern bibles (Psalm 73 in the Latin Vulgate).</note> With the cooperating grace of Christ, I will strive to quell this murmuring in the following pages through many wonders <insert>so granted by God</insert> or miracles shown by divine power near and around our times—indeed, even while it was granted to us to live among men—along with various revelations and the virtues of holy men. These things are established either by the personal experience of my own sight or hearing, or by the reports of those worthy of trust, and, as I believe, they have been made sufficiently credible as a result. But because

<summary>Johannes Nider opens his prologue by addressing skeptics who claim miracles no longer occur; he intends to prove God's ongoing presence through contemporary 15th-century examples.</summary>
<keywords>Johannes Nider, Formicarius, miracles, Council of Constance, Council of Basel, Germany, skepticism, divine revelation</keywords>

<margin>
1 Corinthians 1
Job 13
</margin>

I am now working on moral subject matter; I therefore ask the reader of the following pages not to seek a formal demonstration <note>In medieval scholasticism, a "demonstration" was a logical proof that produced certain knowledge. Nider is asking the reader to accept "probability" or credible testimony instead of mathematical certainty.</note> where a suitable probability is sufficient. Nor should anyone suspect me of easily believing just any person, especially women—whom I suspect, unless they have been proven, often rave in such matters—although this fragile sex is not to be despised, for in that sex God has often done great things "to confound the strong things of the world," according to the Apostle <note>original: "vt confundat fortia mundi". A reference to 1 Corinthians 1:27, where St. Paul writes that God chose the weak to shame the strong.</note>. I know that God, according to the prophecy of the blessed Job, does not need our lie to serve Him <note>original: "noſtro non egere mendacio". Referring to Job 13:7: "Will you speak wickedly for God? and talk deceitfully for him?"</note>. I know that the science of Theology, which I have professed, detests falsehoods. I know, finally, that feigned doctrine is far from the life and the <term>Order of Preachers: The Dominican Order, a Catholic religious order founded to preach the Gospel and combat heresy through education and poverty.</term> and the office I perform. Nor should anyone wonder if I sometimes keep silent about the locations and proper names of persons, because brotherly charity commands it to be done so, and right reason persuades it, where either the seal of confession, or some notable secret, or the danger of <term>vainglory: translated from the Greek-derived "cenodoxiæ," meaning an excessive or empty desire for fame and praise</term> has constrained me to remain silent about certain things, or where there is some other danger to body or soul.

Therefore, I have endeavored to collect five small books under the form of a single volume; this present work is called *The Ant-Hill*, and it is interpreted morally. In it, the *LAZY* one will hold the office of the disciple, and the *THEOLOGIAN* will hold that of the teacher.

The first book will be principally about the rare examples and deeds of good men.

The second about likely good revelations.

The third about false and illusory visions.

The fourth about the virtuous deeds of the perfect.

The fifth about <term>witches: "maleficis," specifically those believed to use supernatural power to cause harm through a pact with the devil</term> and their deceptions.

<summary>Nider defends the credibility of his work by citing theological standards and the need for confidentiality, then introduces the dialogue format of his book and its five-part structure.</summary>

Chapter One. That the properties of ants <note>original: "formicarum". The ant serves as Nider's primary metaphor for the industrious Christian soul.</note> should be examined above the conditions of many other animals. Regarding their sixty properties. Regarding the threefold difference of labors. Regarding the seeking of miracles. Regarding those to whom the Eucharist <note>The sacrament of Holy Communion.</note> was miraculously given, and why sensible devotion <note>An emotional or physical feeling of God's presence during prayer.</note> is sometimes withdrawn.

Chapter 2. What blackness signifies. Regarding certain virgins betrothed to Christ, and why God is accustomed to give more to the simple.

Chapter 3. That God’s wisdom shines more wonderfully in small animals. Regarding monasteries miraculously reformed, and how those who live in "deformed" <note>original: "deformatis". In the 15th century, a "deformed" monastery was one that had fallen away from its original strict religious rule and required "reformation."</note> monasteries can be saved.

Chapter 4. Regarding the threefold good polity <note>Governance or social organization.</note>. Regarding the error of those who disparage chastity. Regarding those divinely liberated from carnal love, and how sterile lands are suitable for protecting chastity.

Chapter 5. Regarding mutual and brotherly assistance, and regarding the threefold degree of those living chastely in marriage.

Chapter 6. How in certain brute animals there is a kind of reason, memory, and concern. Regarding the fact that the lives of Prelates <term>Prelate: A high-ranking member of the clergy, such as a bishop or abbot, who holds authority over others.</term> should not be judged easily, and regarding the holy examples of certain Bishops.

Chapter 7. Regarding the moral city, and the threefold good labor. What good things two General Councils <note>Likely referring to the Council of Constance (1414-1418) and the Council of Basel (1431-1449), both of which Nider attended.</note> have achieved in our time. That a general reformation of the church is currently impossible. That Prelates should not...

Johannes Nider, of the Order of Preachers <note>The Dominicans</note>, a German, inquisitor of heretical depravity, doctor of the sacred page <note>A formal title for a Doctor of Divinity/Theology</note>, was a man endowed with distinguished and notable virtue. Because of his self-restraint in life and especially his great expertise in sacred literature, he was famous throughout the whole world. ### *Sixtus of Siena, "Holy Library," Book 4.* <note>Sixtus (1520–1569) was a renowned Dominican biblical scholar and bibliographer.</note>

# Book One.

## THAT THE PROPERTIES OF ANTS are to be examined above the conditions of many other animals. Concerning their sixty properties. Concerning the threefold difference of labors. Concerning miracles to be sought. Concerning those to whom the Eucharist <note>The Holy Communion or Blessed Sacrament</note> was miraculously given, and why perceptible devotion is sometimes withdrawn.

### CHAPTER I.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial letter 'V' ornate with floral vines and foliate patterns.</image-desc>

GO to the ant, O sluggard, and consider her ways, and learn wisdom; which, having no leader, instructor, nor ruler, prepares her food in the summer, and gathers in the harvest that which she may eat: so says that wealthy Solomon, the foremost Philosopher and Theologian in this matter, in Proverbs 6. In which passage he teaches you, O sluggard, to attend principally to three things: 1. the command of a pious teacher, when he puts forward, *go, and learn wisdom*; 2. the excess of your own lukewarmness <note>original: "teporis," referring to spiritual apathy or sloth</note>, where he adds, *O sluggard*; 3. the example of a skillful animal, when he concludes, *to the ant*, with her properties—which, if you apply them to human morals, you will indeed learn true wisdom. For this same reason, long ago in the early days of our Order <note>The Dominican Order, or Order of Preachers</note>, our brother Thomas of Brabant <note>Also known as Thomas of Cantimpré (c. 1201–1272), a famous Dominican encyclopedist who wrote on the properties of animals</note> wrote a book...

...moralized concerning bees, applying examples and miracles performed in his own time to them, lest forgetfulness—the mother of ingratitude—should abolish such things. Those, mindful of the coming winter, lest the moistened earth should turn their storehouses into grass, cut the seeds they had brought in <note>This reflects an ancient belief that ants bit the ends of seeds to prevent them from germinating and growing inside their nests</note>; these were carrying dead bodies with solemn mourning; and what was more marvelous, in such a great column, those exiting did not block those entering; rather, if they saw any fallen under a bundle or load, they helped by putting their shoulders underneath."

### CHAPTER I.

...rousing lazy minds by such an example, I began to grow weary of my captivity, to seek the cell of a monastery, and to desire the likeness of those ants, where they labor for the common good, and since nothing belongs to anyone as their own, everything belongs to all. Since, therefore, among the small and admirable animals—not even excluding the bee, short in its flights—none is found more sagacious <note>meaning: wise or clever in its instincts</note> than the ant, nor likewise more suited to the moral discipline of man: therefore, according to the general tradition mentioned before, I will recount its properties in the following books and treatises of this little work. I will write nothing of such properties of ants, however, except what the blessed Isidore <note>Isidore of Seville, a 7th-century scholar whose *Etymologies* was a standard medieval reference</note>, Pliny, Solinus, and Aristotle himself hand down, as well as Lord Albert the Great <note>Albertus Magnus, a 13th-century scientist and theologian</note> in his books *On Animals*, or what I have seen through my own experience. There is, therefore, among the properties of ants in general, according to a threefold scale of comparison, a fivefold difference, according to which there will be five books applicable to the good or bad morals of men.

<margin>Ecclesiasticus 11</margin>

*The third difference is considered in size, because some are small, others larger, and others very large.*

### THE ANT-HEAP, BOOK I.

...black, others red, others of a different form and quality, as in Ethiopia. **THE LAZY MAN**. Since you command me to look into the specific traits of ants, and to learn wisdom there, I would wish that you might express their individual conditions, so that having these as a kind of model, we might thereafter be able to more easily and delightfully 
<margin>perhaps more correctly: to choose or to direct.</margin>
\* love <note>original: *diligere*; the margin suggests *deligere* (to choose) or *dirigere* (to direct) as more accurate alternatives for the student's intent</note> our ways. **THE THEOLOGIAN**. ->Let these be in order under the first book.<-

<margin>
60 properties of ants for the subject matter of the whole work.
</margin>
1. In their activity, ants differ in three ways, as was mentioned before.
2. Those which are black are small in the mass of their body, but in power <note>original: *virtute*; implying both physical strength and innate excellence</note> they surpass larger animals.
3. Although they live in a colony, they nevertheless have no King as a leader, nor a teacher.
4. Their social organization <term>civilitas: the way a community organizes its laws and behavior</term> is very different from the governance of bees; for while the bees have a monarchical kingdom, the ants do not.
5. Even if they lack a monarch, they nevertheless obey one another peacefully.
6. In their Republic <note>original: *Republica*; Nider views the ant colony as a self-governing state</note>, they possess a certain reason, care, and memory.
7. Together they construct a home or city, which they cover with various distinct living quarters and small pieces of plants.
8. In their homes they build straight and hidden paths, in which they often live quite secretly.
9. Both males and females go out to work, all together in troops.
10. They maintain their paths very orderly, so that those going out do not hinder those wanting to re-enter by running into them.
11. Outside the home, they walk in a fairly straight and open path to acquire necessary food.

# THE ANTHILL, BOOK I.

...are most sagaciously sought.

4. Nightingales <note>original: *Philomenæ*; in classical mythology and medieval bestiaries, the nightingale is often referred to as Philomela.</note> eagerly seek out and eat ants and their eggs, because they recover from sickness and their voices are made melodious by them.

5. The ant-lion <note>A predatory insect larva, though in medieval lore it was sometimes depicted as a confused hybrid of a lion and an ant that could not eat and thus starved.</note> steals and eats the food of the ants in winter, because in summer, being improvident, it reserves no food for itself.

6. Although the nest of the ants may smell pleasant, nevertheless, if new and tender wood—or a flask <note>original: *lagena*; a large bottle or jug</note> made from such wood—is ground or rubbed harshly over it, they are found to take on a certain notable stench.

7. When the incautious ants walk outside their homes for the sake of gain, they are often treacherously killed by the ant-lion.

8. Where ants are harmful, they are easily put to flight if ashes are sprinkled there in a circular pattern.

9. Ants are said to be so large in Ethiopia that they are compared to dogs. <note>This refers to the "Gold-digging ants" of Herodotus and Pliny, a popular legend in the Middle Ages.</note>

10. Such ants are said to dig gold out of the sand with their feet.

11. These same ants are said to most diligently guard the gold they have dug up—which is of little or no use to them.

12. They pursue to the death those men who watchfully steal the gold from them.

3. Their eggs are fragrant and serve as a medicine for certain sick animals.

4. The eggs receive their growth in a warm place and facing the Sun, where, having been placed by the parents, they first turn into white worms, and from there into an ant...

*SLUGGARD.* I see, and perhaps I am envious, for you call me a sluggard now for the third time—not by my own name, but by a shameful one. You know that since the time I professed my approved religious life <note>referring to taking monastic vows in a recognized order</note>, I have hated sloth <note>original: *acediam*; a specific monastic vice characterized by spiritual apathy, boredom, or listlessness</note>, even if I have not entirely escaped it. *THEOLOGIAN.* I do not assert that you are ensnared by the vice of a lazy man in actual fact, but use the name only for the sake of our mutual comparison. Know that no name, whatever it may be, will harm a person if they are free from the act of the vice it describes. For how did it harm the Apostle Thaddeus <note>Saint Jude Thaddeus</note> that he shared a name with Judas, the betrayer of Christ? Where a difference in character is evident in someone, it matters little that their names happen to match. For just as a word alone grants goodness to no man, so the mark of a shameful name does not take away the gift of virtue from anyone. Unless I am mistaken, this was the very sentiment of Chrysostom <note>Saint John Chrysostom, the 4th-century "golden-mouthed" Church Father</note> when he said in a certain passage: "If you write the name of the devil in golden letters, it will still not lack malice; and if you depict the name of God in some foul characters, it will do no harm to the divine goodness." Therefore, let us not care greatly for the itching sounds of words, but let us labor to make progress in virtues—as we have begun to do—from the properties of the ant.

The first difference and property of ants was recited previously: *That in their activities, ants differ greatly, because some bury the dead; others are often occupied in profitable labors; and others seem to stand in the public ways, striving in a way to show the path to others, so they do not stray.* By these things, it is given to be understood that no person, especially one within the Church, is permitted to be idle in the vice of sloth <term>sloth: translated from *acedia*, a state of spiritual apathy or listlessness considered one of the seven deadly sins</term>, but all must strive to always be occupied in some useful exercise. For within the assembly of the Church itself, there are various exercises modeled after the ants, and three different types of activities that differ greatly in merit before God.

<margin>Three kinds of men. 1.</margin>
Certain people are held in the world by lawful pursuits, but are weighed down by labors concerning physical things—for instance, the mechanics <term>mechanics: manual laborers, craftsmen, or artisans who work with their hands</term>—for the sustenance of themselves and those necessary to them. This especially includes those who serve their neighbor in physical works of mercy. However, they ought not always to persist in these same tasks, but at times should leave them aside to devote themselves to better things. For those existing in the secular world or in infirmity are as if dead, or established in a kind of death, according to that chant of the Church: *In the midst of life we are in death* <note>original: *Media vita in morte sumus*; a famous Gregorian antiphon</note>. For above, the whole of life is in heaven; below, the whole of death is in hell; but here, we are in the midst of life, which is a kind of death. It is for this reason that Christ, wishing to call a certain man to a better life, said to him in Matthew 8: "Follow me, and let the dead bury their own dead." Regarding this, Bernard <note>Saint Bernard of Clairvaux (1090–1153), a highly influential Cistercian abbot and mystic</note> notes in his 19th sermon: It is to be noted in this sentence that sometimes lesser goods must be set aside for the sake of the utility of greater ones.

<margin>2.</margin>
There are others who sweat in profitable labors, but in spiritual goods: namely, the religious <note>members of monastic orders</note> and the clergy, who through prayers and the Canonical Hours <note>the set of daily prayers and psalms recited at specific times by priests and monks</note> drive away invisible enemies from their own souls and those of others, day and night. Of these, the Apostle says in 1 Timothy 5: "Those [priests] who rule well..."

->### THE ANT-HILL, BOOK 1.<-

...for those working lawfully in the world. There was a certain common man, a laborer, a simpleton <term>simplicianus; a term for someone viewed as "simple" or uneducated by the world, but spiritually pure</term> in the eyes of the world, but in truth wiser toward God. He was a citizen of the city of Nuremberg in the Diocese of Bamberg during my own time—I will not give his proper name now, but the good reputation of his life comes to mind. He was the spiritual son <note>original: "filius confessionis"; someone who regularly confessed his sins to a specific priest for spiritual guidance</note> of my predecessor in the Nuremberg priory, namely Brother Eberhard, a man most worthy of trust, as the one standing near me can testify. Indeed, it was through his account that I learned what follows.

<margin>An example of the Eucharist being granted by divine means.</margin> 

This "simpleton," then, was not a beggar in terms of worldly substance, but lived with moderate means according to the standards of the world. In divine matters, however, he was most devoted; for he gave generously to the poor from his own labor and resources through works of mercy. He would at times sharply discipline his body through long pilgrimages, and he used to exercise himself in various ways through meditation on the Passion of the Lord. 

Because his soul began to burn more for God every day through these pious activities, his desire to receive the most divine Sacrament of the Eucharist several times a year never ceased to grow. However, in the aforementioned city <note>Nuremberg</note>, the male sex is accustomed to approach the Sacrament of the Eucharist more rarely than the female sex; and the parish priests are usually more willing to grant it to the latter than to the former. 

Therefore, this servant of God feared to ask for the Sacrament—which he desired with a burning heart—more frequently than was the custom, lest he should appear "singular" <note>singular: in this context, acting in a way that draws attention to oneself or implies one is holier than the community</note>, according to that memorable saying of the blessed 

<margin>Bernard.</margin> 

Bernard: *He who does what no one else does, everyone wonders at.* <note>original: "Qui facit quod nemo, mirantur omnes." A warning against spiritual pride or outward displays of piety that differ from communal norms.</note> He eventually devised, by divine prompting, a way by which he might acquire through equivalence what he was unable to receive through the physical presence of the Sacrament. For he knew that the mercy of God always accepts a good will in place of the deed, provided that one’s own negligence does not <meta>catchword: prevent.</meta>

->## CHAPTER I.<-

...forbids <note>original: "vetat"</note> it. He did, therefore, as much as was in his power to prepare himself for the Sacrament of the Eucharist, especially on the days and at the hours when he likely could not receive the Eucharist from his own priest. For first, if the opportunity presented itself, he would go to sacramental confession beforehand; on the preceding day, he would eat more moderately in place of a fast <term>vice ieiunij; performing a partial fast as a spiritual discipline when a full fast was not possible</term>. Then, with true devotion through meditations, standing at the altar of the heart <note>original: "ara cordis"; a metaphor for the internal, spiritual space where a person meets God</note> before the eyes of the living God, he used to sacrifice himself and rouse his spirit as diligently as he could. Finally, during the office of the Mass, and most especially at the hour of communion, he asked with all the desire he could muster that Divine Mercy would make him a participant in such a great Sacrament, and accept his **good will in place of the deed** <note>original: "bonam voluntatem pro facto"; a theological principle that God accepts the sincere intent to perform a holy act if the act itself is prevented by circumstances</note>.

As evidence of this—so that the body might be subject to the spirit and that Divine Goodness might accept the gift of his good will for the deed—it happened that whenever the priest would take the Sacrament under the appearance of bread into his own mouth, this servant of God, striking his breast, would also open his own lips. And behold, a wonderful thing! For by a divine miracle (as may be piously believed), it happened that when he disposed himself in this way, a certain small particle of the **consecrated host** <note>original: "hostiæ conſecratę"</note> began to adhere to his tongue in a way that was devout, sweet, and perceptible to the senses. It seemed necessary to him either to remove this particle he felt from his mouth—which he feared to do—or, as he actually did, to swallow what he had received. 

He wondered at this many times, and finally began to doubt whether this was truly happening by divine means. One day, after he had heard the divine service and perceived the particle as mentioned before, wanting to be certain once the Mass was over, he put his finger in his mouth to touch his tongue. A certain **white particle**, as his sight confirmed, clung sensibly to his finger. He placed it back in his mouth and consumed it as before. However, throughout the remaining course of his life, he never again merited to perceive such a thing, even though he did not cease from his good works any less than he had before.

# OF THE ANTHILL, BOOK I.

**STUDENT.** <note>original: "PIG." abbreviation for Piger, the "Lazy" student character</note> I would like to know why God chose to withdraw this gift from His servant, who seemed to perform no unlawful act in that physical experience.

<margin>Luke 1</margin>
**THEOLOGIAN.** As I believe, Divine Mercy took away no part of the grace or virtue given freely to him thereafter; rather, He only removed a certain physical sensation. According to our wisdom <note>original: "sophiam"</note> and teaching, there is little or no merit in such a sensation itself. Indeed, such feelings are sometimes a reward given to the imperfect to prevent them from faltering on their path <note>a reference to the "milk" given to spiritual infants before they can handle the "meat" of difficult faith</note>, rather than being a merit in their own right. For this reason, these sweet sensations are often withdrawn from the stronger souls laboring in the vineyard of God, as it is necessary that they be given instead to the weaker, just as the blessed Bernard <note>St. Bernard of Clairvaux (1090–1153), a Cistercian abbot and influential mystic</note> teaches in his *Letter to the Brothers of Mont-Dieu*. Furthermore, the man perhaps was not entirely without fault for hesitating—much like Zechariah <note>referring to the father of John the Baptist who was struck mute for doubting the angel's message</note>—after witnessing so many circumstances of a divine message, in a matter where it was not permitted to doubt.

# THE ANT-HEAP, BOOK I.

...of the saints who are in the heavenly homeland <note>original: "in patria." In medieval theology, "the fatherland" refers to heaven, the true home of the soul.</note> for a long time. However, when this virgin was already quite advanced in years, a disease of the epidemic plague entered the monastery and caused this sacristan, along with many other nuns, to fall ill. 

After this holy virgin had devotedly received all the ecclesiastical sacraments, two sisters were already nearing their final agony. These sisters were lying in a distant chamber and were unaware of the virgin's own illness.

<margin>Angelic songs were heard at the death of a religious virgin.</margin>

They began to hear and see a celestial harmony and the presence of angels around the holy virgin’s location, and they said to those serving them: “Do you hear and see what the heavenly hosts are singing and doing around our sister? When this man realized with his mind's eye that he had been chosen as the shepherd and leader of such a sickly flock, he was immediately moved and visited by divine grace. Changed into a different man, he shuddered at the life he had previously led; he dreaded placing his weak shoulder under this new burden and began to wonder whether he should await the confirmation of his office with the intent of truly reforming himself, or whether he ought to resign from the election.

I say nothing of the lack of physical restraint and the disobedience of souls, without which one can hardly live in such monasteries.

<margin>Various opinions on this matter.</margin>
**THEOLOGIAN:** Regarding this doubt, not only various but even contrary and opposing opinions are given by different people. <margin>1.</margin> Some do not fear to say that all those living in such monasteries are outside the **state of salvation** <note>original: "statum salutis"; the condition of being on the path to heaven.</note>, <margin>2.</margin> a view with which I do not agree. There are others who, on the contrary, dare to affirm that everyone in such monasteries is in a **state of grace** <note>original: "statu gratiae"; being in God's favor and free from mortal sin.</note> if they have kept the commandments owed by secular men and have lived in the accustomed manner of those monasteries beyond what was mentioned; I believe their dogma to is incautious, unless they distinguish their response more carefully. There are, moreover, others who take something of a middle path, whose doctrine hands down **five rules**. By these, anyone who is a member of a religious order—at least one who cannot move to a reformed house (as they say)—can learn whether he walks the path of salvation while in a dissolute and deformed monastery.

<margin>3. The answer is indicated through five rules.</margin>

1. If he keeps those things which must be kept under command even by a secular man: for in these, the primary and Christian religion principally consists.

2. If he keeps the things he professed in his Rule and statutes, specifically those that fall under a direct command: for by acting against these, because they are commanded, his vow of profession seems to be directly violated. To go against this is to gravely offend God, and he who violates such things damns his soul.

3. If, not being provided for from the common goods of the community, he holds only such temporal goods as are necessary for his status...

### CHAPTER 4.

<margin>Aristotle, Book 3 of the *Politics*, Chapter 5. Three types of good political leadership.</margin>

<margin>1.</margin>
A kingdom is a monarchy, or the leadership of a single person, specifically when one person—perfect in all virtues and seeking the common good and the personal welfare of every individual in all things—rules over the entire remaining multitude of people.

<margin>2.</margin>
A second type is Aristocracy, in which several virtuous people, perfected in wisdom and virtue, hold power. They appoint virtuous and prudent men to each individual office. This system is corrupted when wicked and unjust men take control.

<margin>3.</margin>
There is also Timocracy <note>In the Aristotelian sense used here, a "timocracy" is a form of government where property owners or those with a certain status hold power, but still aim for the common good.</note>, in which a multitude of men—who are established above their equals in honors—govern and seek the good of both the rich and the poor. Although all these forms of government are good, the first [Monarchy] is the best, the third [Timocracy] is the lowest, and the second [Aristocracy] is better than the last. <margin>Three corruptions of the same.</margin> Conversely, three corruptions of leadership correspond to these governments; these should not be rightly called political leadership, but rather transgressions of them.

<margin>1. Tyranny</margin>
The first, which is called tyranny, is the worst form of government. It occurs where a king turns into a tyrant who seeks his own benefit in everything, rather than the welfare of his subjects.

The second [corruption] is a lesser evil called oligarchy, in which a few wicked men rule together over both the rich and the poor. They do not intend the good of the community but look only after their own benefit and that of their friends—specifically favoring certain rich or poor individuals—and they distribute offices to such people accordingly.

The third [corruption] is called democracy, which is more tolerable. In this system, many people rule—not the middle class, but the common populace—yet they do not care about the losses of the rich, focusing only on the interests of their own poor. The first, who...

### CHAPTER IV.

...[subjects. Such rulers] are tyrants, and they seek the good of no one but themselves. The second group <note>referring to the corruption of Aristocracy</note> seeks only the good of their rich and poor friends. The third group, however, procures only the good of their own kind, namely the common people. <note>The author is describing the three "corrupt" forms of government mentioned on the previous page: Tyranny, Oligarchy, and a corrupted form of Democracy.</note> It appears that the chosen people of God, Israel, once held these aforementioned three forms of leadership in succession. 

First, they had a single monarch on earth, Moses, whom God—the supreme ruler of the world's monarchy—sent, as recorded in Exodus 3, saying: "Come, I will send you to Pharaoh, so that you may lead my people, the children of Israel, out of Egypt." <note>original: "Veni mittam te ad Pharaonem, vt educas populum meum filios Iſrael de Ægypto."</note> 

The second was when the Lord said to Moses in Numbers 11: "Gather for me seventy men from the elders of Israel, whom you know to be elders and masters of the people; and I will take of your spirit and give it to them, so that they may bear the burden of the people with you, and you alone may not be burdened." <note>This represents the transition to an Aristocratic system (rule by a group of elders).</note> 

The people of Israel underwent a third form of rule, or something very much like it, as described in Judges 17, where it is said: "In those days there was no King in Israel, but everyone did what seemed right in his own eyes." <note>original: "In diebus illis non erat Rex in Iſrael, ſed vnuſquiſque quod ſibi rectum videbatur, hoc faciebat." This refers to a period of popular rule or decentralization.</note> 

I said that all Israel had a single first monarch on earth because, by appointing Moses, God intended Himself to be the King of Israel from heaven rather than from earth; His reign lasted until the time of Saul. Thus, God was angry when Israel first desired an earthly king, and He said to the praying Samuel in 1 Samuel 8 <note>original: "1. Reg. 8." - In the Latin Vulgate Bible, the books of Samuel are often titled 1 and 2 Kings.</note>: "Listen to the voice of the people in all that they say to you. For they have not rejected you, but they have rejected me, that I should not reign over them." And in the same book, chapter 10, Samuel says to the people: "Today you have cast away your God, who alone saved you from all your evils and tribulations." 

Therefore, among a swarm of bees, there is a likeness of a monarchy or kingdom, in which one is the king and leader of the swarm. <note>original: "rex" - While we now know these are queen bees, historical texts often referred to the leader of a hive as a king.</note> Among the multitude of ants, however, no king of the same species is found; rather, they are guided toward their proper ends by Nature—the force that gives nature to all things—namely, by God.

### CHAPTER IV.

## CHAPTER V.

Although ants lack a monarch, they nevertheless obey one another in tranquility. This condition preserves a constant peace and harmony among them, which we find in very few animals. In this regard, they also closely approach the state of innocence <note>The theological concept of humanity's perfected state before the Fall of Man.</note>, in which there would have been no discrepancy <margin>that is, discord.</margin> among humans, if the first-created <term>first-created (protoplasti): A Greek-derived term for Adam and Eve as the original ancestors of humanity.</term> had kept the first commandments of God. Therefore, the Lord sent a deep sleep upon Adam: and when he had fallen asleep, He took one of his ribs and filled the flesh in its place. And the Lord God built the rib, which He had taken from Adam, into a woman, and brought her to Adam. In this creature, it especially teaches what kind of behavior is required...

...at that time. We know, however, that difficulty increases merit, and a greater degree of merit establishes a more eminent rank [in heaven]. Thus, many find it easier to abstain from the eating of meat forever than to attempt to eat it intermittently without the excess of gluttony <note>The author argues that total abstinence is often psychologically easier than practicing moderation, which requires constant vigilance</note>. 

The second question: how ought a prudent confessor or counselor conduct himself toward such persons who are inspired by the purpose of chastity within marriage? 

**THEOLOGIAN:** Regarding the first point, you should know that in any action, or the omission of one, difficulty sometimes arises from the genus and nature of the work—because it is difficult and arduous in itself—while at other times it arises only, or principally, from the person performing it. The first kind of difficulty increases merit, but not the second, which arises from the vice of the subject; and so it is in the examples provided earlier. Therefore, the degrees of marital continence <term>continence: choosing to abstain from sexual relations</term> stand as they should. 

Regarding the second point, know that first, he must recognize with the greatest diligence the natures, conditions, and circumstances of the persons thus inclined toward chastity. Next, if he finds everything points toward chastity, he should be careful not to admit a vow to confirm it immediately; rather, he should teach them to exclude occasions for a lack of restraint. ### CHAPTER VII.

Ants construct a house or city together, which is divided into dwellings and covered with various small pieces of plants. In these acts, a triple and wonderful operation of these animals is suggested. For they build a kind of city for themselves, they construct various dwellings within it, and they cover these against heat and rain with various fragments of plants. In these operations, they have no master of their own species, but God alone, by whose instinct they are guided both in the construction and the maintenance of such things. 

In these traits, the ants specifically bear the figure <note>original: "Typum," a theological term meaning a symbolic foreshadowing or model.</note> of those who belong to general councils <term>General Councils: large assemblies of high-ranking Church leaders (bishops, abbots, etc.) convened to decide on matters of doctrine and discipline.</term>, and especially the prelates. For these men ought to reform the city of the Church Militant <term>Militant Church: the community of Christians currently living on earth, as opposed to those in heaven or purgatory.</term> through their own "buildings"—so far as it concerns them—wherever it suffers ruin. They should build up men in various ways for the service of God and defend and protect them from the heat of vices and the frost of enemies. They ought to conduct themselves in word and example such that they deserve to be guided principally by the Divine Spirit in these tasks. 

For it was in this way that John saw this city descending from heaven, and originally having its source there. <margin>Revelation 21.</margin> "I saw," he said, "the holy city, the new Jerusalem, descending from heaven from God, prepared as a bride adorned for her husband." But, alas! Today the matter has been turned into the opposite. For the greater part <note>original: "potior," here meaning the more powerful or larger part.</note>

Take an example of this from the art of architecture. For give me an architect however skillful, if he lacks suitable material, like wood or stones, he will never construct a house. <margin>
Gregory, *Moralia*, Book 6, Chapter 17 (otherwise 27).
</margin>

Among ants, both males and females go out to labor, all of them in troops. In this, they teach us to avoid idle leisure and sloth, through which fuel is provided for vices. For physical labor—whether it is performed through the exercise of the limbs, or in other chastisement of the body, or in other means of the <term>active life: the stage of Christian life focused on outward works and the struggle against vice</term>—is so necessary to everyone according to common law (whenever one has not given oneself to the contemplation of the mind or the study of books) that without it, no one can rightly pass over to the <term>contemplative life: a state of life focused on the prayerful "vision" of God, often called the "theoric" life</term>. <note>The author uses the term "vita theorica," derived from the Greek *theoria*, meaning "to look at" or "contemplate."</note>

Hence Blessed Gregory says in the 6th book of his *Moralia*, treating that passage in Exodus 19: "Beware," God says through Moses to the people, "that you do not go up into the mountain, nor touch the borders of Israel. Everyone who touches the mountain shall die the death: a hand shall not touch him, but he shall be overwhelmed with stones or pierced with arrows; whether it be beast or man, he shall not live." <note>original: *Caue... ne ascendatis in montem...*</note>

Now, the people are forbidden from the mountain when the law is received from God so that, namely, those who still desire earthly things with weak minds should not presume to contemplate sublime things. Whence it is rightly said: "If a beast touches the mountain, it shall be stoned." For a "beast" touches the mountain when a mind subjected to irrational desires raises itself to the heights of contemplation. But it is struck with stones because, not sustaining the highest things, it is killed by the very blows of the celestial weight. Therefore, those who strive to reach the summit of perfection, when they desire to hold the citadel of contemplation...

<margin>Threefold labor.</margin>
**THE LAZY MAN.** <note>original: "PIG." for *Piger*, the character representing the slothful student in Nider's dialogue.</note> As I perceive from your words, you commend a threefold labor. One, which is performed in the manner of <term>mechanical work: physical labor or manual trades, such as farming or smithing</term> with the hands or feet; another, by which the body is tamed by vigils, fasts, abstinences, <term>hairshirts: garments made of coarse animal hair worn against the skin as a form of penance</term>, and the like; and finally, that by which, while living lawfully among men, one restrains the mind against anger, hatred, love, sadness, joy, pleasure, and against similar passions. It is asked, therefore: which of these labors is better?

**THE THEOLOGIAN.** As far as the nature of the work is concerned, they possess a degree of goodness in the same order in which you heard them. All else being equal, the first seems to be of less merit and less difficulty than the second, and the second less than the last. However, as to which of them—all or only some—are more necessary for a person to acquire perfection, let each person read attentively in his own conscience. For just as it is more necessary for a poor man to be enriched by the labors of his hands <margin>Aristotle, *Topics*, Book 3, Chapter 1.</margin> than to philosophize according to Aristotle, so among those imitating the doctrine of Christ, it is more urgent for many to use a mechanical art for their livelihood than for there to be a need for the second type of exercise, by which the body is worn down. 

Yet, toward the last stage—by which means the passions are conquered and brought to a <term>middle state: the Aristotelian "golden mean," where emotions are balanced and governed by reason</term> in the soul through opportunities found in external things—every imperfect person is bound to strive, as you heard on the authority of Blessed Gregory; because the <term>active virtues: practical moral virtues like justice or temperance exercised in daily life</term> necessarily consist in these. Without the first and second types of labor, however, some can be sufficiently tranquil depending on the place and time, and according to the [arrangements...]

**THE LAZY MAN.** I have often wondered why, in our regions, men are no longer found—as they once were—who dare to attack the body with fasts and abstinences, with whips and other harsh exercises, as many of the canonized saints are read to have done, and the fathers in Egypt and Scythia, whom the *Lives of the Fathers* <note>original: "Vitas-patrum." This refers to the *Vitae Patrum*, a famous collection of hagiographies of the early Christian hermits living in the desert.</note> describes in full. 

**THE THEOLOGIAN.** Although such men are no longer found as frequently as in the past, nevertheless there are still many such devoted people, whom you will hear about shortly in what follows. But first, I want you to know that it can happen for five or six reasons why some are not able to endure such heavy exercises. <margin>Six reasons why some cannot endure bodily exercises. 1.</margin> Namely: from the state of the air, from the physical makeup of the body, from zeal for perfection, from the habit of youth, from the pretense of hypocrisy, and from special gifts. 

For the air, if it is very hot in a certain region, does not hinder digestion (as the <term>physicians: medieval doctors or natural philosophers</term> say), but draws it toward the exterior, and consequently makes men more prone to abstinence. On the contrary, a cold region constricts the pores of the body, and can increase the heat within the stomach through <term>antiperistasis: a philosophical concept where a quality is intensified by being surrounded by its opposite, such as heat being concentrated inside the body when the outside environment is cold</term>. Hence it happens that in our cold regions, some men eat more in the winter than in the summer. It is no wonder, then, if men in hot regions fast more easily.

<margin>2.</margin> The physical makeup of certain individuals also plays a role, as is clear in those who are cold by nature, such as those of a <term>phlegmatic: one of the four humors or temperaments, traditionally characterized as cool, calm, and sometimes sluggish</term> or <term>melancholic: a temperament associated with being somber or analytical, thought to be caused by an excess of "black bile"</term>...

They observe their very hidden paths in an orderly fashion, so that those exiting do not hinder those wishing to re-enter by meeting them head-on. <margin>Response to the first point.</margin>
**THEOLOGIAN.** To the first point I say: he was a martyr, so to speak, in the knowledge of his infused wisdom, but not in the feeling of pain and experience. For from the moment of his conception, he had knowledge of all future things in the higher powers of his blessed soul, where he saw the Word <note>The Logos, or the Second Person of the Trinity</note> most clearly and through infused knowledge; but foreknowing these future things did not move his physical senses to feelings of sadness and pain, except when the time of his passion approached.

<margin>Thomas Aquinas, Commentary on the Sentences, Book 3, Distinction 17, final question, article 5.</margin>
This is what the Holy Doctor <note>Saint Thomas Aquinas</note> means when, in the third book, distinction 17, final question, he says: "Although death was foreseen from the beginning of conception, it was not foreseen as imminent; therefore, it did not cause a disturbance—that is, a dread of the emotions—but only when it was already hanging over him." For this is how we experience fear or pain in ourselves.

<margin>Aristotle, Ethics, Book 3, Chapter 6.</margin>
For a young student of life knows that the end of all terrifying things is death, according to the saying of the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> in the third book of the *Ethics*, and that he himself will die; but because he does not imagine it as near, but as distant, it moves him little or not at all toward sadness. However, it does move a person of feeling if he is old and it is near, if it is forethought in that way.

<margin>To the second point.</margin>
To the second point: I find that Christ was most beautiful in his face and in all the limbs of his body; for the greater part of his life, while living among others, he walked with a cheerful and joyful countenance, and in his words, he perfectly displayed the virtues of affability and <term>pleasantness</term> <note>original: *eutrapelia*; the Aristotelian virtue of social grace, wittiness, or being "well-turned" in conversation</note>. The first is evident from Holy Scripture, from the doctrine of the saints, from approved history, and is proven by the diligence of reason.

<margin>Psalm 44.</margin>

### CHAPTER XI.

<margin>Augustine, *Confessions*, Book 2, Chapter 9.</margin>
Blessed Augustine committed [a sin] through laughter when, as a young man, he stole certain apples from others. Concerning this, he says in his book of *Confessions*: "The laughter was as if from a tickled heart, because we were deceiving those who did not think we were doing it and were vehemently against it." <note>Augustine refers here to his famous youthful theft of pears, which he committed not out of hunger, but for the thrill of doing something forbidden with his companions.</note> No one, however, easily laughs alone, unless something extremely ridiculous occurs to the senses <margin>I added [this] from the original.</margin> or to the mind; at the very least, this laughter was pernicious. Regarding these two types of laughter, Seneca <margin>Seneca</margin> says in his book *On the Four Virtues*: "Laughter is reprehensible if it is immoderate, if it is poured out childishly, or if it is done effeminately." <margin>original: *fractus* ("broken" or "enervated").</margin> Laughter also makes a person hateful if it is proud and loud, or malicious, or stealthy, or evoked by the misfortunes of others.

<margin>Basil, in his *Rules*, discusses this more fully in Question 17, where he seems to look back [at this].</margin>
Regarding the second type of laughter, Blessed Basil says in his *Rule*: "It is a sign of a lack of restraint <term>incontinence</term> <note>In this context, 'incontinence' refers to a general lack of self-control or discipline over one's impulses, rather than specifically physical functions.</note> to behave with laughter through disordered and unsettled manners, whereas joy ought only to be indicated by a slight smile. For it is unbecoming to raise a quivering laugh with sound, which usually happens through a lack of mental restraint even against one's will; such a thing usually softens and dissolves the gravity and constancy of the soul."

<margin>Lives of the Fathers.</margin>
How foreign such laughter should be to those in religious life is shown by an example in the *Lives of the Fathers*, where it is said: While the Fathers were eating together in charity, one of them laughed at the table. Seeing him, Abbot John wept bitterly, saying: "What do you think this brother has in his heart, who laughed when he should rather weep, because he is eating charity?" <note>In monastic tradition, the communal meal was seen as a sacred act of "charity" or brotherly love; laughing was seen as a distraction from the solemnity of that grace.</note>

Virtuous laughter, however, is that which Seneca (cited above) describes as something to be practiced. He says: "Let your laughter not be scurrilous, but a pleasing urbanity. Let your wit be without a 'bite' <note>original: *sine dente*, literally 'without teeth,' meaning wit that does not wound others.</note>, your jokes without vulgarity, your laughter without a loud guffaw <note>original: *cachinno*, a loud, mocking laugh.</note>, and your voice without shouting."

<margin>Thomas [Aquinas] on Job, chapter 29.</margin>

And likewise, he was not weighed down by sadness, which is why he adds: *And the light of my countenance did not fall.* For men weighed down by sorrow are accustomed to have their eyes cast down toward the earth.

<margin>Albert [the Great] on the same.</margin>
And Lord Albert says regarding the same passage: *If I ever laughed,* he says, because he was showing cheerfulness to them, which must be done sometimes; hence Ecclesiasticus 4 says: "Be not as a lion in your house, terrifying your domestics." <note>original: *Ecclesiastici 4*. The warning is against being a domestic tyrant who makes those at home tremble.</note> *They did not believe it,* namely, that it was laughter for the sake of laughter, but rather that it was the cheerfulness of kindness, moderated by great maturity and containing nothing foolish. This follows what is said in Ecclesiastes 2: "I counted laughter as error, and to joy I said: why are you vainly deceived?" And he explains this further, adding: "The light of my countenance," signified by my cheerfulness, "did not fall to the earth," that is, into contempt <note>original: *conculcationem*, literally a "trampling underfoot."</note>, as does the light of those who possess foolish and unrestrained joys, of whom it is said in Wisdom 14: "While they rejoice, they are mad." Abraham possessed this virtuous laughter, of which it is said in Genesis 17: "Abraham fell upon his face and laughed, saying in his heart: Shall a son be born to a man a hundred years old? **FORMICARIUS BOOK 1.**

*Ants do not make food for themselves in the manner of bees, but they store up the food given to them by God and by nature.* In the first group, the refreshment and labor of the "contemplatives" is understood, while in the second, that of the "actives" <note>The "active life" refers to external works of charity and duty, while the "contemplative life" refers to internal prayer and meditation.</note>. For that bread of which it is said in Luke 14, "Blessed is he who eats bread in the kingdom of heaven," is acquired by some through a kind of personal worry and labor, such as by holy teachers and prudent prelates. These individuals, through an effort granted to them by nature—though not without the prompting grace of God—insist upon good works. Of such food, it is said in Ecclesiasticus 14: "Before your death, practice justice, for there is no food to be found in the underworld." <note>original: "Ante tuum obitum operare iustitiam, quoniam non est apud inferos reperire cibum."</note> By others, however—specifically those who are beginners or still imperfect—a recreation of the mind is found with only modest labor, rather than being prepared through exhaustion. Regarding both this and the former, it is said in Proverbs 13: "There is much food in the fallow lands of the fathers, and others are gathered without judgment." <note>original: "Multi cibi in noualibus patrum, & alij congregantur absque iudicio."</note> For there is (as was touched upon above near the end of the first chapter) a grace of God bestowed upon his servants on their journey which consoles the mind. One is <term>sanctifying grace<explanation>original: "gratia gratum faciens"; grace that makes the soul pleasing to God, often working quietly and invisibly.</explanation></term>, which by some is perceived sensibly <note>Felt through the senses or emotions.</note> only slightly, or not at all. The other is <term>freely given grace<explanation>original: "gratia gratis data"; a gift of spiritual "sweetness" or emotional consolation granted by God regardless of a person's current merits.</explanation></term>, in which divine sweetness is sensibly acquired by the gift of God alone, without prior merit. Those possessing the first without the second often labor heavily under the state of virtues and temptations, yet most meritoriously; just as the Apostles of Christ are found to have mourned once the bridegroom was taken away. The second group, however, are not shaken by heavy attacks for the time being, but with the joy of divine consolation, they merit less than others (all things being equal), just like the disciples of the Savior who were unable to mourn in the presence of the bridegroom.

For he had previously asked many wise men in secret what he should think about the aforementioned feeling, but as mentioned, the man only received a full answer during a public sermon.

### CHAPTER XII.

While she was tending her parents' cattle, she was sometimes provoked by her peers—suitors who, as is common at that age, would gesture to her from a distance with insolent intent. But as soon as she sensed the approaching deception, she fled to the safety of prayer, bending her knees and raising her hands to her spouse <note>original: "sponsum." Referring to Christ, to whom she had spiritually pledged her virginity.</note> whom she had chosen. In this way, the plotting of the tempters toward evil was entirely thwarted. 

Consequently, upon reaching marriageable age, she felt a great sweetness in divine service, in prayers, and in private meditations. These devoted exercises of the body toward God made the labor in the house and in the fields so light for her that she completed works that were disproportionate to a woman’s strength. For during the entire period of Lent <term>Lent: The forty-day period of fasting and penitence before Easter.</term>, she fasted strictly, never tasting fish or oil, and very little butter. Meanwhile, in the fields, she would follow the plow and use an iron instrument to break apart the furrows left by the plowshare. This was a task of the greatest labor, especially as the earth there was so unsuitable for cultivation that the plow did not sufficiently prepare the ground for seeds unless the soil was turned multiple times by the plowshare, and unless the clods—which stuck together like glue—were finally broken apart. 

During the winter time, when everything is most strictly frozen, the virgin would often pray before her little bed for an hour or more after her most grueling daily labors. She stayed there so long that the soles of her feet—which had previously become wet in the stable or among the cattle—froze so firmly inside her shoes that when they were pulled off, the skin of the virgin was often peeled away <note>The text highlights this extreme physical suffering as a sign of her "asceticism," the practice of self-denial for spiritual growth.</note>. Divine consolation, which she then felt in her meditations, made all these things easy for her. 

Finally, around her twenty-fourth year, she entered the city of Isny <note>Isny im Allgäu, a town in south-western Germany.</note> together with three sisters, whom she kept as virgins in a state of chastity. There, she gathered such a great multitude of other virgins that in that relatively small town, there were fifty virgins...

**PIGER:** Why is it that throughout this book you seem to have already recounted so many miracles of God's servants? Do not naturalists and philosophers, and those experimenters similar to them, know how to perform certain wonders that bear the appearance of miracles?

**THEOLOGIAN:** Indeed they do, and many abuse such things, either for the vice of curiosity or greed, even though they are purely natural. For instance, consider the white stone called *Aimast* <note>original: "Aimast." This likely refers to asbestos or a similar fibrous mineral described in medieval lapidaries.</note>, about which Lord Albert <note>Referring to Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a Dominican friar and polymath who wrote extensively on the natural sciences.</note> speaks in his book *On the Causes of the Properties of the Elements*, Book 1, Tractate 1, Chapter 10. 
<margin>Albertus Magnus reports wonders concerning the Aimast stone and certain others.</margin>
He says, "What is wonderful is a certain white stone, whose name is Aimast, which attracts fire from a great distance; the fire follows it and is ignited within it. Deceptive priests use it to make lamps on altars, which they claim are lit by themselves, and thus they delude the simple people." Furthermore, fire follows the white *Aimast* wherever it is placed opposite it, whether above, below, to the right, or to the left. This is certain because that stone breathes out something like a spirit of sulfur; by this spirit, fire is attracted to that place. Not only is it attracted, but the fire even moves toward the stone itself, or toward the thing in which its natural place is located in some respect, just as a magnet <term>Magnes: A lodestone or natural magnet, often used in medieval science to explain "occult" or hidden natural forces.</term> is the place of origin for iron. These are his words. 

In the same way, some people carry around a type of wool that "burns" in fire <note>This refers to incombustible material, again likely asbestos, which survives fire while appearing to burn.</note>, which some claim comes from the Salamander serpent <note>In medieval bestiaries, the salamander was a legendary creature that could live in or extinguish fire; "salamander's wool" was a common name for asbestos.</note>, while others assert it is the downy fiber of a certain plant. "I have found," he says, "that it is the 'down of iron.' For where great masses of iron are forged together, sometimes the iron is split, and a vapor of fire flies out, and with [it]..."

FORMICARIUS, BOOK II.

<meta>catchword: ...dicting,</meta>

One of these sisters still lives today, nearly ninety years old—a model of all virtues and an inspiring sight for all virgins. As for the brother, who I believe has happily entered his grave with his virginity intact and in a state equivalent to martyrdom, he became a shoemaker <term>calceator</term> <note>Latin: *calceator*. A maker of shoes or boots; a common trade in medieval Basel.</note>. In this craft, for which his father (surnamed Mulber) was also known, he earned enough to support the aforementioned family until about his twentieth year. At that time, a certain holy man—perhaps foreseeing what was to come—called him to the schools. There, despite the mockery of many, he made such progress in the liberal arts within two years—both at Basel and at the University of Prague—that he scarcely had an equal of his own age in those studies. 

He later returned from his general studies and, after entering our Order <note>The Dominican Order, or Order of Preachers.</note>, came to the convent at Colmar <note>Latin: *conuentum Columbariensem*. Colmar, in Alsace, was a significant center for Dominican reform in the 15th century.</note>. He saw to the reform of the Order in many places and eventually became such a devoted preacher that Germany had no equal to him at that time. For he corrected vices without fear and with great courage; because of this, he was troubled for a long time by various people. At last, he departed from this light happily (as I hope) through a long illness that he had preferred, possessing a certain merit of martyrdom. I write about this history quite freely because I often had the honor of being a traveling companion to this holy man, and even today I have a great and good acquaintance with his living sister.

**PIG.** <note>Piger, the "Lazy" or "Dull" student, a character used as a foil to ask questions of the Theologian.</note> Since it pleases you to recount certain revelations, it would be helpful if you would explain with what degree of certainty you believe such things to be true.

For there he defines contemplation or meditation as the cause of devotion, and he argues against the opposing view in this way: If contemplation were a cause of this kind, then those more suited for contemplation would have greater devotion; but we see the opposite, because devotion is frequently found more in certain simple men and in the female sex, in whom a lack of contemplation is found. He responds there: Knowledge and whatever else pertains to greatness provides an opportunity for a person to trust in himself and not hand himself over entirely to God; and from this it follows that such things sometimes occasionally hinder devotion. Meanwhile, in simple people and women, devotion abounds by suppressing pride. If, however, reason perfectly subjects knowledge and any other perfection to God, then devotion is increased by that very fact.

### CHAPTER II.

...a significant division arose regarding the choice of a pastor. <margin>
Why bishops today do not shine with miracles as they once did.
</margin>
**THEOLOGIAN.** The reason for this is that now, unlike in the past, their calling to the height of the cathedral summit <note>original: "cathedralis culminis"; referring to the bishop's throne or see.</note> is not from the Holy Spirit, but their promotion frequently comes from vainglorious and greedy clergy and laity. I pass over in silence those raised to the chairs of pontiffs who are bound to know the two testaments <note>The Old and New Testaments.</note>, as signified by the two horns of the mitre <note>The two peaks of a bishop's hat (mitre) were traditionally interpreted as symbols of the Old and New Testaments.</note>, yet none of whom knows how to speak grammar correctly—the first basics for children. For such men afterwards, in the governance of churches, shine with such "miracles" as are usually found in the perverse courts of secular men.

### CHAPTER II.

...you and the princes make them pontiffs <term>Pontiff: Here used as a general term for a high-ranking bishop or prelate.</term>, who shine with your miracles and wonders, not God’s. For when the Holy Spirit promoted bishops in the early church, they gave sight to the blind, the ability to walk to the lame, and returned life to the dead; they brought peace to the lands, and through these acts, they brought in citizens for heaven. Now, however, bishops filled with your diabolical spirit shine with those same "powers," because you are accustomed to rob those who see of their eyes, those who walk of their feet, and the healthy of their lives, while you take peace from the earth through your wars and remove religious devotion from the path to heavenly life. 

*PIG.* <note>Piger: Latin for "The Sluggard," the interlocutor in this dialogue who represents the questioning or skeptical student.</note> These "miracles of evil" of which you speak, and which the common people seem to throw in the clergy's teeth, are more frequent in Germany <note>original: "Alemania"</note> than in any other part of the world; perhaps because many dioceses are now so hedged in with the thorns of temporal affairs that, in their lives, morals, concerns, and even their dress and horses, they are considered princes of worldly warfare rather than pastors of souls or bishops. They are so overwhelmed by these pomps that they cannot attend to or provide for the salvation of souls. 

*THEOL.* <note>Theologus: The Theologian, who provides the moral and doctrinal answers.</note> The common people do not stray far from the truth in this, but I wish <margin>Psalm 138.</margin> our eyes did not see their imperfection <note>A reference to Psalm 139:16 (138 in the Vulgate): "Thine eyes did see my substance, yet being unperfect."</note>, from whose <margin>Psalm 54.</margin> streets usury and deceit have not yet departed, and in whose city we have often—or rather, too often—seen iniquity and deceit. The proof of this is seen in the Blessed Gregory <note>Saint Gregory the Great (c. 540–604), a Pope known for his immense administrative wealth used for charity.</note>, who was once the wealthiest bishop of both the city and the whole world. <margin>Book 1, chapter 6</margin> You have heard, moreover, above and just now of many good prelates in Germany who commendably presided over both their wealth and the souls in their care. Therefore, it is not the use, but the abuse of the clergy’s temporal status that is everywhere to be condemned...

## CHAPTER III.

Ants have two eyes by which their bodies are guided. Because of the smallness of their heads, ants have eyes situated upon certain appendages <note>original: "additamenta"</note> that emerge from the head like two hairs. Through this, we are taught clearly enough that we ought to use two eyes—namely, those of the body and of the soul—for the proper governance of the whole person. It is obvious to everyone what the eyes of the body are.

<margin>Augustine, *On the Trinity*, book 12, chapters 3 & 7.</margin>
But the eyes of the soul are the <term>Practical and Speculative Intellect: In medieval philosophy, the "practical" intellect is the mind's ability to make decisions about actions and morals, while the "speculative" intellect is the ability to contemplate universal truths and God.</term>, according to Augustine in Book 12 of *On the Trinity*, and as stated in the gloss on 1 Corinthians 2.

<margin>The Ordinary Gloss <note>A standard medieval collection of biblical commentaries.</note></margin>
For first, as if with a "left" eye, we ought to look upon lower and earthly things, without which we cannot sustain life in this world. Second, however, one must contemplate higher and eternal things, without which we cannot reach the goal of our eternal happiness. The Prophet <note>The author of the Psalms, traditionally King David.</note> mentions both the eyes of the body and the soul where he says:

<margin>Psalm 123.</margin>
"Behold, as the eyes of servants look to the hands of their masters, as the eyes of a handmaid to the hands of her mistress, so our eyes look to the Lord our God until he has mercy on us." Although there is a great agreement between the physical and mental eyes, there is no less a difference between them. Both physical and mental eyes are pairs; both necessarily require light; and it is necessary for them to shine with cleanliness and purity. Furthermore, just as nature has protected the first [physical eyes] with many small layers—namely seven—and three fluids <note>In medieval medicine, the eye was thought to be composed of seven "tunics" or membranes and three "humors" or fluids.</note>, as the art which they call <term>Perspectiva: The medieval science of optics, which studied the physics of light and how the eye functions.</term> teaches, so too is it necessary to provide for the second [mental eyes] most cautiously through grace and one's own diligent effort. <margin>Psalm 17</margin>

For the former, physical light is needed; for the latter, a divine ray. The former are stained by material dust, but the latter by phantasms, errors, lack of knowledge, ignorance, and sins. When the former are active and in physical light, they recognize many differences among visible things, but at that moment, the latter—namely the intellects—are hindered more by such things. For this reason, those wishing to imprint the <term>Art of Memory: A collection of mental techniques used to organize and recall large amounts of information, often by visualizing "memory palaces."</term> usually flee from bright places; and God is known to have been seen by Moses in the darkness, according to the testimony of Holy Scripture.

### CHAPTER IV.

Divination <term>Divination: the practice of seeking knowledge of the future or the unknown by supernatural means.</term> which relies on a false opinion is superstitious and illicit, and therefore one must consider what is true regarding the foreknowledge of the future through dreams. Now, dreams are sometimes the cause of future events—for instance, when someone’s mind, made anxious by what they see in their sleep, is led to do or avoid something; and of such things Solomon speaks, saying: *Dreams have caused many cares.* <note>Though credited to Solomon, this is a reference to the Book of Sirach (Ecclesiasticus) 34, often associated with Solomon’s wisdom in the medieval period.</note> Sometimes, however, dreams are the cause of certain events insofar as they are traced back to some common cause for both the dreams and the future events. And according to this, foreknowledge of the future happens most often through dreams. ### CHAPTER IV.

Therefore, the cause of dreams is sometimes indeed internal, and sometimes external. The internal cause of dreams is twofold: one is mental <term>animalis; derived from *anima* (soul/mind), referring to psychological origins</term>, insofar as things occur to a person's <term>phantasia; the faculty of the mind that stores and combines sensory images</term> while sleeping, which the person’s thoughts and affections dwelled upon while awake. And such a cause of dreams is not a cause of future events; therefore, dreams of this kind have only an accidental relationship to future occurrences, and if they sometimes happen to coincide, it is by chance. At other times, however, the internal cause of dreams is physical, for from the internal disposition of the body, a movement is formed in the imagination corresponding to that disposition—just as it occurs in dreams to a person in whom cold <term>humors; the four bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—that medieval medicine believed determined health and temperament</term> abound, that he is in water or snow. Experience also teaches concerning things touching from the outside: if someone surrounds a sleeper's finger or hand with cold water, he will immediately dream that he is lying in water. For this reason, physicians say that dreams should be attended to in order to recognize internal physical dispositions. 

The external cause of dreams is likewise twofold, namely physical and spiritual. The physical cause is insofar as the sleeper's imagination is changed either by the surrounding air—as has already been exemplified by the water—or from the influence of a celestial body <note>Medieval science held that the movements and "impressions" of the stars and planets could physically affect the human body and mind.</note>, so that certain images appear to the sleeper that conform to the celestial arrangement. The spiritual cause is sometimes from God, who reveals certain things in dreams through the ministry of angels, according to that in <term>Numbers 12</term>:
> If there be among you a prophet of the Lord, I will appear to him in a vision, or I will speak to him through a dream. <note>original: "Si quis fuerit inter vos propheta domini, in visione apparebo ei, vel per somniũ loquar ad illũ."</note>
Sometimes, however, through the operation of demons, certain images appear to sleepers, by which they sometimes reveal certain future things to those who have entered into illicit pacts with them. Thus, therefore, the Doctor <note>St. Thomas Aquinas.</note> concludes there in his response: if anyone uses dreams to foreknow the future, according to how dreams proceed from

### CHAPTER V.

An ant that happens upon another while blind will cling to the one with eyes most firmly, and will not let go until it has been led back to the nest. In this, we see how piously divine mercy has provided for such creatures; by its instinct, an ant deprived of sight is saved by the diligence of another that sees. By such diligence, we can understand those simple people who, though they possess divine dreams or revelations by God’s gift, do not see their true meaning. Instead, by the guidance of another, they learn what they could not know by their own effort. This is like the simple Samuel, who was inexperienced in divine visions. <margin>Three teachings regarding dreams</margin>

Third, that the means of acquiring the **discernment of spirits** in this matter is achieved through a savor that is not only internal, but intimate, bestowed by him—namely, the Holy Spirit—who alone is more interior to every thing than that thing is to itself.
