<margin>
Six rules to be observed regarding dreams in which evils are thought to be signified beforehand.
</margin>
<margin>1.</margin>
First, do not believe in such dreams definitively or assertively unless you have received the indubitable gift of interpretation, such as Jeremiah obtained, who says in Jeremiah 26:
> "In truth the Lord sent me to you, to speak all these words in your ears." <note>original: "In veritate misit me dominus ad vos, vt loquerer in auribus vestris omnia verba hæc."</note>

The reason for this rule is that the causes of dreams are sometimes things that are signs of no future event, but only of past images, or other natural factors that do not actually designate the things dreamed. Or they may come from demons, who long to make those who believe in dreams become so accustomed to their influence.

<margin>2.</margin>
The second rule is that you should not always drive away all dreams whatsoever, especially those which might be signs of future tribulation, if you perceive them frequently proving true for you in ways that are good and useful for the soul. This is because sometimes they are gifts of God preserving us from evils, lest we be led into temptation. For "foreseen arrows strike with less force," as Blessed Gregory says.

<margin>
Gregory, Homily 35 on the Gospels, part 3.
</margin>
The third rule: 
When a dream of something ill-fated occurs to you, then with a brave heart and God's help—without confidence in your own strength—resolve to keep yourself composed. For the strengthening of the mind through those natural faculties which God has bestowed in the freedom of the will must be put into action and used. It is through these means that the philosophers (as Seneca teaches in *On the Remedies of Fortuitous Events*) <note>Seneca the Younger was a Roman Stoic philosopher whose writings on endurance and fate were highly respected by medieval Christians.</note> patiently endured terrible things.

<margin>4.</margin>
The fourth rule: 
Flee from the occasion of an evil that likely looms ahead to the best of your ability, so that you do not, for example, provide the cause of guilt... <note>The text cuts off here at "cul-", likely leading to "culpæ" (guilt/fault) on the next page.</note>

### CHAPTER VII.

Let us move to another characteristic [of the ant], which is that ants return to their nest along a single, quite "royal" line; one does not block another on the path, but sometimes they seem to offer each other a covenant of peace with a kiss of the mouth, as it were. In these creatures, a certain unbroken friendship is demonstrated to us—peace and tranquility—which are the effects and fruits of divine love <note>original: "charitatis." In this context, charity refers to "Caritas," the highest form of Christian love for God and neighbor.</note>, and are truly the gift of those inspired by the Holy Spirit. Regarding these, the Apostle says in Galatians 5: "The fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, long-suffering, goodness, kindness, gentleness, faith, modesty, self-control, and chastity." Therefore, those men in whom such signs are found show a high probability of divine inspiration. Because of this, the Apostle adds: "If we live by the Spirit, let us also walk by the Spirit; let us not become desirous of vain glory, provoking one another or envying one another."

**THE STUDENT:** Few "moral ants" <note>The student uses the allegory of the ant to refer to virtuous Christians.</note> are found in our time, I suspect, who maintain such signs of unity and peace toward themselves and their neighbors, and who are led within by a divinely inspired spirit, according to the mandate of the Apostle which he sets forth in that same passage:

> But I say, walk in the spirit, and you will not fulfill the desires of the flesh. <note>original: "Dico autem spiritu ambulate, & desideria carnis non perficietis." — Galatians 5:16.</note>

**THE THEOLOGIAN:** I refuted a similar question and such a suspicion earlier in Book 1, Chapter 6. However, so that you may recognize that in our own time there have been sons and daughters of peace and pupils of the Holy Spirit of both sexes, I will provide you with two examples out of many.

<margin>A man deaf and mute from birth predicts through nods and signs the return of a priest from the city of Rome, and the downfall of his guardian.</margin>
There was in the city of Constance <note>Constance (Konstanz) was a major ecclesiastical city in Germany, famous for the Council of Constance (1414–1418).</note> a certain man, poor in possessions and, as it seems, deaf and mute from birth. Yet he was not inexperienced in the prophetic spirit; he was humble in his life and dress, and he strove to maintain peace with men and, even more so, with God, in purity of soul and chastity of body. His name was... <note>The name is left blank in the original manuscript.</note>. This man, as I have learned from many trustworthy people, used to point out sometimes future things and sometimes even hidden matters that lay beyond human diligence—I do not say "predict" them, because he lacked the use of a tongue, but foreshadow them through clear signs. Indeed, in our brothers' friary at Constance, many admit to having experienced such things themselves.

I once had a relative of this sort in the college of the said city, which is called St. Stephen's. He was a canon priest, very devoted to God and the "Princes of the Apostles" <note>A traditional title for St. Peter and St. Paul.</note>. On the journey, however, while at an inn one night, he accidentally fell from a height. ...signs, I say, which lasted so long that the aforementioned virgin, the manager of his house, and no one else in the city of Constance knew anything of the priest’s arrival by human <margin>perhaps: by sign <note>The marginal note "f. indicio" suggests a variant reading or clarification that the knowledge came via a sign rather than typical human reasoning.</note></margin> judgment. This mute man, though poor in possessions, was supported by a certain rather wealthy citizen of Constance, who loved the mute man little less than if he were his own natural son. Meanwhile, a day came in which the citizen arranged to travel by boat across the adjacent lake to another city near the water. While the citizen was still in his own house about to set out on his journey, the mute man saw and considered this; wherefore, by such nods as he was able, he urged his master not to entrust himself to the boat. But the citizen refused. 

After he left the house, the mute man followed him, dissuading him from the journey he had begun in whatever ways he could. Finally, near the ship, with wretched groans—as he had done before—he tried to stop his master; for he foreknew that if he sailed, he would immediately die in the waters. But his efforts achieved little. And when the ship departed from the shore with his master, the mute man remained on that same shore (as it is said) and, with many tears shed and a mournful appearance, lamented his master’s sorrowful departure. Consequently, as adverse fortune moved the ship across the waters, the citizen was drowned that same day. Thus, it was made clear not only to the city but to all the surrounding country that the mute man was illuminated by the Spirit of God.

For the mind of a prophet, as Saint Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the influential Dominican friar and philosopher.</note> teaches in his *Summa*, is instructed by God in two ways. One way is through **express revelation**. The other way is through a certain **instinct** <note>original: "instinctum" — an internal divine impulse or "nudge" rather than a clear vision or voice.</note>, which human minds sometimes experience even without knowing it, as Blessed Augustine says in the second book of *The Literal Meaning of Genesis*. 
<margin>Chapter 17.</margin> 
Therefore, regarding those things which the prophet knows expressly through the spirit of prophecy, he has the greatest certainty and holds it as a fact that these things have been divinely revealed to him. Hence it is said in Jeremiah 26: *In truth the Lord sent me to you, to speak all these words in your ears.*

<margin>Some editions read: "known."</margin> 
But regarding those things which he knows by instinct, he is sometimes in such a state that he cannot fully discern whether he has *thought this by some divine instinct or by his own spirit. Not everything we know by divine instinct is manifested to us with prophetic certainty. For such an instinct is something imperfect within the category of prophecy.

<margin>Homily 1.</margin> 
Hence, Blessed Gregory <note>Gregory the Great (c. 540–604), Pope and Church Father.</note>, writing on Ezekiel regarding the previously mentioned prophet Nathan, says: "It should be known that sometimes the holy prophets, when they are consulted, bring forth certain things from their own spirit out of a great habit of prophesying, and they suspect that they are saying this from the spirit of prophecy." Therefore, do not wonder if sometimes those things which were 
->predicted<-
by that mute man did not come to pass.

Regarding the second doubt, you cannot be resolved unless you understand certain grades of prophecy, which the Holy Doctor <note>Referring to Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the Dominican philosopher whose work Nider is paraphrasing here.</note>, in the place cited before, establishes. For there are five. 

The first—ascending from the lowest—is when someone is moved by an **internal instinct** <note>original: "interior instinctu" — a divine nudge or impulse to act without necessarily receiving a verbal message or vision.</note> to perform certain outward actions, as is said of Samson in Judges 
<margin>1.</margin>
the fifteenth chapter: that the spirit of the Lord rushed upon him, and just as wood is consumed by the heat of a fire, so too the bonds with which he was tied were broken and loosened. And because of this mode of prophecy, I shared the second example with you, because this grade seemed to apply in the opening of the mouth of that holy woman <note>Referring to the woman from the previous page whose lockjaw was cured so she could receive the Eucharist.</note>. 

The second grade of prophecy is when someone is illuminated by an **internal light** to recognize things to be known, or things to be 
<margin>2.</margin>
done, pertaining to human preservation or social life—things which, however, 
<margin>I have added a negation from the original source.</margin>
*do not* exceed the limits of natural knowledge, as is spoken of regarding Solomon in <note>original: "3. Reg. 4." — 1 Kings 4</note>, who spoke parables and discussed trees, from the cedar that is in Lebanon even to the hyssop that grows out of the wall, and treated of beasts, birds, reptiles, and fish. And all this was from divine inspiration, for it is stated beforehand: *God gave Solomon wisdom and very great prudence.* These two grades, however, are below prophecy properly so-called, because they do not reach supernatural truth. Remember, however, that I do not wish to speak of prophets "properly so-called" in every instance. 

The 
<margin>3.</margin>
third grade is when some supernatural truth is manifested to someone through an **intelligible light** by an **imaginary vision** <note>In medieval theology, an "imaginary vision" (visio imaginaria) is not "fake," but rather a vision perceived by the internal faculty of the imagination rather than the physical eyes.</note> through the likeness of physical things leading toward a supernatural truth; and such was the prophecy held by all those who are numbered in the order of the prophets in the text of the Bible.

### CHAPTER VII. ###

<meta>catchword: instinct—</meta>

These are also specifically called prophets for this reason: because they performed a **prophetic office**. Hence, they spoke in the person of the Lord, saying to the people, "Thus says the Lord." This was not done by those who wrote the **sacred writings** <note>original: "hagiographa" — referring to the third division of the Hebrew Bible, including books like Psalms, Proverbs, and Job, which were considered divinely inspired but distinct from the "Prophets."</note>, many of whom spoke more frequently of those things which can be known by human reason. They spoke not as if in the person of God, but in their own person, though still with the assistance of **divine light**. 

The fourth grade is when some supernatural truth is revealed through **intelligible light** <term>intelligible light: a direct divine sharpening of the intellect that allows a person to understand truths without needing a visual or sensory "picture."</term> without an imaginary vision. In this way, David is called a prophet par excellence, because he received the revelation of intelligible and supernatural truth without a vision of the imagination, and because he understood and expressed the mysteries of the **incarnation of Christ** more fully than even Moses. 

However, you should not understand this to mean that anyone in this life understands things, even supernaturally, without **mental images** <note>original: "phantasmatibus" — in the philosophy of Aristotle and Aquinas, these are "phantasms" or sensory impressions stored in the mind, which the intellect uses to think.</note>, because this is contrary to the **Philosopher** <note>A standard medieval reference to Aristotle.</note> and to **Dionysius** in the first chapter of *The Celestial Hierarchy*. For the illustration of the divine ray in this present life does not occur without the veils of mental images of some kind, because it is natural to man, according to the state of this present life, that he does not understand without a mental image. Sometimes, however, the mental images that are drawn from the senses in the common way are sufficient, and a divinely produced imaginary vision is not required; in such cases, prophetic revelation is said to occur without an imaginary vision. 

The fifth and highest grade is when supernatural truth is shown nakedly to the intellect through supernatural light without an imaginary vision— 
<margin>
Augustine, Book 12 of *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, chapters 26, 27, and 28.
</margin>
as was communicated to Moses and Paul: namely, to see the **divine essence**, according to Augustine in his book *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*. All these points are taken from the **Holy Doctor** <note>Thomas Aquinas.</note>, through which it is now clear enough which paths are the right ones through which, by divine influence, knowledge is gained.

### *Concerning the care to be taken for possessing a treasury of virtues. And concerning soldiers working virtuously for the state, or for the faith.*

## CHAPTER VIII.

All [ants] observe one single place in which they place and hide away their treasures, so that, evidently, they might gather during the harvest what they will eat. And this condition of our little beasts <note>original: "beštiolarum" — a diminutive term for the ants, used throughout this work to show how much humans can learn from "lesser" creatures.</note> teaches everyone in this present life that the fruits of the virtues they are able to acquire should be hidden away in a safe place, like treasures of the soul, in heaven and not on earth. Hence the Ordinary Gloss <margin>Ordinary Gloss <note>The *Glossa Ordinaria* was the standard medieval collection of biblical commentaries used by scholars.</note></margin> upon the words from Proverbs 6: "The ant prepares her food in the summer and gathers in the harvest what she may eat," says this: "If an animal lacking a ruler, devoid of reason, and with nature as its guide provides for its future, how much more should you—created in the image of God, called to behold His glory, and aided by such great teaching—gather the fruits of good works in the present for the Creator himself <margin>restored from the original in place of "all"</margin>, by which you may live eternally in the future." For this life is compared to the harvest and to summer, because now, amidst the heat of temptations, is the time for gathering the merits of future rewards. The Day of Judgment is compared to winter, because no opportunity remains for working for one's life; instead, each person will then be compelled to bring forth from the granary of their former affection <margin>original: "actionis" — of action</margin> what they have stored up. Hence, in the final chapter of 1 Timothy, the Apostle [Paul] says to his disciple: "Command the rich of this world not to be high-minded, nor to hope in the uncertainty of riches, but in the living God, who provides us all things abundantly for our enjoyment; to do good, to become rich in good works, to [give] easily..."

At that same time, the sect of the heretics had a captain distinguished by his bold malice, named Zischa <note>Jan Žižka (c. 1360–1424), the famed Hussite general known for his innovative wagon-fort tactics and for never losing a battle.</note>, who disposed himself to avenge all the things previously mentioned. For one day he arranged two battle lines of armed men: the first, a strong force of four hundred men, to whom he entrusted the task of burning the villages of the faithful around Iglavia on the morning of the following day, and thus provoke the soldier of Christ to leave his city. But he gathered a second, much larger expedition, in which he himself, following the first, planned to bring aid to it if it were attacked. 

Therefore, the first battle line of the infidels appeared in the fields outside Iglavia in the morning, as had been ordered, and provoked the soldier of Christ to come out. He immediately sent a messenger to a certain nearby place to call for some armed men, and invited the city's mercenaries to go out with him to scout the enemy's army and to attack it if the opportunity presented itself. Seeing this, the city's mercenaries said to the soldier: "The defense of the city has been primarily entrusted to us, and it is not expedient that so few of us should attack a force so disproportionate to our arms." Then, having called his own men together, the soldier, in the manner of a Maccabee <note>Refers to the leaders of the Jewish rebellion in the 2nd century BCE, who were seen by medieval writers as the ideal models for Christian knights defending the faith against superior numbers.</note>, said:

> "Behold, you have heard: these men will not attack the treacherous. I ask you, therefore, let us attack the enemies of Christ; for I hope..."

When he was carried into the city, all the common people lamented; but, by the grace of Christ, on the following day he began to possess perfect reason. And as the soldier himself told me, he was fully healed of all his wounds in a short space of days, not so much by human medicine as by divine gift. Another condition presents itself, namely, that the nest of the ant-colony emits a certain sharp, pungent, and yet delightful odor. A nest, as we know, *is properly the habitual dwelling and home of all fertile and prolific birds.* For the birds of the air, says the Savior, have their nests (Luke 9). This delightful odor, in truth, signifies the fragrance of virtues, one's reputation and example, and the sound doctrine of Christ. Hence the Apostle says in 2 Corinthians 2: "Thanks be to God, who always leads us in triumph in Christ Jesus, and through us spreads the fragrance of the knowledge of Him in every place. For we are the good odor of Christ to God, among those who are being saved and among those who are perishing: to the one an odor of death leading to death, but to the other an odor of life leading to life." <note>original: "Christi bonus odor sumus Deo" — Paul's metaphor suggests that the lives of believers should spread the "scent" of the Gospel to those around them.</note>

Among these visions, as I often learned from her, she foresaw through the divine spirit things which she could not have known by human means. Having finally been deprived of her husband, although she was still of marriageable age, she did not wish to prefer any other man to Christ, whom she had chosen. *PIG.* A doubt has often crept into my mind: whether good angels and spirits "possess" certain servants of God, both men and women, for good by entering into them, just as there is no doubt that evil spirits besiege those handed over to them for evil?

...according to Dionysius, they <note>Referring to angels.</note> are the purest and most radiant mirrors; they do not harm, but rather perfect, illuminate, and advance the human mind toward divine service. The opposites of these qualities are what the demon inflicts upon the bodies he possesses.

<margin>
He proves in various ways that good angels possess some people for their own good.
</margin>
That good angels do, in a certain way, "possess" or occupy certain servants of God is evident from experience, from the examples of the Church Fathers, from reason, and from Holy Scripture. Regarding experience: just as we see those possessed by a demon, or those familiar with them—such as **sorcerers** <note>original: "maleficos" — a term often used for those practicing harmful magic or witchcraft.</note> and their disciples—take on deformities of the eyes, the face, or gestures that are horrible for other people to look upon (which are undoubtedly the effects of the demon’s most malicious presence), so too do we find the opposite. We see that those who serve God and the virtues with all their might—especially those who are chaste in body—possess a pleasing face, kind gestures, and a most humane gaze, even when seen by sinners. For charity, joy, patience, kindness, and similar virtues are (as the Apostle says in the fifth chapter of Galatians) the effects and **fruits of the Spirit**.

<margin>
A wife's graceful appearance vanished and was replaced by a horrid one due to the commission of adultery; however, through the sacrament of penance, her face recovered its original beauty.
</margin>
I once knew a noble and devout **knight** <note>original: "militem" — a soldier or member of the knightly class.</note>, of whom I shall speak later in the tenth chapter of the fourth book. He had a beautiful wife who had been secretly deceived for a short time by a certain adulterer, to whom she had become attached and "infected" by a clinging, stuck-together love <note>original: "conglutinato amore" — a vivid metaphor suggesting an illicit, messy emotional bond.</note>. When the husband, a prudent man who wished to heal the soul of his lost wife, discovered this, he summoned her in secret. He saw that her face (as the knight later reported to me) had become exceedingly horrid to look at. Through holy and pious warnings, he persuaded her to feel **contrition** <note>Sincere sorrow for one's sins arising from a love of God.</note> for her crime and to seek the **sacrament of penance**. He eventually led her to fulfill this through the grace of God. Once this was done, as she was leaving the priest after receiving her sacramental penance, it seemed to her chaste husband that she had totally recovered that original beauty of her face, which she had previously and visibly seemed to have lost.

This point is also clear from the examples of the Fathers. For the holy father Equitius, of whom the blessed...

### CHAPTER X.

<margin>
Gregory, *Dialogues*, Book 1, chapter 4. The example of a good angel possessing Blessed Equitius and constantly urging him to preach.
</margin>
Blessed Gregory relates in the first book of his *Dialogues* that Equitius appears to have been possessed by a Seraphic angel. Although Equitius held no sacred order <note>meaning he was not an ordained priest</note> and had not been officially sent to preach by the Supreme Pontiff, he was nonetheless set on fire with such fervor to convert the souls of the faithful from the love of the world to divine service that he ran about everywhere—through churches, fortresses, villages, and the individual homes of the faithful—to stir the hearts of his listeners toward love for the heavenly fatherland. When his friend Felix—who was "happy" by both name and nature <note>original: "Felix re, & nomine"</note>—asked him about the cause of this behavior with great wonder, Equitius replied: "I also ponder those things you say to me, but one night a beautiful young man stood by me in a vision and placed a medicinal iron tool—that is, a lancet <term>fleubotomum: a surgical tool used for bloodletting; here used metaphorically as a spiritual instrument to 'cut' the tongue loose for speech</term>—upon my tongue, saying:

> 'Behold, I have put my words in your mouth; go forth to preach.'

And from that day on, even if I wished it, I cannot remain silent about God."

<margin>
Vincent of Beauvais, *Historical Mirror*, Book 30, chapter 28. Another example regarding Saint Peter the One-Eyed.
</margin>
We read, moreover, in Vincent’s *Historical Mirror*, that a certain Abbot of the Cistercian order asked Saint Peter—of the same order and surnamed "the One-Eyed" <note>original: "monoculo"</note>—how he was able to persevere always in the same state of equanimity. Peter replied: "When I was a novice, a certain spirit seemed to visibly enter into me; from then until now, that power and that profound affection have always dominated me in a certain way.

<margin>
Psalm 79.
</margin>
It rules me and leads me like the sheep of Joseph <note>This refers to Psalm 80 in modern numbering: "Give ear, O Shepherd of Israel, you who lead Joseph like a flock."</note>; when I am scattered among outward things, it frequently gathers me back inward; it compels me to focus when I am unwilling to pray; and it sometimes makes me unaware of the things that strike my eyes or ears."

Furthermore, this opinion is not at odds with the Holy Scriptures, but is rather in harmony with them. ### CHAPTER X.

Ants greatly hate foul-smelling things, such as sulfur, burnt stag's horn, and oregano; if these are poured over the ants' nests, they migrate from them to another place. Therefore, those who wish to drive them away from their dwelling-place put the powder of burnt stag’s horn in it, or smoke them out with sulfur or oregano. By foul and sulfurous things, Holy Scripture gives us to understand the sins of Venus <note>original: "Venerea," referring to sexual lust or carnal acts</note>. Hence, in Genesis 19: "The Lord rained sulfur and fire upon Sodom and Gomorrah," so that foul and abominable things might punish those men whom lust had defiled. And in Ecclesiasticus 9, it is said of incontinent <note>lacking self-restraint</note> women: "Every woman who is a harlot..."

Of the first book, chapters 18 & 28. <note>Refers to previous sections in Nider’s *Formicarium* (The Ant-Hill) where related themes of spiritual struggle and virtue were discussed.</note>

*SLOTH:* What, I ask you, according to God, could those women have done if they had been slaves, rather than manumitted <term>manumissæ</term> <note>original: "manumissæ." A Roman law term for slaves who have been formally granted their freedom.</note> freedwomen, or free-born?

*THEOLOGIAN:* Even then, against their will, no one would have had a just dominion over them to command them to enter into a marriage contract in which there was a danger to their proposed chastity. For in the New Testament, only God is excepted in such a case, as He alone has full dominion over the body and soul, over property and reputation. Hence, just as in the Old Testament (according to the Holy Doctor <note>A standard title for St. Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the most influential philosopher-theologian of the Middle Ages.</note>) no one dared to abstain from marriage without a special command from God, so in the New Testament no one, except God, can justly put marriage before the choice of anyone who is unwilling, if it would mean the loss of their chastity.

*SLOTH:* Why then does the Apostle say in the third chapter of Colossians: "Children, obey your parents in all things"? And why does he later add: "Obey your fleshly masters in all things"? <note>The "Sloth" is quoting the New Testament (Colossians 3:20 and 3:22) to challenge the idea that a woman or slave can ever disobey their superiors.</note>

*THEOLOGIAN:* A distinction must be made here, as Saint Thomas says in the *Summa* (2.2, Question 104). There are two ways in which it may happen that a subordinate is not bound to obey his superior in all things. First, because of the command of a greater power. * For as the Gloss says regarding the thirteenth chapter of Romans concerning those who "resist the power of God and acquire damnation for themselves": "If a local official <term>curator</term> <note>original: "curator." A minor administrative official in the Roman system.</note> orders something, * must you do it if it is ordered against the command of a proconsul? Again, if the proconsul himself orders one thing and the emperor another, is there any doubt that the former should be disregarded and the latter served? Therefore, if the emperor orders one thing and God another, the emperor must be disregarded and God must be obeyed." Secondly, an inferior is not bound to obey a superior if the superior commands something in which the subordinate is not subject to him. For Seneca says in the third book of *On Benefits*: "He errs who thinks that slavery descends into the whole man; for the [better] part of him... <note>The author is quoting the Stoic philosopher Seneca to argue that while a body may be enslaved, the mind and spirit remain free.</note>

the better part is excepted; though bodies are subject and bound to masters, the mind is indeed its own master <term>sui iuris</term> <note>original: "sui iuris." A legal term meaning "of one's own right," referring to a person who is not under the legal control of another.</note>. And therefore, in those matters that pertain to the inner movement of the will, a person is not bound to obey another human, but only God. However, a person is bound to obey another human in those things which are to be performed externally through the body. Yet even in those matters which pertain to the nature of the body, a person is not bound to obey another human, but only God, because all people are by nature equal—for instance, in those things pertaining to the physical maintenance of the body and the generation of offspring. Whence, neither are slaves bound to obey their masters, nor children their parents, regarding the contracting of marriage, or the preservation of virginity, or anything of this kind. But in those things that pertain to the arrangement of human acts and affairs, a subordinate is bound to obey his superior according to the nature of that superiority; just as a soldier obeys the leader of an army in matters pertaining to war, a slave obeys a master in matters pertaining to the performance of servile works, a son obeys his father in matters pertaining to the discipline of life and domestic care, and so on for others.

### CHAPTER XII.

<margin>On the life of virtuous old age.</margin>

Only in old age do they take up wings and fly in the manner of birds. Indeed, I have seen this with my own eyes, that in the same ant-hill wings first seemed to grow on some, on others the wings matured, and those who had already attained higher wings were stretching themselves out by flying into the heights. In these ants, it is appropriately suggested to us that once the vices of gluttony and lust have been put to death—and not before, but in the "old age" of a virtuous life—we can indeed be enriched with the gifts of the peace and tranquility of contemplation. For by "old age," a long life of merit can be appropriately understood, and by "wings," the instruments of contemplation. 

We are not speaking of just any old age, for we know it is written: *The child shall die a hundred years old, and the sinner being a hundred years old shall be accursed* <note>Isaiah 65:20</note>. ->### BOOK II OF THE ANT-COLONY (FORMICARIUS)<-

in her dress, in her withdrawal from the world, and in those things which pertained to the worship of God, she was blameless before all men. However, she lived with a conscience so timid and **scrupulous** that I hardly remember having found her equal in this regard. For even after making a pure and complete **sacramental confession** <note>original: "confessionem sacramentalem"; the formal act of confessing sins to a priest for absolution</note> of her life, she was frequently tormented by heavy **scruples** <note>original: "scrupulis"; in a religious context, this refers to "scrupulosity," a state of obsessive anxiety where a person fears they have sinned when they have not</note> concerning whether her past confessions had been insufficient. Even in the smallest matters, where there was no sin or only a slight one, she feared that the fall of a **mortal crime** <note>original: "mortalis criminis"; a grave or "deadly" sin</note> was present. Thus, she enjoyed no peace in the house of her conscience; for whatever she did, or omitted from the category of good works, she always suspected that a notable sin had been present. 

Therefore, from these excessive fears, her natural constitution—belonging to the **fragile sex** <note>original: "sexu fragili"; a common medieval trope regarding the physical and emotional susceptibility of women</note>—began to decline greatly, and her bodily strength decreased daily. This was because she did not judge definitively, but rather feared, that she was always full of grave sins. She herself was afraid, as were her **confessors** <note>priests who hear confession and provide spiritual guidance</note> and the virgins living with her, that if she were caught near death in such a state of most scrupulous conscience, she might perhaps be caught in the snare of despair by the **malignant enemy** <note>the Devil</note>. 

Therefore, prudent men and doctors of souls, seeing that her bodily failure led to a grave danger for her soul, explained to the virgin—who was in danger of losing her use of reason—that she was by no means bound to certain **fasts of the Church** <note>original: "ieiunia ecclesie"</note> as a healthy person would be. For they knew that the daily labor with which she was burdened, because she was poor in possessions (for she served the other virgins), along with her past fasts and abstinences, would not provide fuel for lust, but were rather sufficient for preserving **chastity** <note>original: "castitati"</note>. But at this, a greater sadness invaded her heart when she saw herself deprived of the **instruments of virtues** <note>spiritual disciplines like fasting</note> which the common people of the faithful use. For one day, quite unexpectedly—though she was barely or not quite fifty years old—she fell ill and began to fail day by day. At that moment, every **scruple** and disordered fear left her completely. She said to Brother **Johannes Wolfhardi**, whom she had chosen as her special confessor because he was a devout man: "Behold, Father, you know how prone to error I was, and how excessively timid in my conscience; but by God's grace, do not fear, for it has all departed. I piously and confidently hope for and believe in the grace of forgiveness for the sins I have committed and confessed." And so, invoking the Blessed Apostle Peter and his disciple **Apollinaris** <note>Saint Apollinaris of Ravenna, traditionally said to be a disciple of St. Peter</note>, whom she had most especially loved in her life, heart, speech, and deeds, she finally passed away devoutly from that same illness, fortified by the **nourishment of the Church** <note>original: "ecclesiæ alimentis"; referring to the final sacraments</note>.

We once had in the reformed convent at **Colmar** <note>original: "Columbariensi"; a city in modern-day France, then part of the Holy Roman Empire</note> a certain brother named Peter. From the time of his early conversion, even before he first entered the convent at **Nuremberg** <note>original: "Nurenbergensi"</note>, he had been an exemplar and mirror of religious life, distinguished by the integrity of all his virtues. For he was always [ready] to collect **alms** <term>charitable donations for the support of the monastery</term> from door to door...

<header>CHAPTER XII.</header>

<sig>M</sig>

He was ready, obedient within the house, diligent day and night in the choir, and friendly to all the brothers. However, he possessed a conscience that was—beyond what can be believed—timid, <term>scrupulous</term> <note>overly concerned with minor details of sin or ritual</note>, and **fainthearted**. He feared even when things were safe, and far too much so, as it seemed. For this reason, the more **discerning** <note>original: "discretiores"; brothers with greater spiritual maturity and judgment</note> brothers often teased him playfully about these things, for they knew he bore with an even mind everything that he did not perceive to be an offense against God. 

And although he had later been ordained as a priest, was physically strong, of a lively complexion, and barely thirty years of age, yet—as we have gathered from many indications—this constant fear damaged his **vital organs** <note>original: "vitalia"; the life-force or internal organs</note> too much. Consequently, one day quite unexpectedly, he fell into some sort of illness, which immediately forced him to take to his bed. 

While he lay in the infirmary in good faith, having the perfect use of his reason, gentle in his patience, and fervent in his solid devotion, though motionless, he suddenly and unexpectedly began his final agony. With religious gestures, he closed his final day. For only shortly before, on the preceding day, he had confessed in the usual manner and had celebrated Mass. He had always led such a life in the Order that, in the judgment of discerning men, there was no sign of danger regarding this unexpected and sudden death—at least not that it was a "bad" or perilous death for his soul. And I trust in the Lord that this unexpected passing could not harm him; but perhaps divine mercy, lest one so **faint of heart** fear death or its circumstances too much, decided to immediately grant an end to living in the body to a soul that was pleasing to Him.

## ON FALSE AND ILLUSORY *visions*.

*How quantity is manifold. How some pretend to be the souls of the deceased and to have revelations. Concerning women crying out in jubilation during a sermon, and what should be thought of such things.*

### CHAPTER I.

"God found wickedness even in His angels, nor are the stars clean in His sight," as noted in the same book, chapter 25 <note>The author refers to the Book of Job 4:18 and 15:15/25:5</note>. It is therefore not surprising if in our little beasts—from whom we are commanded by Solomon to learn our ways <note>A reference to Proverbs 6:6: "Go to the ant, O sluggard; consider her ways and be wise."</note>—some defects of deprivation and harm are found, in which they carry the type and likeness of certain evil or foolish men. In these creatures, we can learn to beware of vices no less than we are able to perceive virtues in their good properties. 

Just as among ants, regarding their material body, a great and manifold difference is found in the size of their mass—namely, that some are very small, others large, and the rest very large, which (as will be said below) cause more harm to humans—so among evil men, a great diversity of error is found. For this reason, the Apostle <note>St. Paul</note> in 1 Corinthians 14, advising his followers against the craftiness of errors, said: "Brothers, do not become children in your thinking, but be infants in malice, and be mature in your thinking" <note>original: "Fratres nolite pueri effici sensibus, sed malitia paruuli estote, sensibus autem perfecti sitis"</note>. And more clearly in Ephesians 4: "Let us no longer be children tossed to and fro, and carried about by every wind of doctrine through the wickedness of men, in craftiness for the schemes of error. But speaking the truth in love, let us grow up in all things into Him who is the head, Christ. From Him the whole body, joined and held together by every supporting ligament, according to the effective working in the measure of every part, makes the body grow for the building up of itself in love" <note>original: "Iam non simus paruuli fluctuantes... in ædificationem sui in charitate"</note>. But alas, today many do not grow this way; instead, they increase in malice.

# THE ANT-HEAP, BOOK III.

<margin>Chapter 5.</margin> Without the discernment of spirits <term>discretionis spirituum: the theological skill of determining if a vision or impulse is from God, the self, or the Devil</term>, this cannot be done sufficiently, as was touched upon in the second book. For there are infinite ways in which the ancient enemy <note>original: "hostis antiquus" — a traditional title for Satan</note> is accustomed to delude the unwary, by which he is found to have sometimes deceived even the greatest men. 

For I learned from the Archdeacon of Barcelona, Lord John—a man highly notable in both divine and human law—that before the time of the Council of Constance <note>A major church council (1414–1418) held to end the Three-Popes Schism</note>, when the schism had already continued for a long time under different supreme pontiffs called in their respective obediences <note>The "Obedience" was the term for the group of countries following a specific claimant to the papacy</note>, some of whom resided in Rome and others of the opposing party in Avignon, Pedro de Luna <note>The birth name of the Avignon Pope Benedict XIII (reigned 1394–1423), eventually declared an antipope</note> was residing there. When he was besieged by enemies, he fled in secret, entering the sea by a galley on the Rhône River. 

<margin>A certain abbot deceives Benedict 11 (otherwise called 13), known before as Pedro de Luna, with a false prophecy.</margin> And when, in a certain town (whose name does not occur to me now) situated above a distant sea port, the townsfolk were warned by a certain abbot on the day preceding the arrival of the said Pope Benedict to prepare themselves to receive the said supreme pontiff, everyone laughed at the said abbot. This was because the Pope had previously departed from Avignon in the greatest secrecy, nor did the Pope intend in any way to enter the said town, nor had he sent anyone ahead there; instead, he had sailed a long distance past the same town, for a stretch of about fifteen miles. 

And behold, a contrary wind forced the galley with the Pope to enter the said town. When he was unexpectedly received there, the Pope learned of the abbot’s oracle <note>A prophetic pronouncement</note> and inquired how he had known of his arrival beforehand. And he received an answer from the abbot that he had read this prophecy long ago in a certain book, which contained that the same Pope was to suffer many things from his adversaries, that he was to be besieged, that he was to come to the aforementioned town, that he was to enter into persecution again, but finally he was to go to Rome, and there, having obtained peaceful possession in the union of the Church and with the schism settled, he was to find rest.

**PIG:** If they were perfect people, men or women, I would probably believe in the signs of such devotions; but when the imperfect do such things, perhaps they should be feared as fictions rather than held as a rule.

**THEOLOGIAN:** Here you could certainly be deceived again and sin gravely in rash judgment. For such things happen not only to the perfect, but also sometimes to those beginning to serve God, as Isaac expresses in the same place.

*Concerning the Bears to whom tyrants are compared. How much common prayer avails, and how private works of mercy are shown in the cases of wayward nuns and a woman wonderfully entangled in marriage trials.*

### CHAPTER III.

Bears are devoured by ants; specifically, these ants heal the bears if they are sick, which is why they are sought after most wisely by sick bears. <note>This refers to a medieval bestiary belief that bears, when feeling ill or having eaten Mandrake, would seek out ants to eat as a medicinal cure.</note> How the simple and good faithful are to be understood through the "ants" has been repeated often; now, however, it must be added who the "bears" are that lie in wait for such people. Indeed, in Holy Scripture, the characteristic of a tyrant or a persecutor is usually designated by the name of the Bear. Hence, through the cruelty of Nebuchadnezzar, king of the Chaldeans—with which he persecuted the inhabitants of Jerusalem and destroyed the city—he is called a "lurking bear" in the third chapter of Lamentations. There, in the persona of the holy city, Jeremiah laments thus: *He has blocked my ways with hewn stones, he has subverted my paths; he has become a lurking bear to me, a lion in hiding.* <note>original: "vrsus insidiãs... leo in absconditis." Quoting Lamentations 3:9-10.</note> *He has subverted my paths and broken me; he has left me desolate.* And Solomon, in Proverbs 28, says even more clearly: *A hungry bear is a wicked prince over a poor people.* 

Wicked lords, however, are "sick" when they exercise unjust power over their subjects, because every disordered passion of the soul is its own sickness. Yet often, by divine ordinance, it is arranged that after the common people have been punished <note>The author suggests that tyrants are sometimes used by God as a "scourge" to discipline the people.</note>, the tyrants recognize their own malice, coming to their senses and ceasing their persecutions, as if they have now been entirely healed. Just as we read in the last chapter of 4 Kings <note>In modern Bibles, this is 2 Kings 25, regarding the release of King Jehoiachin.</note> and the last chapter of 2 Chronicles.

## CHAPTER XII.

<margin>The sisters' feelings regarding the reform.</margin>
The sisters all protested against the reform with one voice, and consequently, through their relatives, they threw the entire city into a state of division. Some said the reform was good, while others said it was by no means so, calling it instead a "pernicious novelty" <note>original: "nouitas est perniciosa." The "Observant Reform" sought to return monasteries to a strict adherence to their original rules, which many established inhabitants saw as an unwanted and radical innovation.</note>. For many months, therefore, work was carried out on this matter so that the holy work might be completed in peace, but because of the conflicting opinions of the city’s counselors <note>term: "consulum" — members of the city council or magistrates who held significant power over local religious houses.</note>, the business was delayed day by day. Meanwhile, the Master of the Order sent for eleven holy reformers—women who came from a monastery that had already been reformed—and they were introduced into the monastery of the sisters of Saint Catherine by stealth, rather than openly, for fear of certain citizens without whose consent nothing effective could be done. The council of the said city eventually reached this decision: that the sisters of Saint Catherine ought to be reformed by that process which had begun among them, but only if and to the extent that they were not forced into this reform against their will. Hearing this, we who bore the burden of the war against the wrath of demons almost despaired of the perfection of the holy reformation, because it was known to all that not one of the sisters was willing to undergo it. Therefore, in a matter so desperate in the eyes of men, I decided that we must turn to God through public prayers. And because I was preaching daily at that time during the Advent of the Lord, on that day when the messengers of the council were to publicly test the will of the sisters, I spoke briefly to the people during the sermon in this manner:

> "Good people, <note>original: "Boni pueri," literally "Good boys" or "Good children," a common paternalistic address from a preacher to his congregation.</note> it is clear to you how labor is currently being undertaken for the reform of the sisters of Saint Catherine. Until now, I have made no mention of this from the pulpit; now, therefore, I ask that each person here present pray to the Most High, so that in such a business the will and good pleasure of Almighty God may be done."

Now, some of the council’s messengers felt a certain displeasure regarding the method of this reform. And when the sisters were asked for their consent and had withdrawn to one side, after a short delay—hardly longer than it takes to recite the Psalm *Have mercy on me, O God* <note>original: "Miserere mei Deus," the 51st Psalm, a central text of penitence.</note>—by the inspiration of the Spirit of God, they all consented to the reform. Coming then into our presence and that of the messengers, they offered themselves to the reform with tears and kneeling. We were overjoyed beyond measure at this, and our adversaries were confounded. And because the city council had placed this holy business at the sisters' own discretion—which it now perceived had changed for the better—it therefore ordered this conclusion to be fully executed to the best of its power; and so that place is today completely reformed.

Furthermore, there lived recently in the church of Mainz <note>original: "Maguntina." Mainz was a major ecclesiastical and political center in the Holy Roman Empire.</note> a provost among the highest rank of canons—a cleric in name only. He was of noble birth, but in arms he was a soldier, in dress a mercenary, and in his morals entirely dissolute. Although he lived off the very generous revenues of the altar <note>term: "beneficijs" — an ecclesiastical office that provided a steady income (a "benefice") to the holder.</note>, he nevertheless fled from the canonical hours <note>The set times of daily prayer—such as Matins and Vespers—that clergy were strictly required to recite.</note> as if they were poison. Moreover, he was so handsome of body that the Empress, who is alive today, is reported to have said she had never seen a more beautiful man. Living for some time in this lifestyle to the scandal of many, he cared for no man's exhortations or corrections. Therefore, the hand of God unexpectedly touched him with leprosy, which day by day cut him off from the company of men against his will, and thrust him into a certain house of his own in Mainz. There he remained for a long time, full of impatience and void of the fear of God; at last, he became so deformed in body that he had no equal in the leper colony.

For a long time, it remained hidden from this woman how many snares and shackles she lay bound in under the power of the devil, entangled in his net. At last, however—I believe through the works of mercy in which she always persisted—she was enlightened in some measure around the thirty-sixth year of her age. While I was preaching in the aforementioned diocese, she came to me for the sake of counsel after having consulted many others. These previous advisors, as I discovered, had not helped the woman's soul with their foolish advice, but had rather destroyed or neglected it. And when she overflowed with such great weeping that you would have believed her another Mary Magdalene—except that she did not fall at the feet of a sinner <note>The author, Nider, humbly refers to himself as the "sinner" whose feet she did not fall at, unlike the biblical Mary Magdalene at the feet of Jesus.</note>—and I asked her what sorrow she held, she finally added:

> "Father, I am a sinful woman, ready to repent in every way possible for me and to make satisfaction. I have had four husbands; the one I have now is not mine. I contracted marriage with all of them **through words of the present** <note>original: "per verba de praesenti." In medieval canon law, a marriage was legally binding the moment a couple exchanged consent using the present tense (e.g., "I take you now"), even without a priest or ceremony.</note>, and of these, three remain alive today."

Upon hearing this, I was quite stunned, knowing that one must apply the greatest effort to such complexities if one wishes to untangle anyone. Therefore, having diligently investigated the case, which I had not known before, I learned that there was a difficulty regarding all those still living; for regarding the dead husband, if any bond had existed, it was dissolved by the end of his life.

I perceived that the first husband among the living had previously contracted marriage with another woman, albeit clandestinely <note>A "clandestine" marriage was one performed in secret, without the public banns or witnesses required by the Church, yet it was often still considered valid and binding.</note>, and thus the woman was free from him in the **court of conscience** <term>court of conscience (Latin: *forum conscientiae*): The internal moral standing of a person before God, which may differ from their legal status in a public church court (the *forum externum*).</term>. 

She had also contracted marriage with the second husband clandestinely, and the marriage was consummated by the carnal act; but since she denied this under oath before an ecclesiastical judge, she was divorced from this second husband. 

With the third husband, she afterwards contracted marriage **in the face of the church** <note>original: "in facie ecclesiae." This refers to a formal, public wedding ceremony, usually conducted at the church door or altar, making it "official" in the eyes of the law.</note>, with whom she then shared a home and had certain children. 

I was greatly anxious about what I should advise between these two men so that the soul of the adulteress might be saved. For both men were...

And so that this would not be a lie, she would turn this in her mind toward an **illness of the soul** <note>original: "animæ infirmitatem." This is an example of "mental reservation," where a speaker uses a phrase that is technically true in their mind (sin is an illness of the soul) even if the listener understands it physically.</note>. For it is certain according to our faith that through mortal crime, everyone undergoes the death not only of the soul, but even the perpetual death of the body. She did as she had thought, and with divine grace smiling upon her, the husband—who was previously lacking in self-restraint—began to have compassion for the woman, whom he had often learned was truthful in other matters. For many years now, he has kept her untouched, only as a sister; nor have I heard anything bad from elsewhere regarding any adultery by the man. A reference to the "Josephite marriage," a tradition where a husband and wife live together in total continence, modeled after Mary and Joseph.</note>.

**THEOLOGIAN.** The woman's words contained the truth and carried its weight, though perhaps not according to every man's understanding. ### CHAPTER IIII.

Nightingales <note>original: "Philomena"</note> greedily seek out ants and their eggs to eat, because they recover from sickness by eating these, and their voices are made more resonant. Now, as Lord Albert <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a Dominican scholar and one of the most famous medieval scientists and theologians.</note> relates in Book 23 of *On Animals*, the Nightingale is named from *philos* and *menos* <note>Greek: "love" and "strength/passion"</note>, because it sounds sweet, for it loves sweet songs. Or it is named from *philos* and *mene* <note>Greek: "love" and "abiding/month"</note>, because while it competes in song with another, it would rather lose its life than give up its song out of defeat. For with its beak and throat, it mimics almost every kind of music, and sometimes kills itself with its own singing. In this bird are symbolized greedy and covetous princes and men who, with persuasive and sweet or cunning words, oppress simple folk in material matters,

...in earthly matters or in the soul, just like defenseless little ants and their fruits. Regarding this, the blessed Jeremiah complains in the person of the Lord in Jeremiah 5, saying: "Among my people are found wicked men, lying in wait like bird-catchers, setting snares and traps to catch men. As a cage is full of birds, so are their houses full of deceit; therefore they have become great and rich, and they have bypassed my words most wickedly; they have not judged the cause of the widow, they have not directed the cause of the orphan, and they have not judged the judgment of the poor."

And regarding similar people, the prophet says in Ezekiel 33: "Their heart follows their greed, and to them it is like a musical song that is sung with a sweet and pleasant sound."

That the sweet words of men are equivalent to sweet sounds is taught in Ecclesiasticus 40 <note>Also known as the Book of Sirach.</note>, where it says: "The pipe and the psaltery <note>A stringed instrument similar to a zither or harp.</note> make sweet melody, and a sweet tongue is above them both."

**THE STUDENT:** <note>original: "PI G." for "Piger," meaning "The Sluggard" or "The Lazy Student," the character who asks questions.</note> Is it not rightly the case that, in a reciprocal way, a wicked woman does something similar with the honey-sweet words of her mouth to deceive unwary men?

**THE THEOLOGIAN:** Women indeed do this, but with a different art of deception—not like men, who often use tyranny and power after their deceit and trickery. For this reason, Solomon warns his son against such things in Proverbs 5, saying: "Pay no attention to the deceit of a woman, for the lips of a harlot <note>original: "meretricis"</note> are like a dripping honeycomb, and her throat is smoother than oil, but her end is as bitter as wormwood <note>A plant known for its extreme bitterness, often used as a metaphor for sorrow or poison.</note>, and her tongue is as sharp as a double-edged sword."

And again in chapter 6 of the same book: "Keep, my son, the precepts of your father, that they may guard you from the wicked woman, and from the flattering tongue of the stranger. Let not your heart lust after her beauty, nor be captured by her glances."

And he says even more clearly in chapter 7: "Say to wisdom, 'You are my sister,' and call prudence your friend, that she may guard you from the strange woman, and from the outsider who makes her words sweet; she has ensnared..."

# CHAPTER IV. 205

...for with many words and the flattery of her lips, she led away the senseless youth passing through the streets. <note>original: "enim vecordem iuuenem..." — this completes the citation from Proverbs 7 begun on the previous page.</note> **THE STUDENT:** It was not recently, but long ago when I heard such warnings in Holy Scripture <note>original: "sacra scriptura"</note> against women, that a doubt struck my mind: Why is the fragile sex not protected more in the sacred writings—so that they might guard themselves against the deceits of men—than the masculine sex, which is known to be of a more constant mind? Furthermore, when mention was made at a monastery of our order in Colmar <note>original: "Columbaria," the Latin name for the city of Colmar in Alsace.</note> among the sisters of our order concerning the blessed John Chrysostom <note>An influential 4th-century Church Father whose writings often contained harsh critiques of female behavior.</note> and certain other saints who, as the scripture says, spoke out quite enough against women; a certain nun who had a smattering of grammar <note>original: "sciola grāmaticæ"</note> heard this and said in anger: "You men have put forward far too many writings against our fragile sex; if we had the ability <gloss>The response of a defiant woman.</gloss> to write and speak as you do, we would have long ago returned the favor to your 'faithfulness.'" **THE THEOLOGIAN:** To address your second point first, know that no prudent man has ever brought any evil charge against the female sex itself, for he does not doubt that it was created good by God. Hence, in Holy Scripture, where we are warned about women, an adjective describing malice is almost always joined to the name of the woman, as is evident in the books of wisdom. Thus, the blessed Job used a prudent style; because his wife was the only one left in his whole house by the devil to be his persecutor, he responded to her:
> You have spoken like one of the foolish women,
because he did not wish to reproach the sex created by God, but rather the foolishness attached to the woman. In the same way, other ecclesiastical writers, when they command us to beware of women, mean a wandering harlot, a bold prostitute, or some other evil woman, and it is she whom they detest.

...because they are closer to God by nature, they are therefore more shamefully infected when defiled; they are freer in body and soul, and thus like wanderers, they are more easily deceived; they are hotter in their physical constitution <term>complexione: the medieval medical theory of the four "humors," where a "hot" temperament was associated with activity but also passion.</term>, and so they are more quickly inflamed to evil; they are more elegant in body, and thus are more quickly desired by women; and they are more eminent in rank and office, and therefore others are more scandalized by their bad example.

<margin>1.</margin> First, I say that men are closer to God by nature than women are, which is why the Apostle says in 1 Corinthians 11: *But I want you to know that the head of every man is Christ, the head of woman is man, and the head of Christ is God.* <note>original: "Volo autem vos scire..."</note> And again: *A man indeed ought not to cover his head, since he is the image and glory of God, but woman is the glory of man. For man was not made from woman, but woman from man. Indeed, man was not created for woman, but woman for man.* <note>original: "Vir quidem non debet velare..."</note> Where the <margin>Ordinary Gloss</margin> <gloss>The *Glossa Ordinaria*, the standard medieval biblical commentary.</gloss> says: Man is said to be the image of God because he was principally created in God's image, and in him, reason <note>original: "ratio"</note> naturally flourishes more than in woman, as if he himself were reason.

<margin>2.</margin> Second, men are freer in body and soul because authority <note>original: "dominium"</note> resides with them; hence they can stand and walk where and when they wish, and speak with anyone they like. But when freedom is taken into abuse, it becomes an occasion for sin for many. In contrast, in the third chapter of Genesis, it is said to the first woman by the Lord: *You shall be under the power of the man, and he shall rule over you.* And in 1 Peter 2: *As free people, and not using your freedom as a cloak for malice, but as servants of God.*

<margin>3.</margin> Third, men are hotter in their physical constitution, and therefore they are more quickly inflamed toward evil. <margin>4.</margin> Fourth, men are more elegant in body than women in their stature, height, and in the beauty of their limbs. The Creator seems to have established a similar pattern in almost every species of animal, such that He always created the male more eminent, and indeed more beautiful: as is clear in the peacock, the pheasant, the duck, the pigeon, and in many others. For the sake of this fact, it is specifically said of the first man in the first chapter of Genesis: *Let us make man in our image and likeness, that he may rule over the fish of the sea, and the birds of the air, and the beasts, and the whole of creation, and every reptile that moves upon the earth.* <note>original: "Faciamus hominem..."</note>

<margin>5.</margin> Fifth, men are more eminent than women in rank and office. Hence, in 1 Timothy 2: *Let a woman learn in silence with all subjection; but I do not permit a woman to teach, nor to have dominion over a man, but to be in silence.* For Adam, he adds, was formed first, then Eve: *And Adam was not seduced, but the woman was seduced into transgression.* <note>original: "Adam enim... prius formatus est..." The author is citing St. Paul to argue for a natural and divinely ordained hierarchy between the sexes.</note>

### BOOK III OF THE ANTHILL ###

...she was quite clever, and being moved by the divine word, she experienced certain inspirations and revelations that appeared, on the surface, to be quite beautiful and in harmony with Holy Scripture—though by what spirit they were truly sent, I do not know. I have come to doubt them because, as I discovered later, she secretly harbored an excessive love for wine and for her own personal freedom. To tell the truth, and to admit my own youthful folly, I was at that time quite gullible regarding such things. For I used to take great delight whenever I encountered a person who appeared <margin>another reading: in my judgment</margin> to be truly devout, and who I heard had received some new divine insight through their devotion. Drawn by a certain curiosity toward these novelties, I applied myself to them more fervently than I did to the established passages of Scripture—even though, by the grace of Christ, I never actually strayed from those biblical truths.

However, because the aforementioned woman lived under no one's authority or vow of obedience, she traveled freely wherever she pleased. She always maintained an appearance of virtue, for without such a facade, no person of faith is ever truly led astray. Eventually, to her own misfortune, she insisted on going on a pilgrimage to a certain shrine of the Blessed Virgin, and she got her way.

At that same time, there lived in that place a certain man of the cloth—alas, he was a monk in name only. He was a priest, but one filled with seductive talk and a lack of self-control, skilled in the "bird-trapping" of lost souls. Joining the woman on her journey, he progressed from conversation to acts of service, and from service to a close friendship. Through this intimacy, the poor woman soon found herself in the very jaws of a demonic nightingale <note>original: "daemonicae philomenae." The nightingale—Philomela in myth—was a common literary metaphor for song, but here Nider uses it ironically to describe a predatory seducer who uses "sweet" words to devour his prey.</note> waiting to devour her. From that point on, her soul became entirely "captive to love" <term>philocapta: a Latinized Greek term for being ensnared or captivated by erotic love</term> through the man’s words and gestures. Eventually, through his frequent visits, he seduced and violated her. She mourned this loss so immoderately—lamenting the "treasure" <note>A common metaphor for a woman's virginity or chastity.</note> of her virtue that had been stolen beyond recovery—that she would have taken her own life with a sword, had the weapon not been wrestled from her hands by her very corrupter.

She eventually came to me seeking counsel, but she would not follow my advice; she had already ventured too deep into the demon’s throat. For I commanded her that she should in no way allow that man to approach her, and that she herself...

<margin>the defiler is struck by illness</margin> The defiler himself, however, was immediately struck by a grave illness. He recognized his crimes and—as I truly believe regarding the virgin <note>possibly referring to his repentance toward the woman he wronged</note>—he repented from the heart. Having duly received all the sacraments of the Church, he departed this life with such good signs of his predestination that I have never recognized the like in anyone else at their deathbed. For I believe that divine mercy looked upon the man’s past good deeds, which, as is clear to me, he had performed for many years while serving God devotedly in his younger days.

<margin>Gregory, *Morals on Job*, book 5, chapter 16.</margin>
Blessed Gregory shows what this signifies in the fifth book of his *Morals on Job*, explaining that passage from Job 4:11: *The tiger perished because it had no prey.* He says: In the translation of the Seventy <note>The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note>, it does not say "Tiger" at all, but rather: *The <term>ant-lion</term> perished because it had no prey.* <note>original: *Myrmicoleon*</note>. Indeed, the ant-lion is a very small animal, an enemy to ants, which hides itself under the dust; there it kills the ants as they are carrying grain, and once killed, it consumes them. In Latin, it is called either the "Lion of Ants" or, more precisely, "both ant and lion." It is rightly named both "ant" and "lion" because to birds or any other small animals it is an ant, but to the ants themselves, it is a lion. For it devours the ants like a lion, but is itself devoured by the birds like an ant. And further below: This

<margin>Gregory, ibid., chapter 17.</margin>
shows that the ant-lion bears a resemblance to the demon and the hypocrite. Truly, the apostate angel <note>Lucifer or Satan</note>, having been cast down from the heavens to the earth, besieged the minds of the righteous—who prepare for themselves a refreshment of good works—upon the very path of their actions. When he overcomes these minds through his snares, he kills them unexpectedly, just like ants carrying grain. He is rightly called an "ant-lion," that is, a lion and an ant; for as we have said, he is a lion to the ants, but an ant to the birds. This is because the ancient enemy is strong against those who consent to him, yet weak against those who resist. For if one yields to his suggestions, he is like a lion that can by no means be endured; but if he is resisted, he is crushed like an ant. Therefore, he is a lion to some and an ant to others, because fleshly minds can scarcely endure his cruelty, while spiritual minds trample his weakness with the foot of virtue. Heretics, therefore, because they are proud of their presumption of holiness, speak as if exulting: *The ant-lion—or certainly the tiger—has perished, because it had no prey.* For whom does Eliphaz <note>one of the three friends of Job in the biblical narrative</note> signify by the name

<margin>Gregory, chapter 16.</margin>
of the "Tiger," if not the blessed Job, noted for his variety <note>likely referring to Job's varied trials or the multifaceted nature of his character</note>...

### BOOK III OF THE ANTHILL

<margin>Out of hatred, a prostitute is introduced into the chamber of a pious priest to blacken his reputation.</margin>
Because he sowed [the word of God] graciously and through the holiness of his life—by which he showed himself a mirror of virtues—he won the souls of many for his Creator. From this, he acquired great favor from the people. However, conversely, he incurred a very great hatred from the clerics who should have been his brothers in that same church. Indeed, in comparison to him, the lives of the wicked clerics seemed filthy. Since they did not dare to persecute the holy man openly, nor to strip him of his <term>benefice</term> <note>A church office that provided a living or income</note> and honor, they devised a most wicked lie in hypocrisy against him. 

For they secretly procured a key to the holy man’s chamber, and while he was away, they let in a woman of ill repute during the day. They instructed her to start a fire within the chamber and to cry out for help from the room toward the streets. Hearing this, the rivals—rising from their ambush as if they wished to help the woman—would join in, following a pre-arranged reward. It was carried out exactly in this order. For when the woman cried out in the already burning chamber, the clerics ran from their ambush, calling upon the secular neighbors for assistance. When they saw the woman in the chamber, the good man’s entire reputation was blackened; thus, the innocent man was forced to yield both his reputation and his position. 

Finally, after a long time had passed, the principal author of this wickedness, being at the point of death <note>original: *in extremæ infirmitatis articulo*</note>, confessed the matter to a priest. This priest refused to absolve him unless he restored the man's reputation publicly. Therefore, having summoned witnesses worthy of belief, this wicked man—lest he be cast into eternal shame—confessed the cause and the sequence of the aforementioned betrayal, and so he finally restored the innocent man’s reputation. 

Furthermore, hypocrites or very bitter pretenders are sometimes found among simple men. Scarcely three years have passed since there was in the city of <term>Regensburg</term> <note>original: *Ratisponensi*</note> a certain vete-

...and with a spoon most greedily put it into his mouth, and so the wretch was immediately suffocated. Furthermore, there are found among these people hypocrites who are far worse: namely, heretics. Indeed, every heretic is a hypocrite in that he feigns himself to be a Catholic and a virtuous man—which he is not—but not every hypocrite is a heretic. For there currently runs and creeps through the regions of <term>Swabia</term> <note>original: "Sueviæ"; a historical region in southwestern Germany</note> among certain persons of both sexes—laity and clergy, monks and nuns alike—a heresy and a hypocrisy so enormous that I do not dare to fully describe it, lest I stain the ears of the innocent <note>original: "innocentum maculem"</note>. 

For this sect asserts that it is permitted to lie at one's pleasure, to keep no oaths or agreements, and even to kill the most innocent person, even if it were one’s own father or mother. They never fast, except so that they are not caught by others while eating; they consume <term>dairy products</term> <note>original: "lacticinia"; typically forbidden during fasts</note> and meat when someone else eats during the season of <term>Lent</term> <note>original: "quadragesimali tempore"; the forty days of penance before Easter</note>. Where they can do so secretly, they work on the feast days of the Church, yet remain idle on other days. In their hearts, they despise all ceremonies of the Church as the "works of animalistic men, not spiritual ones." And what is worse, they affirm that the glory of virginity, abstinences regarding clothing, and the hardship of one's bedding are merely "bodily superstitions," and they teach their followers to renounce such things. 

They claim that the only perfection and virtue lies in a certain "highest contemplation of the spirit," which has no flesh and bones; yet they themselves, as I know, live not only carnally but in the most bestial manner. For they boast that they have reached such a peak of perfection that nothing can be counted as a sin against them. Consequently, they consider it a very small matter whenever they disobey the <term>Supreme Pontiff</term> <note>The Pope</note> or other pastors of the Holy Church. Furthermore, in the heat of sexual intercourse between a man and a woman—where even according to the <term>pagans</term> <note>original: "ethnicos"</note> reason is swallowed up and man is made like a beast—they say that the highest contemplation and most excellent <term>ecstasy</term> <note>original: "raptum"; literally a "seizing" or carrying away of the soul</note> consist, because...

If you ask about their clothing or habit, know that they do not use a uniform one. Instead, they sometimes cover themselves in clothing however costly and extravagant, and at other times in very cheap clothing, according to the place and time, so that they might not be betrayed. For by the very fact that they believe themselves <term>incapable of sin</term> <note>original: "impeccabiles"</note>, they think every kind of dress is permitted to them without any fear. They change it frequently so as to remain hidden; otherwise, they would be more quickly discovered. 

When they are together, if you wish to know their words, they sometimes use amorous or whorish language with one another, behaving in the manner of pimps. But if they are living among others, they use words more subtle, elegant, sublime, spiritual, and metaphysical than can be believed, as far as the...

# BOOK III OF THE ANT-HILL

in the **German language** <note>original: "lingua Theutonica"</note>, so much so that scarcely anyone can understand them correctly, even a literate person. In this tongue, they wrap up high-minded sentiments about the spirit, about abstraction, about various lights, about divine persons, and about the degrees of contemplation. For this reason, certain German books of their subtle sermons seem to serve their malice well; they speak using such vocabulary that some people—unless I am mistaken—have either foolishly or dangerously written them, or permitted them to be written. At the very least, these works seem to have been falsely attributed to certain honorable and ancient doctors of religious orders by certain **Beghards** <note>A lay religious movement in the Middle Ages, often suspected by the Church of harboring heretical "Free Spirit" views</note> or heretics. Thus, they hide the virus of their own depravity under the aforementioned words and offer the poison of their heretical malignancy to others.

As a foundation for their error, they twist these authorities of the Apostle to their own reprobate sense: *If you are led by the spirit, you are not under the law* <note>Galatians 5:18; original: "Si spiritu ducimini non estis sub lege"</note>. They do not notice what is immediately added: *Now the works of the flesh are manifest, which are fornication, uncleanness, immodesty, luxury* <note>Galatians 5:19; original: "Manifesta sunt opera carnis..."</note>, of which these people are full. Then, they allege for themselves that other passage from the same place: *You, brothers, have been called unto liberty* <note>Galatians 5:13; original: "Vos in libertatem vocati estis fratres"</note>. They do not attend to what follows: *Only make not liberty an occasion to the flesh.* And so, to bring these matters to some conclusion: to kill the simple, they use ornate words; the toxin of death is offered there; physical exercises are disparaged by them; they are moved to meditate upon I-know-not-what "spirit"; and finally, all their disciples slide down into the works of the flesh, even though they may appear outwardly to be like tigresses <note>A metaphor for being "spotted" or "marked" with external signs of piety that hide a predatory nature</note> full of virtues.

## CHAPTER VI.

*Although an anthill may have a pleasant scent, yet if fresh and tender wood, or a jar made from such wood, is rubbed or scraped harshly against it, it is found to take on a certain noticeable stench.* By the anthill, the dwelling of simple, good people is designated; and by the scent proceeding from it, the awareness of a good reputation is signified, as was established above.
<margin>Book 2, Chapter 9</margin>
But by the new and fresh wood, bodies can be signified from which the moisture of carnal passions has not yet been drawn out by the heat of charity. If, therefore, men or youths—indeed even old men—frequently visit the house or dwelling of any women, even holy ones, without evident necessity and usefulness, they will easily stir up the stench of their own reputation in the nostrils of others.
<margin>2 Corinthians 2</margin>

# THE ANTHILL, BOOK III.
