# BOOK III OF THE ANT-HILL

<margin>She comes to her senses and revokes her errors.</margin>
...we showed how many distinguished and learned men had been deceived by careless revelations and led astray by an "angel of Satan" <note>A reference to 2 Corinthians 11:14, where Paul warns that even Satan can disguise himself as an angel of light to deceive the faithful.</note>; and we demonstrated in many ways how fragile the female sex <note>A common medieval trope (*infirmitas sexus*) suggesting women were more susceptible to spiritual deception without male or clerical guidance.</note> can be when not supported by the testimony of Holy Scripture. Then, through the grace of Christ, she herself began to come to her senses and promised that she wished to follow me and my companion in all things. Believing herself to have been deceived, she made a voluntary sacramental confession <term>sacramental confession: a formal confession to a priest intended to seek absolution for sins and reconcile with the Church</term> to me regarding everything she had committed since her youth in order to cleanse her soul. She offered herself to publicly revoke her error and to perform penance. And so, three days later, before the city of Regensburg <note>original: *Ratisponensi*</note>, she carried out everything previously mentioned to full effect, while many in the crowd wept out of joy and mercy.

<margin>Matthew 10. Luke 12.</margin>
**PUPIL:** Since nothing is hidden that is not also commonly brought to light even in this life <note>Referring to the Gospel passages where Jesus says "nothing is covered that will not be revealed."</note>, was it discovered afterward whether she had any leader <note>original: *haeresiarcham*; literally a leader or founder of a heretical sect.</note> in her error, or any disciple?

<margin>The causes of the error.</margin>
**THEOLOGIAN:** Not at all; she had only a malignant deceiving spirit. Through an internal impulse, she had accepted this spirit as an "angel of light" in false revelations. She had not presented these matters for examination to any experienced or learned man to see if they were truly from God, nor had she sufficiently called for divine help against the spirit of error. Furthermore, she was unable to help herself through acquired knowledge or the basic principles of Holy Scripture. Thus, it is no wonder if, relying on her own wit, she deserved to be so gravely deceived by presuming too much of herself.

## CHAPTER VIII.

->**Ants, where they are harmful, are easily put to flight if ashes are scattered there in a circle.**<- By this it is clearly given to be understood that when simple men wish to be harmful to their neighbors, they can repent of their undertakings and return to themselves no better than through the humbling of themselves and the acknowledgement of their own fragility. For ashes designate the humility of human weakness; hence in Genesis 18, Abraham said to God, so that he might be heard as a humble man: *I will speak to my Lord, though I am but dust and ashes.* <note>original: "puluis & cinis"</note> And Tamar, humbled by her brother's violation, is read in 2 Kings 13 <note>In modern Bibles, this is 2 Samuel 13. Tamar was the daughter of King David.</note> to have sprinkled ashes on her head. Hence in Lamentations 2 <note>original: "Threnorum"</note>, it is said of those humbled in the captivity in Jerusalem: *The virgins of Jerusalem have sprinkled ashes upon their heads.* And the King of Nineveh, by repenting humbly, cast his garment from him, and was clothed in sackcloth, and sat in ashes, as seen in Jonah 3. *Why is earth and ashes proud?* says the author of Ecclesiasticus 10 <note>Also known as the Book of Sirach; a book of ethical teachings.</note> concerning man. For *all flesh is grass, and all its glory is like the flower of the field; the grass is withered and the flower has fallen, because the spirit of God blew upon it. Truly the people are grass,* in the fortieth chapter of Isaiah. *Our body shall be as extinguished ashes,* said the wise man in Wisdom 2. Therefore, when we do not humbly acknowledge ourselves inwardly through true self-knowledge, we immediately become puffed up with pride and quickly begin to be harmful to ourselves and our neighbors. Hence, if we neglect to sprinkle ourselves with the ash of humility, through the requirements of divine mercy and justice, we often fall into errors or open vices, so that we may rise again more humble after our fall than we seemed to be when we stood upright.

In it was written that the sisters should begin and continue to hold all temporal goods in common, according to the rite of the holy fathers; otherwise, divine vengeance would follow.

### CHAPTER VIII.

...they imitate any other men in such a way that, unless they are seen, they cannot be distinguished at all. Some, without shame, produce so many rhythmic sounds from their lower parts at will that they even seem to sing from that area <note>This refers to the practice of ventriloquism or "flatulism" which historical authors often viewed with suspicion or as a curiosity of the body's control</note>. I myself have experienced a man who could sweat whenever he wished. It is known that some weep when they want to, and pour out tears abundantly. 

Now, there is something even more incredible to many, which several brothers have experienced in very recent memory. There was a certain priest named Restitutus <note>A priest mentioned by St. Augustine in 'The City of God', Book 14, Chapter 24</note> in the parish of the church of Calama <note>An ancient city in what is now Algeria</note>; whenever he pleased (for he was asked to do these things by those who wished to witness this marvelous thing firsthand), upon imitating the voices of someone lamenting, he would so withdraw himself from his senses and lie there so much like a dead man, that not only did he not feel those pinching or pricking him, but sometimes he was even burned when fire was applied, without any sense of pain until afterward from the wound. Furthermore, it was proven that he did not keep his body from moving by resisting the pain, but by simply not feeling it, because just as in a deceased person, no breath could be found in him. Nevertheless, he later reported that he had heard the voices of men, if they spoke clearly, as if from a great distance. 

Thus says Augustine. Therefore, such people who can easily alienate themselves from their bodily senses by nature can perform wonders in the sight of others, whether by their own industry, or by the cunning of demons, or by the ministry of good angels.

One thing I know: the instincts of good spirits are true, but false ones are sent by evil spirits, or arise from bodily phantasms <note>mental images or delusions</note>, by which many are deceived in various visions. In these matters, if the daughter (who was quite young when she claimed to be a prophet) had imitated her mother’s humility and silence, I believe she would have walked more safely and with less shame to herself and her kin. 

Consequently, at the same time that the daughter brought her aforementioned revelations into the public eye, this mother, perceiving this in her monastery at "The Stones," was greatly terrified (as I have heard). She feared an unfortunate outcome for the matter, and although this woman was a widow of such great repute, she nevertheless suffered very frequently, almost until the final days of her life, from a certain fantasy <note>original: "phantasiam"; here meaning a persistent delusion or obsessive thought</note> by which she imagined she ought to eventually leave the monastery and build a certain new hospital. ### CHAPTER IX.

Ants are said to be in Ethiopia that are horned and large, so much so that they resemble dogs in their form, as Isidore <note>Isidore of Seville (c. 560–636), an archbishop whose *Etymologies* served as the standard encyclopedia of the Middle Ages.</note> relates in the 12th book of his *Etymologies*, chapter 3, along with the following three properties. Finally, Albert <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a Dominican scholar and saint known for his extensive writings on natural science.</note> says the following in the 26th—or last—book of his work *On Animals*:

> If we are to believe those things written in the letter of Alexander <note>Referring to the *Epistola Alexandri ad Aristotelem*, a popular medieval fictional account of Alexander the Great's wonders in India.</note> concerning the marvels of India, then there are in India ants as large as dogs or foxes, having four legs and hooked claws.

So he says. If their inner greatness of industry and ingenuity corresponds to their physical size, they are certainly most cunning. Now, through this monstrous and especially unusual likeness to dogs, the atrocious heretics <term>haeretici: those who hold beliefs contrary to established Church dogma; here Nider specifically targets the Hussites of Bohemia</term> can be aptly understood. > Look out for the dogs, look out for the evil-doers, look out for the "mutilation." <note>original: "concisionem"; St. Paul uses this word as a mocking play on "circumcision," suggesting the false teachers are merely cutting the flesh.</note>

# BOOK III OF THE ANTHILL

...through Germany, you preached the same crusade against them. Then, when the general Council of Basel <note>A major church council (1431–1449) that dealt with church reform and the Hussite conflict.</note> summoned them to appear, you served for a long time as one of the council's messengers, and later as an envoy to those same heretics, conversing with them frequently. I ask that you briefly summarize their sects so that I may understand them.

*THE THEOLOGIAN.* What you ask would require a massive volume, even if I were able or willing to grant your request. Nevertheless, <margin>John Wyclif, a leader of heresy, around the year 1375.</margin> this is how their rise and ruin came about. 

Less than sixty years ago, there lived in England a certain secular priest and professor of arts, sharp in intellect and charming in eloquence, but in his errors, writings, and life he was not merely a heretic, but a heresiarch <term>heresiarch: the founder or leader of a heretical movement</term>, named John Wyclif. In his small books written in English and Latin, he sought to subvert the commonweal of both laypeople and clergy with new doctrine. Those who have stayed there know how many people—then, afterward, and even now—have been made secret heretics in England by his articles <note>original: "articulis"; here referring to Wyclif's specific theological propositions condemned by the Church.</note>.

In my own time, a certain Bohemian—who was later burned to ashes at the general Council of Constance <note>The Council of Constance (1414–1418) was called to end the Papal Schism and address the "Bohemian heresy."</note>—namely Master of Arts Jerome <margin>Jerome of Prague, a disciple of Wyclif, brought heresy from England to Bohemia.</margin>, having studied in England, greedily drank down this poison. Afterward, he poured it out abundantly through books and his own voice in the capital city of Bohemia, at the University of Prague. Because of this, the aforementioned university was divided, and many of the more prominent theologians departed from there. 

Then nearly all of Bohemia began to rebel against the Roman Church, and it was filled almost everywhere with erroneous doctrines; so many sects of heretics existed there that they can hardly be counted. <margin>Three main sects of Bohemian heretics.</margin> Three principal sects, however, persisted for a long time: namely, the "Old Praguers," who were more tolerable; the "Orphans"; and the "Taborites," who were the worst of all. They burned churches and monasteries; they spared no nun, nor monk, nor the Carthusians...

And although they were all heretics and schismatics, nonetheless, by divine permission, they were equally blinded and punished by such an incredible error that at times one sect would attack another, so that the victor might kill the vanquished: heretic killing heretic, and schismatic killing schismatic. 

There was only one sign in which they all agreed: namely, to communicate "under both kinds" <note>original: "sub utraque specie"; the practice of the laity receiving both the bread and the wine during the Eucharist, which was the central demand of the Hussites.</note> in the most divine sacrament of the Eucharist. <margin>Why the wicked sometimes prevail over the good</margin>

This is clear from the gathering of Israel against the Benjaminites; the Israelites were first defeated twice despite being honorable, and only once did they emerge as victors over the Benjaminites, as told in the twentieth chapter of Judges. Also, in the second book of Maccabees, chapter 6, many chosen faithful were slaughtered under the most cruel persecution of Antiochus; they were defenseless as if without God’s help in the eyes of men, but not in the eyes of God. 

**THE SLUGGARD.** Certainly, it is quite surprising why divine justice permitted such a great evil to rage in such a kingdom, especially since previously the simple folk and the nobles there held to strict abstinences and fasts on Fridays. 

<margin>In Bohemia, on Fridays, dairy products and eggs are not usually eaten. Romans 11.</margin>

They placed more weight on the eating of dairy products or eggs on those days than some people in other lands care about the transgression of the Church's fasts. 

**THE THEOLOGIAN.** Those judgments of God are hidden, and who has known the mind of the Lord? <note>original: "quis nouit sensum domini?"; a reference to Romans 11:34.</note> We know, however, that abstinence from the foods you mention is commendable, but rather to be praised is a constant thriftiness in living, humility in the use of temporal things, tranquility in social interaction, and—against lazy idleness—a diligence in lawful labor. 

<margin>The cause of the heresies in Bohemia.</margin>

Furthermore, we know—and the Bohemians themselves admit this publicly—that in their land, more than in other kingdoms, there was a great excess in food and drink, a frequent atrocity of violence even to the shedding of blood, a slothful idleness in many things without any use, and a feigned brazenness for committing corruption <term>frontositas: literally "brow-ness," meaning a bold or shameless face, here used to describe a lack of moral shame in business or behavior</term>. For how many thousands of Christians, I ask, have been captured in our time...

**T H E O L.** Offhand, I am aware of no such specific sect. Indeed, he stood out as such a wonderfully singular and singularly wonderful heretic that, to my knowledge, he had no equal. For in the aforementioned university, after studying the *trivium* <term>Trivium: The three foundational liberal arts consisting of grammar, logic, and rhetoric.</term> for some time, he listened to the lectures given by the masters of sacred theology, not yet "infected" as he would later become. Afterward, having been ordained a priest, he went down to Hungary, and there he held the office of preaching and the administration of the sacraments. Meanwhile, having a small amount of knowledge in the arts, he acquired a distaste for the rites of the Christian faith. By syllogizing—or rather, by false reasoning—privately debating with himself about the articles of faith and all the ceremonies of the Church, these things seemed to him to be greater delusions than they had appeared before. To put it briefly, this wretched man reached the point where he believed nothing at all of those things which belong to the Catholic faith, except insofar as he could clearly and effectively prove them through philosophical demonstration—as a natural philosopher would say; just as it is demonstrated that there is one ruler of the whole universe and a first cause.

He therefore mocked all the ceremonies of the faithful, thought little of the doctrines of the Christians <note>original: "Christicolarum," literally "Christ-worshipers"</note>, and despised all the sacraments of the church. He did not admit the Old Testament and set no value on the New; he considered the glosses <note>marginal or interlinear explanations of scripture</note> and the Doctors <note>authoritative teachers of the Church</note> of both to be nothing but nonsense, as well as all those who followed them. Yet, despite all this, while living as a hidden heretic, he administered many ecclesiastical sacraments—namely baptism and the like—and frequently celebrated the office of the holy mass.

It happened one day that a certain man, dressed in sacred vestments and about to go toward the altar to celebrate the office of the holy mass, was making his preparations. To him, the heretic said: "Do you wish to consecrate the son of a foolish woman again?" <note>original: "Visne iterum consecrare fatuæ filium?"—a blasphemous reference to the Virgin Mary and Christ.</note> or he spat out some other similar detestable and miserable word. Taking this blasphemy badly, the other man, once the divine services were finished, approached the treacherous man privately, saying: "Did you say to me as I was celebrating, whether I wanted to consecrate the son of a foolish woman again?" The accused replied that he had, and did not deny it; indeed, he began to vomit even more of the poison of his infidelity than before.

Upon hearing this, he was betrayed to the bishop, captured, imprisoned, and examined, and was found to be exactly as I have described. Meanwhile, the legate of all Germany, the Lord Cardinal of Piacenza <note>Branda da Castiglione (1350–1443), a powerful diplomat and church reformer.</note>, arrived with three devoted, prudent, and highly learned professors of both theology and canon law. They visited the accused in prison so that his soul might be saved, and they took care to try to bring the wanderer back to his senses through pious persuasions, but they made no progress at all with the prideful man. For when questioned about the various sects active at that time—the Wycliffites <note>Followers of John Wycliffe, whose ideas influenced the Hussite movement.</note> and Bohemians <note>Followers of Jan Hus.</note>, the Waldensians, Arians, Jews, Saracens <note>A medieval term for Muslims.</note>, and any other perfidious groups—he constantly mocked them all and persisted only in his own error. ### CHAPTER XI.

You have jumped to the very question I intended to ask you to solve: Why does our most merciful Lord allow so many heresies to swarm over his Church, his most beloved bride? But since you have already touched on this in your answer, please add some examples to the benefits you mentioned. **THEOLOGIAN:** You will be able to see this in many things said previously and in those that follow.

<margin>A falsely holy recluse, who was predicted to receive the stigmata <note>The five wounds of Christ.</note> on a certain day, is exposed and put to shame.</margin>
Shortly before the time of the Council of Constance <note>A major 15th-century church council held in Germany.</note>, there was a famous recluse <note>An "anchorite" or woman living in religious solitude.</note> in the town of Cells <note>Modern-day Radolfzell am Bodensee.</note> near Constance. She was a high-level "contemplative" who was said to possess great holiness—at least by those who have no idea how to
<margin>1 John 4 <note>Refers to the verse: "Beloved, do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits to see whether they are from God."</note></margin>
test spirits to see if they are from God. It was rumored that many of the more devout secular clergy from Constance and the surrounding area sought refuge in her for divine consolation, as if she were a mother. I knew some of them personally; they were men of no small status. This woman often showed herself lying as if in a trance or an ecstatic rapture. Upon returning to her senses and waking up, she would then reveal secrets that she could not have known. After these displays, certain priests who were far too trusting of such "little women" <note>original: "mulierculis" — a diminutive often used dismissively by medieval writers to imply weakness or gullibility.</note> began to place their faith in the holiness of this recluse.

The time came when it was spread as truth and constant fact throughout the city of Constance that, on a specific named day, the marks of the five stigmata of Christ would certainly appear on the hands, feet, and heart of this woman. When that day arrived, a great many notable people—both layfolk and clergy—left the city and came to Cells. The priests of this "false prophetess" were also present at this spectacle, enlarging their fringes <note>original: "magnificantes fimbrias" — a biblical allusion to the Pharisees in Matthew 23:5, signifying a boastful or hypocritical display of piety.</note> and leading the newcomers to see what they called "the wonders of God."

### FORMICARIUS <note>The Ant-Colony</note>, BOOK III.

At this word, the murmuring was silenced for a little while. Finally, after a great part of the day had passed and the crowd was departing, nothing but the greatest confusion was brought upon all who had believed in the woman’s delusions and her "revelations." For everyone present, perceiving the manifest lie, was ashamed to have come.

Hear of an event that occurred within the last ten years. There was a schoolboy, about thirteen years of age, in the city of Ravensburg in the Diocese of Constance. Having gone missing from his lodgings, he was sought everywhere for many days throughout the aforementioned city. Finally, he was found outside the city, lying atop a certain tree called a pine, located about half a league or a full league <note>A league is an old unit of distance, usually about three miles.</note> away. He had no visible wound, nor did any rope appear by which he might have strangled himself or been strangled by another; nor was there any clear footprint of a killer. 

Immediately, many of the common people began to worship him as if he were a martyr secretly murdered by the Jews. <note>This refers to the "blood libel," a common and unfounded medieval myth that Jewish communities committed ritual murder of Christian children. Nider here describes it as a product of popular superstition rather than fact.</note> They began to fabricate the most lying miracles supposedly performed by him, to erect wooden and stone chapels, and to appoint guardians for the pilgrims. They gathered money dedicated to this "new martyr" and—as if the highest proof of martyrdom had been established—they offered <term>veneration</term> <note>original: "duliam." In Catholic theology, *dulia* is the honor given to saints, as opposed to *latria*, the worship reserved for God alone.</note> to this unknown "saint." 

A verbal battle broke out between the laity and the clergy over who the boy was; some said that the opinion of the boy was favorable, while others contradicted them, saying: "By no means; those who believe such things so quickly lead the crowds astray." During this disagreement, the boy was buried by the local Bailiff in a nearby castle, and the official would not allow anyone to approach the place of the grave until the truth of the matter could be revealed. But the credulous commoners refused to abandon their supposed martyr. Because they could not reach the grave, they instead frequented the site of the supposed martyrdom: specifically, that pine tree in the fields—or rather, in the woods.

### CHAPTER I.

In approaching the fourth little book in order, which deals primarily with the virtuous deeds of the perfect and with those who act negligently regarding such matters, we first encounter this property of ants: that in the course of their life they differ greatly among themselves. For some are in eggs, others are newly born larvae <note>original: "vermiculi," literally "little worms"</note>, while others are now able to reproduce and perform vigorous works. Progress in spiritual matters is suggested to us in this way: that just as ants grow in body, so we should receive growth in the soul. The precursor of God <note>John the Baptist</note> provided an example of such growth for us, where it is said of him in the first chapter of Luke: *The child grew and was strengthened in spirit.* <note>Luke 1:80</note> And in the second chapter of the same book, it is said of the one whom he had foretold <note>Jesus</note>: *But the child grew and was strengthened, full of wisdom, and the grace of God was upon him.* <note>Luke 2:40</note> Finally, regarding him at twelve years of age, it follows again there: *Jesus advanced in wisdom and age, and in grace before God and men.* <note>Luke 2:52</note> Not that the [grace] of Christ...

To respond to that first authoritative text, you should know that according to the literal sense, this authority and its meaning depend on the preceding verse and on what follows immediately after. The sense of these is that it is safer, regarding the protection of chastity, to live with an unjust man than with a woman who is doing good deeds. Hence the text reads as follows:

> Do not gaze upon every person’s beauty, and do not linger in the company of women. For from clothing comes the moth, and from a woman comes a man’s iniquity. <margin>Ordinary Gloss.</margin>

# CHAPTER II.

[The end of the previous word]... under the name of "fruit," new and tender fruits can be understood; concerning this, it is said in Job chapter thirty-nine: *The ostrich leaves her eggs in the earth; do you perhaps warm them in the dust?* <margin>Gregory, *Moralia in Job*, Book 31, Chapter 5 (otherwise 7).</margin> Saint Gregory <note>Pope Gregory I (c. 540–604), whose "Moralia in Job" was a foundational text for medieval biblical interpretation.</note> says in the thirty-first book of his *Moralia*: "What is expressed by the eggs, if not the offspring that are still tender, which must be cherished for a long time so that they may be led to become living, winged creatures? Indeed, eggs are insensible in themselves, but when warmed they are converted into living, winged creatures. So, without a doubt, it is certain that little listeners and children remain cold and insensible unless they are warmed by the solicitous exhortation of their teacher. Therefore, lest they grow sluggish if left in their insensibility, they must be cherished by the constant voice of teachers until they are able to live through understanding and fly through contemplation." To have left eggs in the earth <margin>Ibid. Chapter 6 (otherwise 7).</margin> is to provide no example of heavenly life to one's children. *You perhaps warm them in the dust*, as if He <note>God, speaking to Job.</note> says: as I do, who warms them in the dust, because I ignite the souls of the little ones—even when placed in the midst of sinners—with the fire of my love. ### THE ANT-HEAP, BOOK III.

...he ran, having grabbed a club, and attacked the heretics standing near the town with persistent words and blows. They, having drawn their swords, defended themselves and struck the fool <term>fatuus</term> <note>original: "fatuum"; in this context, a "holy fool"—someone perceived as mentally simple but possessing deep, often provocative, religious devotion.</note> with such immense wounds—the scars of which I saw later—that they left him for dead, as they thought. Thus fell Christ’s little poor man <term>pauperculus Christi</term>; and after the heretics withdrew, he lay for a long time rolled in his own blood. At last, however, having recovered his strength, he arose and began to approach the castle by climbing up. The guards on the walls were amazed at where and when the fool had left the castle. Opening the gates for him, they found him wounded with lethal injuries. For among other places, he was completely pierced through by swords near the nipples—a place which, when the wound is deep, is always known to be a fatal injury. 

Now, the fool always held Jews in the greatest hatred, but heretics even more so. When a certain Jew, highly skilled in surgery <term>chirurgia</term>, was brought in as a doctor, the fool would by no means allow him to approach, as if he were death itself. "Far be it from me," he said, "to be healed by a heretic!" Instead, he ran to the cook in the kitchen; being hungry, he ate a morsel of food <margin>with him [the cook].</margin> with him, and within a few days he was healed without any bandages or medical art. In everyone's judgment, he was healed by divine power alone, since he was aided by almost no human protection.

<margin>The lodgings of the Catholics remained untouched while the plague raged everywhere in the houses of the heretics.</margin>

<margin>The three-fold degree of charity.</margin>
Even with the authorities already mentioned, the blessed Augustine and his followers have stood firm, distinguishing a three-fold degree of charity: the beginning, the progressing, and the perfect—just as is found in all living creatures: their birth, their growth, and the perfection of their state of increase. *PIG.* <note>Abbreviation for "Piger," meaning "The Sluggard," the student character in this dialogue.</note> Can you bring forward anyone from the number of people you know who, from their earliest age, has maintained the state of baptismal innocence in the perfection of spiritual life right through to old age? *THEOL.* <note>Abbreviation for "Theologus," the teacher character.</note> Since, according to the common law, no one knows whether they are worthy of hatred or love—as the most wise Solomon says in Ecclesiastes 9—I dare even less to judge another’s servant. 

<margin>Romans 14.</margin>
However, since I believe you understand the question only from the perspective of human conjecture, I have seen many such people—especially regarding the dignity, excellence, and status of virgins, of whom I have made some mention in several places above and will do so below—who preserved their baptismal innocence until their final old age, and (as I hope in the Lord of all) entered the grave of the deceased free from mortal sins and with an abundance of merits. *PIG.* You seem to contradict Holy Scripture by placing women above men in goodness.

# BOOK IV OF THE ANT-COLONY

But the indiscreet person, becoming prideful in his own good deeds, falls more heavily; whereas the discreet person, when repentant, returns to the rule of discretion, and henceforth acts more strongly and cautiously. For often the fault of the strong becomes an occasion for virtue, and the virtue of the weak an occasion for sin. Furthermore, if you wish to condemn all women based on the second authority <margin>The second passage is explained in multiple ways.</margin> <note>The "authority" refers to the biblical verse from Ecclesiastes 7:28: "One man among a thousand I have found, but a woman among all these I have not found."</note>, you will be opposing Holy Scripture itself and the catalog of the saints, which canonizes virgins, married women, and matrons in an innumerable multitude. 1. The first interpretation is the one already mentioned regarding original sin <note>Meaning that no human, male or female, is born without sin, except Christ.</note>.

3. ### CHAPTER I.

...as is commonly said, there is "no one" in the church when there are very few people there compared to the great multitude that usually gathers; it is in this same manner that it is spoken of <margin>Aristotle, *Physics*, Book 2, chapters 5 and 6.</margin> in the second book of the *Physics*: "That which is only a small distance away is counted as almost nothing." The sixth sense [of the passage], according to the interlinear gloss <note>The *Glossa Interlinealis* was a standard medieval commentary where notes were written between the lines of the biblical text.</note>, is that "man" signifies reason or strength (for the word *man* [original: *vir*] denotes the strong, derived from "virtue" or "strength" [original: *virtus*]), while "woman" signifies sensuality <note>In medieval psychology, "sensuality" referred to the lower, animal-like faculties of feeling and desire, as opposed to the higher faculty of reason.</note>, over which reason is placed as the leader. Now, sensuality is prone to perpetual corruption, although it can be regulated by reason.

**STUDENT** <note>The text uses "PIG." for *Piger*, representing the "Slothful" or "Slow" student.</note> Is the sin of fornication or adultery therefore greater in a man than in a woman?

<margin>Question. Thomas Aquinas in the *Sentences*, Book 4, Distinction 35, single question, article 4.</margin>

**THEOLOGIAN** The Holy Doctor [Thomas Aquinas] responds in the fourth book, 35th distinction, that they relate to each other as "things that exceed and are exceeded by one another" <note>This is a scholastic way of saying they are unequal in different ways; one is worse in one aspect, the other is worse in another.</note>. This is because in a woman there is more of the "moist humor," and therefore they are more easily led by their desires; but in a man there is more "heat," which excites desire. 

But nonetheless, speaking plainly and all other things being equal, a man sins more in <term>simple fornication</term> <note>Sexual intercourse between two unmarried people.</note> than a woman, because he possesses a greater share of the "good of reason," which ought to prevail over any movements of physical passions. 

However, regarding the harm done to a marriage, the woman sins more than the man. This is partly because it is more against the law of nature (since it was never lawful for a woman to have multiple husbands, whereas the situation was different for men regarding multiple women) <note>A reference to the Old Testament patriarchs who practiced polygyny, which medieval theologians used to argue that a woman having multiple partners was a more fundamental violation of the "natural order" of parentage.</note>, and partly because it causes more harm to the offspring, whose parentage she makes uncertain. And because the violation of marriage is a more serious sin than simple fornication, it follows that, speaking simply, an adulterous woman sins more than an adulterous man, all other things being equal. 

Thus says Saint Thomas. Furthermore, Lord <margin>Albertus Magnus.</margin> Albert [Albertus Magnus]—who is to be believed more than many others in this matter insofar as it concerns natural science—says in the first chapter of the first treatise of his ninth book *On Animals*: "When," he says, "girls are chaste and turn their minds away [from desire], they remain so until the very end of old age, such that they are never defiled, nor do they even experience the pleasure of sexual intercourse..."

### CHAPTER II.

...under the name of [fruits], one can understand things that are new and tender. From this, regarding that passage in the thirty-ninth chapter of Job: *The ostrich leaves her eggs in the earth; perhaps you warm them in the dust?* <margin>Gregory, *Moralia in Job*, Book 31, chapter 5, otherwise 7.</margin> Blessed Gregory says in the thirty-first book of his *Moralia* <note>Gregory the Great’s *Moralia in Job* was a massive, influential commentary that interpreted the Book of Job through moral and mystical lenses.</note>: "What is expressed by eggs, if not offspring that are still tender, which must be cherished for a long time so they may be led to become living winged creatures?" Indeed, eggs are unfeeling in themselves, but once warmed, they are transformed into living birds. In the same way, it is certain that young listeners and children remain cold and unfeeling unless they are warmed by the diligent encouragement of their teacher. Therefore, so that they do not grow sluggish if left in their own insensitivity, they must be nurtured by the constant voice of teachers until they are able to live through understanding and "fly" through contemplation. To have left eggs on the earth is to provide no example of the heavenly life to one's children. <margin>Ibid. chapter 6, otherwise 7.</margin> *Perhaps you warm them in the dust*, as if He [God] were saying: "as I do, who warm them in the dust," because I ignite the souls of the little ones placed in the midst of sinners with the fire of my love.

Because, therefore, according to this opinion of Blessed Gregory, the fruit of good works is expressed by "eggs," <margin>Three conditions of a good work.</margin> so too through the **whiteness**, **smallness**, and **length** of eggs, three necessary conditions for good works are understood: that they be bright through innocence, small through humility, and long through perseverance. For God and His saints are often accustomed to rewarding such works miraculously, beyond the common law of nature.

<page-num>271</page-num>
<header>CHAPTER III.</header>

<margin>Understand that "it is testified" <note>original: *testatur*</note> is implied, or something similar; and "they saw the saints."</margin>
...writings, as famous men [testify], that the saints obtained from God special favors for us, which they had earned. And since it is clear that God performed many miracles through them during their lives that were beyond nature <note>original: *super naturam*; refers to the supernatural or miraculous.</note>, why should it not be believed in a similar way that—being certain of their predestination and without any harm to their humility—they confidently obtained from Him whom they loved most dearly those very things about which you are in doubt? For it is certain that many, by a special privilege, did not doubt that they were in a state of grace and would finally possess the gift of perseverance. Yet, we must not be so presumptuous regarding the privileges obtained by such saints that we think we will be entirely saved in the end just by showing them some small honor, regardless of how badly we have behaved in the meantime. Let such an understanding be far from the hearts of the faithful; rather, we ought to serve the Lord God and His saints with special devotion in good hope, while in the meantime making our calling sure through good works, according to <margin>2 Peter 1</margin> the commandment of Blessed Peter.

...in the affairs of the state <note>original: *reipublicæ*; referring here to the public business or the governance of the commonwealth.</note>. When, therefore, he entered the city of Speyer <note>original: *Spirensem*</note> with a considerable retinue, and a multitude of those proscribed and exiled from said city approached the horse upon which the king sat, they touched the trappings and equipment, and thus entered the city along with the prince. For it is the custom of Germany <note>original: *Germanię*</note> that those proscribed by cities, hoping to obtain grace through the prayers of a prince who is about to enter, join him as he enters a city. Later, once the principal officials have been gathered, the prince, having heard the reasons for their proscriptions, is accustomed to intercede for the defendants if he so pleases, or to remain silent if he prefers. 

Therefore, the city council having been summoned, the king wished first to hear the reasons for the offenses of all those who had entered the city under his protection. Various things were reported, including the grave crimes of various individuals, which nevertheless (to speak in common terms) were not considered "infamous" according to secular justice <note>original: *secularem iustitiam*</note>—such as theft, or robbery punishable by death (which is there avenged by the wheel <note>original: *rota*; a brutal form of capital punishment involving a wagon wheel.</note>), or heresy, or the abomination of the vice against nature <note>original: *vitij contra naturam*; a historical legal term for non-procreative sexual acts.</note>, nor similar things—but rather other crimes of homicide, wounding, discord, and the like. 

At length, however, the leading men of the city and friends from the adjacent regions interceded on behalf of a certain man born in Speyer who had entered the city along with the others. He was a man of no low birth, and they sought for him to be able to remain there safely from then on. However, as the pious prince wished to know the exact cause of this man's exile, it was stated—and truly so—that during a certain game he had blasphemed God not just once, but many times. Then, moved by zeal for the honor of God, the king replied that petitions should be offered for all the others, with this man alone excepted. "Others," he said, "dearest citizens, have sinned against men; I humbly ask that you be willing to spare such men. And behold, by the will of God, although she had previously been physically strong, the virgin immediately began to grow weak and take to her bed. By divine inspiration, she felt that she would soon be taken from this light <note>A common metaphor for departing the world of the living</note>.

### CHAPTER V.

When an ant-hill is disturbed, the ants are accustomed to diligently pick up their eggs and carry them back to the nest. In this, the great faithfulness which the ant has toward its own offspring <note>original: "fructum," literally fruit or offspring</note> is shown; while suffering persecution in external matters, it entrusts its eggs to safer places so they are not harmed. In this regard, the ant distances itself greatly from the negligence of the ostrich, which forgets its eggs and seems not to care what becomes of them. Regarding this, it is said in the thirty-ninth chapter of Job: *The ostrich leaves her eggs in the earth; she forgets that a foot may trample them, or a beast of the field may crush them.*

# THE ANT-HILL, BOOK IV.

...most [devoutly] they approach the office of the altar daily.

<margin>Two simple and chaste virgins, zealous for souls.</margin>
For there were two sisters by the same mother <note>original: *vterinæ ſorores* — sisters sharing the same womb</note>, beautiful virgins living at the same time as myself, in a house near the borders of the Diocese of Constance <note>A major bishopric in medieval Germany/Switzerland</note> toward the Adige <note>original: *Atheſim* — a river in Northern Italy</note>. The younger was named Anna, and the elder was called Margaret. They were born of peasant stock if one looks at the flesh, but they were noble in virtue if the goodness of their character is weighed. The younger was of such simplicity in worldly matters that I can scarcely recall seeing her equal. Indeed, in the art of counting—in which even small children (so to speak) are well-practiced—she did not know how to count well beyond ten. And yet, in those matters which pertain to God, the meaning of many homilies and whatever is necessary for the basics of a true Christian—such as the Lord’s Prayer, the Apostles' Creed, the Ten Commandments <note>original: *decalogo*</note>, and similar things—nothing was hidden from her. This was because, like a **clean animal** <note>A biblical reference to animals that "chew the cud," a common medieval metaphor for someone who "ruminates" or meditates deeply on scripture.</note>, her virginal heart meditated on such things day and night. The elder sister, however, in her natural wit and as far as could be seen from the outside, far surpassed her younger sister in her God-given character. When she first reached marriageable age, she endured many persecutions from a certain Christian who was a **noble in name only**, but in reality a tyrant. Seeing that she was beautiful in face and fit for childbearing <note>original: *prolificationi accommodam*</note>, he desired to join her in marriage as if she were a slave—though she was in fact free by status and by her family name—so that he might thereby amass more servants for himself. The devoted virgin resisted as much as she could, because, inspired by God at a tender age, she had dedicated her virginity to Him. The tyrant, on the other hand, lay in wait, disturbing the virgin’s home by frequently sending young men, so that on one occasion, had she not been divinely aided by fleeing the place, she would have been captured and bound by the officials of the aforementioned noble until she agreed to a marriage union.

### CHAPTER V.

Yet she persevered so constantly in her purpose of **chastity** <note>original: *castitatis*</note> that at last she was permitted to remain unmarried in her own **cottage** <note>original: *tugurij*</note>. This was situated in a certain **village** <note>original: *villagio*</note> in such deserted places and so near to the forests that it was commonly called "the end of bread" <note>original: *finis panis* — a nickname for a region so harsh that grain could not be grown for food.</note>. This was because not even barley can grow there as fodder for the beasts, owing to the cold of the eternal snowy mountains lying nearby. It happened one summer, on a certain feast day, that a **storm** <note>original: *tempestas*</note> so unexpectedly powerful rose up in the air near the village that the **virgin** <note>original: *virgo*</note> testified she had scarcely seen its like. It brought down through the torrent—which at other times used to flow modestly through the village—stones so massive that, by human estimation, it seemed the cottages of the poor would be overturned instantly by the rush of the floodwaters, and men would be suddenly killed by the stones and drowned.

<margin>The holy virgin turns away a stony storm that would have killed many through prayer and by holding up the image of the crucified Christ.</margin>
In this **calamity** <note>original: *calamitate*</note>, the virgin set little value on property or bodies, feeling compassion only for the souls of the country folk who were about to perish; she had seen them living at times with only slightly more reason than beasts. For she primarily feared that, dying from a sudden death without **contrition** <note>original: *contritio* — the theological state of being truly sorry for one's sins, necessary for salvation</note>, they would pay eternal punishments by divine judgment. Having seen these dangers while she stood at the door of her house, she ran with great speed to her cell, where she was accustomed to offer the support of her **prayers** <note>original: *orationum*</note> to the Creator while meditating before a certain carved **crucifix** <note>original: *crucifixum*</note> which she loved dearly. She seized it with the utmost haste and, returning to face the most horrible wind, held up the aforementioned crucifix and prayed with great groans:

# CHAPTER V.

<margin>She sees a sign by which she understands that the plague would also rage there.</margin>
...[where] she has had her home for many years now as an invalid. She is of necessity nourished by the alms of others in a holy life, but in worldly goods, she is poor beyond belief. When she was younger and very simple and upright—just as she is today—seeing that a **plague of epidemic** <note>original: *pestilentia epidimię*</note> was killing many in the neighborhood, she thought of moving her place of residence to a certain village where the infection of the air was not felt at that time. However, she was afraid to go there <note>original: *illô, id est, illuc*</note>, doubting whether she would perhaps have guardians for her **chastity** <note>original: *castitatis*</note> there, as many were laying snares for her. But one day, while she was at prayer, she saw a great bolt of lightning being sent into that same place, and suddenly it occurred to the innocent virgin that the disease of the epidemic was destined to devastate and consume many people there as well. For it happened afterward just as the outcome of the event proved; and as I piously believe, based on many other holy works and inspirations of this virgin, she was moved by a good spirit so that, by fostering good works in her **little nest** <note>original: *nidulo* — a continuation of the book's central metaphor comparing the home of a holy person to an ant's nest</note>, she might serve her Creator in peace.

*What do herbs and their fruits and juice signify? Concerning the wisdom to be learned from the wonders of God in wood and stones through images produced by nature.*

### CHAPTER VI.

The foods of **ants** are fruits and the juices of herbs, parts of which they also separate and carry back with them to the nest. In **sacred speech** <note>Theology or the Bible</note>, "fruits" sometimes designate works, and at other times the delight that follows true wisdom. Hence the Savior says: <margin>Matthew 7</margin> "By their fruits you shall know them." # THE ANT-HEAP, BOOK IV.

...as a vine I have yielded the sweetness of fragrance, and my flowers are the fruits of honor and integrity <note>original: *vitis fructificaui...* — a quotation from the Book of Ecclesiasticus (Sirach) 24:17, where Wisdom speaks of herself</note>. The soul glories in the taste of this fruit in the second chapter of the Song of Songs, where it says: "As the apple tree among the trees of the wood, so is my beloved among the sons. I sat under the shadow of him whom I desired, and his fruit was sweet to my throat." And in the third chapter of Proverbs: "Blessed is the man who finds wisdom, and he for whom prudence flows. Her acquisition is better than the trade of gold and silver; her fruits are first and most pure." For "The fruit of the righteous is a tree of life, and he who wins souls is wise," as seen in Proverbs chapter 11. By "herbs," knowledge is also designated; whence it is said in Job 38: "He shall bring forth green herbs," namely, God.

<margin>Gregory, Book 29 of the *Moralia*, chapter 14 (elsewhere 18).</margin>
Blessed Gregory says in the 29th book of his *Moralia*: "We sometimes take 'herb' to mean knowledge and the teaching of eternal greenness <note>In medieval theology, 'greenness' (*viriditas*) often symbolized spiritual life and vitality</note>, just as it is said through Jeremiah:

<margin>Jeremiah 14</margin>
The wild donkeys stood on the cliffs; they drew in the wind like dragons, and their eyes failed because there was no herb." In this place, then, what else do we understand by "green herbs" but the knowledge of holy doctrine or appropriate good works? Therefore, the deserted land is rained upon so that green herbs may be produced from it; for when the Gentile world received the rain of holy preaching, it germinated both the works of life and the words of doctrine. Thus, the **ants** eat from the fruits or the juice of herbs whenever any wise and faithful people receive some knowledge of serving the Creator with devotion from the things wonderfully created by God. For that Wisdom through which all things were created poured out her wisdom "upon all her works, and upon all flesh," as is said in the first chapter of Ecclesiasticus.

**THE THEOLOGIAN** <note>original: *THEOL.* for *Theologus*</note>: You ought to believe that all things from the highest [hinge] of things...

### CHAPTER VI.

...[created] by the authority of God <note>original: *cardine Deo creata* — literally "created on the hinge of God," implying His central role or command</note> for the prudent, who duly observe them as if they were certain tracks for hunting God and divine matters. For they are lamps lit for the acquisition of happiness, mirrors of divine wisdom, vessels filled with divine knowledge, fingers pointing out the highest good to us, books containing the wisdom of God, and like the servants or messengers of the supreme Lord. Hence, it is said against those who do not consider such things in God’s creatures in the thirteenth chapter of Wisdom: "All men are vain in whom the knowledge of God is not present, and who, from those things which are seen, could not recognize him who is; nor, by attending to the works, did they acknowledge who the craftsman was." <note>original: *Vani sunt omnes homines...* — quoting the Wisdom of Solomon 13:1</note> He who speaks in the first chapter of Romans is a witness to these things: "For the invisible things of God from the creation of the world are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made, even his eternal power and divinity; so that they are inexcusable," namely, the philosophers. But to the foolish, all these things are turned into a toxin and a poison through their abuse, according to that passage in the fourteenth chapter of Wisdom: "The creatures of God were made for hatred, and for a temptation to the souls of all men, and a snare for the feet of the foolish." <note>original: *Creaturæ Dei in odium factæ sunt...* — quoting the Wisdom of Solomon 14:11</note>

**THE SLACKER.** <note>original: *PIG.* — short for *Piger*, the "Lazy" or "Slacker" student character in Johannes Nider’s *Formicarius* (The Ant-Heap)</note> Give some specific examples.

**THE THEOLOGIAN.** Barely twelve years have elapsed since, not far from the city of Nuremberg in the Diocese of Bamberg, an apple tree grew in an open and common field, which remained in its vigor for many years, as follows. This tree, above all those we have heard of in our times, was of a wonderful condition. For at the beginning of summer, namely in the spring, it bloomed, grew leaves, and towards autumn produced apples after the manner of other trees. Furthermore, every year in the harshest and most inclement winter—always and only on the night of Christ's birth, when the Virgin of Virgins brought forth the Son of God while the flower of her integrity remained intact—it produced small green apples the size of a man's thumb <note>original: *artus vnius virilis* — literally "one male joint," likely referring to the length of a finger joint</note>...

produced [shoots the length] of a finger. Furthermore, at that time of year, the region is usually covered in deep snow for two months before and after, locked in frost, and swept by the most rigid winds; all the shrubs and trees suffer these same hardships during that same season. The wonder of the miracle was increased by the fact that the little apples <note>original: *pomella*</note> sprouted neither before nor after, but only on the aforementioned most sacred night <note>Christmas Eve</note>. For unlike other garden trees, it was not nourished with manure, the soil was not dug up around it with a hoe, nor was it protected by any fence. For this reason, every year, many trustworthy witnesses among the <margin>perhaps of the aforementioned</margin> officials from the city of Nuremberg and the surrounding areas of the Diocese of Bamberg used to hurry there and keep watch the entire night to verify the truth of the matter. 

Indeed, there is a tree similar in every way in another location within the said diocese. I myself saw a little apple from that same tree presented in the town of Forchheim, in that same diocese, for the Master General of our Order <note>The Dominican Order</note>, Bartholomew Texier, to see. Among the abuses of this world, the greatest alone is the stubbornness of an old man who, being very near to death, does not dread the arrival of death; who, placed as if at the door of this world, looks outside, yet does not attend to his departure from this present life, nor does he * consider his entry into the future life. For there are three messengers of death: accident, sickness, and old age. <note>original: "Tres sunt enim nuncij mortis, casus, infirmitas, & senectus."</note> Accident announces doubtful things, sickness announces grave things, and old age announces certain things. Accident announces a hidden death, sickness a visible death, and old age a present death. From the uncertainty of death, fear should follow; from the gravity of sickness, pain; and from the certainty of old age, not stubbornness, but affliction and humility.

<margin>3. Cassiodorus.</margin>

### CHAPTER VII.

...he would have considered it a sin to omit. The generous stipend <note>original: "stipendium"</note> that he received from the Duke of Austria for his lectureship, he spent entirely on the construction, reformation, and devout decoration of poor convents out of reverence for the Virgin of God. Whenever it was his turn to lecture among the doctors on Saturdays <note>In the medieval tradition, Saturday was the day specifically dedicated to the Virgin Mary.</note>, whatever the theme of the text happened to be, he so aptly turned the middle of the lecture toward the praise of Mary that those who heard him were frequently amazed. At those times, he often burst into such tears of devotion that he could hardly form intelligible words for the school because of his weeping. In the aforementioned prayers, which he completed in great number every day, and in the collects <note>Brief, formal prayers used in the liturgy of the Mass.</note> of the masses he most devoutly celebrated, he gave his whole mind as much as possible to the often-mentioned Virgin. Indeed, one would hardly see anyone seized by "heroic love" <note>original: "amore hereos" – a medieval medical and literary term for an intense, obsessive romantic passion or "lovesickness."</note> for a worldly girl serve her as diligently as he served the most blessed Virgin. Nor in these things did he neglect the duties proper to the Virgin’s Son <note>Referring to Christ.</note>, or the obligations of his own body or his religious order. For until the very end of his life, which was around his eighty-fourth year, he devoted himself to abstinence and fasting; he never slept in a bed, but in a state of mortification <note>original: "maceracio" – likely referring to sleeping on a hard floor or a rough mat as a form of penance.</note> within the convent; he wore wool against his flesh; and he was so devoted to silence that he was never or very rarely seen conversing with anyone, unless he was occupied in the office of the Vicariate of his order, or at mealtime outside the refectory. But even then, by the virtue of <term>eutrapelia</term> <note>The Aristotelian virtue of "well-turned" or pleasant conversation; the ability to be witty and charming in a balanced, virtuous way.</note> he was more gracious to everyone than can be believed. If he moved from one desk in the library to another, or if he was entering or leaving it, or if he was passing toward or from his chair in the schools, in that tiny interval of time—so as not to lose even a small moment—he would repeatedly whisper the Angelic Salutation <note>The "Ave Maria" or "Hail Mary."</note>. Therefore, as the day of the <term>Nativity of the Blessed Virgin</term><note>September 8th.</note> approached, he devoutly confessed to me sacramentally in his cell. Immediately afterward, he prepared himself for the <term>Sacrament of the Eucharist</term> by walking on foot to the chapel of Saint Martin, where he heard Mass and received communion. When the Mass was finished, he asked for the <term>holy oil</term><note>The Sacrament of the Anointing of the Sick, formerly called Extreme Unction.</note> and received it devoutly. Then, walking back to his cell, he was unable to walk further. But on the following day, specifically on the very feast of the Nativity of the Virgin, with his sight and hearing intact, using clear reason, and in the best of hope, he began his <term>death-struggle</term><note>original: "agonysare." In this context, it refers to the final spiritual and physical battle before death.</note>. Sensing his final agony, he broke out into <term>Angelic Salutations</term><note>The "Hail Mary" (Ave Maria) prayer, based on the angel Gabriel's greeting to Mary.</note> according to his custom, and continued them until he was unable to close his lips completely; for with half-closed lips, he formed the words of the angel by stammering. He thus made an end of his life so graciously that we who were present saw no sign of horror in the man now dead; rather, the cheerfulness of his face and his bearing generated a joy of devotion in all who stood by.

<header>CHAPTER VIII.</header>

### *What the grains of barley or wheat signify, and how God sometimes heavily punishes grave sins today with lightning, or temporal death, or dispossession.*

<margin>chapter 19, or 22.</margin>
They select grains of wheat, but they care little for barley and nothing at all for chaff. Through the wheat, the chosen of God, or their good and high works, are designated; but through the barley, inferior works are meant, and through the chaff, evil things. Regarding that passage in Job 37, *the cloud desires the wheat* <note>original: "frumentum desiderat nubes"</note>, the Blessed Gregory says in the twenty-seventh book of his *Moralia* <note>Referring to the *Moralia in Job*, a massive and influential work of scriptural exegesis by Pope Gregory the Great (c. 540–604).</note>: "Who are all the chosen, if not the wheat of God to be stored away in heavenly barns? These now endure the chaff on the <term>threshing floor</term><note>The *area* or threshing floor is a traditional metaphor for the Church on earth, where the "wheat" (the saved) and "chaff" (the damned) live together until the final judgment.</note>, because in this purification of the holy Church they bear the contrary ways of the reprobate, until the internal <margin>a. b. here. original: "this."</margin> farmer separates these with the <term>winnowing fan</term><note>A tool used to toss grain into the air so the wind blows away the lighter chaff, leaving the heavy grain behind; a common symbol for divine judgment.</note> of judgment, and receiving his chosen ones into the celestial dwellings like now-clean grains, he delivers the chaff to eternal fires." 

<margin>Matthew 3</margin>
Hence it is well said through John [the Baptist]: *His winnowing fan is in his hand, and he will thoroughly cleanse his floor, and gather the wheat into his barn; but the chaff he will burn with unquenchable fire.* But this wheat, until it comes to the perfection of its fruits, waits for the rains of the clouds so that it may grow, because the mind of the good is infused by the words of those preaching, lest it be dried out from the moisture of <term>charity</term><note>In this context, *caritas* or divine love, which keeps the soul "hydrated" against the "heat" of worldly temptations.</note> by the sun of carnal desires. The heavenly farmer saw this wheat rising in the world and desiring the clouds when he said: *The harvest is indeed great, but the laborers are few; pray therefore the Lord of the harvest to send laborers into his harvest.*

Therefore, those who are called "wheat" in one place and "harvests" in another, or who are called "clouds" here and "workers" there, are so named because holy preachers are both clouds and workers: they are clouds through their doctrine, and workers through their way of life. They are clouds because they pour forth words, and workers because they do not stop practicing what they preach. And again, regarding that passage in Job 31: *Instead of wheat, let thistles grow for me; and instead of barley, thorns* <note>original: "Pro frumento oriatur mihi tribulus, & pro hordeo spina"</note>, the Blessed Gregory says in his twenty-second book: "In the wheat, the spiritual work that refreshes the mind is symbolized; but in the barley, the management of earthly matters is represented." In this earthly management, while we are often forced to serve the weak and the worldly, we prepare sustenance as if for beasts of burden; and the very practice of our works, like the nature of barley, contains something of a mixture of chaff.

The priest fell to the ground with his clothes scorched; lying there, he finally realized he was alive and that his companion had died. From that time forward, he cherished chaste virgins, preached more cautiously thereafter, and became a devoted protector and supporter of all religious persons.

# BOOK IV OF THE ANTHILL

...having their residence in that same city. It occurred to the citizens and the city council, and they decided that the wall surrounding the city should be reinforced by a new outer wall <note>Latin: *antemurale*, a defensive rampart built in front of the main city wall.</note> around the entire circuit of the whole city like a kind of cloak. This work was to be paid for in sections by each of the associations of craftsmen, which <margin>German: everywhere Guilds or perhaps crafts.</margin> they call ***Zunftas*** <note>The Latinized version of the German word *Zünfte*, meaning guilds.</note>. 

But since great expenses were required for this work, the town itself pressured all the monasteries and convents—both those of the mendicant <note>Orders that lived by begging and were traditionally exempt from certain taxes, such as the Franciscans and Dominicans.</note> orders and those that held property—to pay for a portion of the walls according to their rate, just as the ***Zunftas*** were required to pay. And so that each would know through what length of space the wall ought to be built by them, certain marks were painted on the main wall opposite the outer wall to be erected for each of the guilds and monasteries, so that it might be clearly seen in which place the boundary and end of each payer was located. 

The city itself, or rather the town’s administration, hired the craftsmen, the materials for the wall, and the workers for that project, and initially paid the expenses for all of these; but afterward, it received the ready money from each group. Seeing this, our brothers <note>The Dominicans, the order to which the author, Johannes Nider, belonged.</note>, and those of the Order of Friars Minor <note>The Franciscans.</note>, and the Hermits of Saint Augustine—since these convents are located there—claimed that they were poor and unable to pay for such a work, even for their share. Indeed, they cited canonical decrees <note>Laws of the Church which often granted tax exemptions to religious houses for secular infrastructure.</note> against being coerced into this, but they achieved nothing among those unrefined people. 

The outer wall was therefore built, and the signs were first placed and the boundaries fixed for the citizens, and for the rent-producing or property-owning monasteries as was said before; then for the portion of the three mendicant orders; and finally for the ***Zunftas*** of the seculars or craftsmen. And after the work was almost perfectly finished in its circuit, it is believed that by the divine and just judgment of God, the outer wall collapsed all the way to its foundation in a single hour,

In that same city, at that same time, several others were divinely punished with physical death. When the brothers refused to give up the location of the corner, the aforementioned **consuls** <note>The city councilors or magistrates.</note> of the city appointed themselves as judges; being biased in their own cause, they issued a judgment against the convent and in favor of the wine-growers regarding the said corner. When the wine-growers were called together, one of them was lowered into the well by a rope to retrieve the pitcher, but by divine permission, he was immediately and suddenly suffocated there and died.

Furthermore, in our own time, a certain **innkeeper** <note>original: *caupo*; an owner of a tavern or lodging house.</note> in southern **Franconia** <note>A historic region in south-central Germany.</note> was punished for his malice no less justly by the permitting judgment of God. For there lives today a famous **robber** <note>original: *prædo*; in this context, a "social bandit" or knightly highwayman rather than a mere thief.</note> named **Wolfenmayser**, who, although he is lawless and has been a plague to many, is nevertheless accustomed to maintaining certain standards of mercy and justice toward those he captures. For he never binds a captive in stocks or thongs, never subjects them to **interrogations** <note>original: *quæstionibus*; a common euphemism for judicial torture.</note>, nor inflicts corporal punishment. Instead, if he finds ready money on someone, he takes it by force, yet he leaves enough for the victim’s expenses to reach the next inn. If someone he detains has a horse, a cloak, clothing, or better weapons than the robber or his men possess, he takes them by way of exchange, giving his own or his men’s cheaper items in their place—the worse for the better, to be sure—yet in such a way that he never allows anyone to leave his presence naked. As a Christian himself, though a sinner, he loves the faithful of the Catholic faith in his words and hates the enemies of the faith; he devoutly hears the solemnities of the Mass daily on bended knees whenever he can, though at times he is no less focused on his loot.

For a long time, the city of **Rothenburg** <note>Rothenburg ob der Tauber, a prominent imperial city in Franconia.</note> pursued this man with arms as a public enemy, especially of their **commonwealth** <note>original: *reipublicæ*.</note>, but he has evaded them all even unto this day. # CHAPTER VIII.

When the **innkeeper** <note>original: *caupo tabernarius*; a host of a public house or tavern.</note> of a public lodging had received a **courier** <note>original: *baiulum*; often a porter or carrier of goods.</note> who appeared fearful and pale, he asked the **messenger** <note>original: *cursor*</note> what trouble he was having. To him, the messenger said in secret: "I know that our enemy **Wolfenmayler** <note>spelled Wolfenmayser on the previous page; a known highwayman or "social bandit."</note> is nearby and frequently uses the roads for ambushes. I am carrying money for my masters, who are citizens; I beg you to swear an oath and keep faith with me—do not hand me over, but rather direct me on my way so that I do not fall into the hands of the enemy." To this, the innkeeper replied: "Rest easy, for this very night I will show you a safe way to escape." The innocent man trusted the traitor, and in the morning toward daybreak, he set out on his journey with his host, the innkeeper. Yet that same night, the innkeeper had secretly sent word through a messenger to the aforementioned robber, telling him to come without delay in the morning to a prearranged spot on the path, where he would find a sufficient prize.

Therefore, in the morning, the robber found the innkeeper with the messenger. He forced the messenger to throw down the money he was carrying for his masters, and the innkeeper described the messenger's cargo so explicitly that the messenger saw clearly he had been betrayed. He obeyed the robber’s command unwillingly and groaned in spirit. Then the robber approached the traitor, threw his arms around the man's neck, and said to the despoiled messenger: "Look here! This man betrayed you to me against the natural laws of hospitality. He is truly worthy of hanging. Choose one of two things: either he shall hang you with a **noose** <note>original: *laqueo*</note>, or you shall **hang him** <note>original: *furcabis*; literally "to place on the fork" or gallows.</note>, and afterward you shall be free." The messenger was at first terrified by this choice, but in order to save his own life, he chose to hang the traitor with the noose. 

Finally, the robber said to the man he had robbed: "You have lost your money because I am plundering my enemies; do not fear, you are not at fault, but rather the traitor who has now paid the penalty for his malice. I will therefore write a letter for you and seal it, in which I will excuse you to your fellow citizens and write clearly how this matter was handled." Thus, he gave the messenger some money for his expenses, as was his custom, wrote the letter of excuse for him as he had promised, and sent him away unharmed.

If seeds are damp or stained with mud, the ants dry them so that they become parched and arid. For by the "seeds," our works are signified; but by the "moisture and mud," the infection and injury of our works are designated. These things God does not love, but the devil is accustomed to love and seek out; wherefore it is said concerning this in Job 40: *Under the shadow he sleeps*, <note>original: *Behemoth scilicet*; referring to the biblical beast, interpreted here as a demon.</note> namely Behemoth, *in the secrecy of the reed, in moist places.* The blessed Gregory says in the thirty-third book of his *Moralia*: "What else is designated by 'moist places' but lust? <note>original: *luxuria*; in medieval Latin, this specifically refers to carnal lust or excessive indulgence.</note> Just as pride is expressed by the 'reed' and the glory of pride, is not the lust of the body expressed by 'moist places'?" Indeed, there are two vices that rule over the human race with great cruelty: one of the spirit, and the other of the flesh. For pride lifts up the spirit, while lust corrupts the flesh. Thus, the ancient enemy, either casting the human race down through pride or pressing it down through lust, *sleeps in the secrecy of the chamber and in moist places*; because he holds damned man under the power of his dominion either through the pride of the spirit or through the corruption of the flesh. Indeed, he possesses some in both: for when the spirit of pride elevates them, no shame for their corruption turns them back from the <term>swelling</term> <note>original: *tumore*; a metaphor for the 'inflation' or 'puffiness' of pride.</note> of their own height.

# THE ANTHILL, BOOK IV.

->*That no one should ground themselves in earthly things. Concerning those forewarned of death by divine oracles, and concerning why the laity should not seek vengeance against the clergy.*<-

### CHAPTER X.

**A**nts skillfully collect grains, hulling them <note>original: "decorticant." The author is describing the biological observation that ants bite off the radicle of seeds to prevent them from germinating in the nest.</note> so that they do not sprout, and hide them away in secret. In this, the wonderful sagacity of this animal is seen. For if it did not hull the grain, the power of sprouting would remain; the grain would send a root downward into the earth and, growing upward, it would lift itself too high by germinating and turning green. In doing so, it would be destitute of all nutritional value <note>original: "virtute." Nider uses this word to mean both the physical "strength" or "essence" of the grain and the moral "virtue" of a person.</note> and would provide no food for life, but would instead nullify almost all the ant's past labor. Other animals, lacking this industry, seem foolish in comparison to the ant, because they collect whole grains in heaps without cutting them; they think they are feeding on 

<margin>Luke 1 <note>A reference to the *Magnificat* (Luke 1:53): "He has filled the hungry with good things, and the rich he has sent away empty."</note></margin>
solid food, but being rich, they are sent away empty. But this ant, providently avoiding this, though hungry, shall be filled with good things. While other little beasts think themselves rich, they are sent away as if empty. Hence, through the foresight of this tiny animal, simple and upright men are aptly symbolized. These are the ones who gather the "grains of virtues" from the lives of their neighbors; by following these virtues in their own work, they hide them in a secret place so that they do not begin to sprout before the eyes of others. If they were to sprout, the men might seek vainglory, and thereby lose their virtue and their reward in this world—just as fools are known to do, of whom it is said in the fifth chapter of Job: *I saw a fool with a firm root, and immediately I cursed his beauty.* <note>Job 5:3.</note> Regarding this, Blessed Gregory <note>Gregory the Great (c. 540–604), whose *Moralia in Job* was a standard medieval commentary.</note> says in

### BOOK IV OF THE ANTHILL

<margin>Thomas [Aquinas], Summa Theologiae, Part 1-2, final question, article 9.</margin>
Conversely, some who began with a bad start conclude with a good end. This gift [of final perseverance] is of such great dignity and difficulty, according to the teachings of the Holy Doctor <note>St. Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the influential Dominican philosopher and theologian.</note>, that it does not fall under any person's own merit, even though it can be piously and continuously obtained through prayer for oneself; this is because merit relies on justice, whereas prayer or petition relies on divine mercy. And we have various examples of this in our own day.

<margin>Emperor Rupert, deferring Extreme Unction out of a vain superstition, was almost overcome by a demon as he lay dying.</margin>
In our own time, there was a King of the Romans named Rupert <note>Rupert of the Palatinate (1352–1410), who was elected King of the Romans (the title for the ruler of the Holy Roman Empire before being crowned Emperor by the Pope) in 1400.</note>, whom we mentioned above in the third chapter of this book. Before his election, he was merciful in both deed and name, and after long and holy works, he fell into a certain lethal sickness and almost died defeated by a demon. For he fell into a grave illness, and although he had received the sacrament of the Eucharist, he craftily withdrew himself every day to avoid receiving the holy oil of anointing <term>Extreme Unction: The sacrament of the Anointing of the Sick, which in the Middle Ages was often associated with the final moments of life.</term>. He had swallowed—from where I do not know—a diabolical instinct (as it seemed) by which some most superstitiously believe that they must altogether depart this life after receiving a sacrament of this kind. 

Therefore, the prince delayed receiving the sacrament because of the danger of death. But doctors of divine and human law <note>Theologians and lawyers.</note>, whom he always loved, exhorted the man with words and persuaded him not to <margin>perhaps: defer</margin> *stop* <note>The original Latin text uses the word "defineret" (to finish/stop), but the marginal note suggests "f. differret," indicating a likely scribal error and that "defer" was the intended meaning.</note> such a healthy antidote for both soul and body.

At last, they achieved their goal through the smile of divine grace. When the prince was being anointed in the presence of learned clerics, and as the prayers which speak of the health of both the "inner" and "outer" man <note>A common medieval way of referring to the soul (inner) and the body (outer).</note> were multiplied, he said quite cheerfully: "In truth, if I had known this sacrament was so powerful for both, as I now hear, I would have requested it most devotedly long ago."
