### *The moral significance of winter and summer. On avoiding sloth, and why we should not be terrified by the sudden death of good people who have led a virtuous life.*

## CHAPTER XII.

In winter, ants rest and enjoy the food they collected during the summer. Thus, Proverbs 30 says: "The ants are a weak people, who prepare their food in the harvest." <note>original: *Formicæ populus infirmus, qui præparat in messe cibum sibi.*</note> By "winter," a time when it is not possible to sow or plow, the future life of blessedness <note>The afterlife or heaven, where labor ceases.</note> is signified. For this reason, the Savior forewarned his followers when speaking of the Day of Judgment in Matthew 24, saying: "Pray that your flight may not be in winter or on the Sabbath." 
<margin>Jerome on Matthew chapter 24.</margin>
As Blessed Jerome says regarding that passage: in the first case, the severity of the cold prevents one from traveling to the wilderness or hiding in the mountains and deserts; in the second case, traveling would be a transgression of the religious law.

By "summer," however, when it is time for reaping, working, and sowing, our present life of labor is understood. This is why Solomon says in Proverbs 6: "Go to the ant, O sluggard, and consider her ways, and learn wisdom; she prepares her food in the summer, and gathers in the harvest what she may eat." And again in the same place: "If you are diligent, your harvest will come like a fountain, and poverty will flee far from you." Conversely,

The terror of sudden death—when a wicked life has preceded it—is, quite literally, the most "terrible of all terrors" in this life;

<margin>To whom sudden death is to be feared.</margin>
it is of such people that it is said in Job 21: "They spend their days in prosperity, and in a point of time they go down to hell." <note>original: *Ducunt in bonis dies suos, & in puncto ad inferna deſcēdunt.* A reference to Job 21:13.</note> Such a man was he who said to himself in Luke 12: "Soul, you have many good things laid up for many years; rest, eat, drink, and be merry." <margin>Augustine, *On Christian Discipline*, Chapter 2.</margin>

### CHAPTER XII.

<margin>Augustine, *The City of God*, Book 1, Chapter 11.</margin>
...for the pagans used to argue against the Christians: "Many have been consumed by a foul variety of many kinds of deaths." <note>original: *Multi multarum mortium fœda varietate consumpti sunt.* The pagans were mocking Christians who died in the Sack of Rome (410 AD), suggesting their God did not protect them from gruesome ends.</note> Augustine responds: "If this is to be borne with difficulty, it is a burden common to all who have been procreated into this life. This I know: no one has died who was not eventually going to die. The end of life makes a long life and a short life the same thing. What does it matter by what kind of death this life is ended, when he for whom it ends is not forced to die again? When, however, innumerable deaths in a way threaten every mortal under the daily accidents of this life—as long as it is uncertain which of them will come—I ask whether it is better to suffer one by dying, or to fear them all by living? But it is one thing that the sense of the flesh flees in weak fear, and another thing that the reason of the mind, carefully unfolded, proves. Death is not to be thought of as bad if a good life has preceded it; for nothing makes death bad except what follows death. Therefore, those who are necessarily going to die should not care much about what happens to make them die, but rather where they are forced to go by dying." Thus he speaks. For you ought to note that the delay of death holds more pain than death itself, and to fear death is more cruel than death itself. Whence Ovid says in his *Book of Epistles*:

<margin>Ovid in the letter of Ariadne to Theseus.</margin>

**U**LTIMATELY, in this fifth book, it remains to conclude our work by discussing witches <note>original: *maleficis*. While this can mean "evildoers" generally, in Nider’s 15th-century context, it specifically refers to those practicing harmful magic or witchcraft.</note> and their deceptions, categorized under the various properties of ants. Now, ants are diverse in their colors: for some are black, others red, and others pale. Through the colors of such creatures, the various conditions of vices can be understood; although these animals are good in themselves, as are all of God’s creatures. For just as through whiteness and the brightness of garments—according to the Blessed Gregory—the purity and cleanliness of virtues are represented, so too through colors that deviate from whiteness, to a greater or lesser degree, the impurity of vices is usually understood, as sacred testimony declares. Hence it is that the Blessed John, in the sixth chapter of the Apocalypse <note>The Book of Revelation</note>, saw one black horse among four different colors of horses. **THE SLUGGARD:** I desire to know first in how many ways, and in what manner, witches, the superstitious, and those like them are ruled, ridden, and driven mad by demons—who, I do not doubt, are varied in their vices and blacker than coals in their malice, according to that passage in Lamentations 4 <note>original: *Threnorum iiii*</note>: *Their faces are blackened more than coals, and they are not recognized in the streets.*

**THE THEOLOGIAN:** The human mind, weighed down by the mass of the body in the exile of this life and trapped in its prison-house, is deluded by many kinds of phantasms <note>mental images or hallucinations</note>, about which we will speak in what follows. However, as far as is sufficient for the present, three types of rare and wonderful appearances of the internal or external senses can occur.

<margin>Three ways in which wonders are seen.</margin>
For some, while awake, see wonders out of divine grace; others through defects of the brain; and others from the cunning of the demon. Through the first, certain prophets are established; through the second, those known as "maniacs" are deceived; and through the third, many are deluded by demonic influence.

...having said the aforementioned things, he recited what follows. For he named to us a certain soldier of the Rhine <note>original: *Rheni*; referring to the Rhineland region of Germany</note> well known to him, whose son was living at that time. This soldier had always stood out among almost all the nobles of Lower Germany <note>original: *Alemaniæ*</note> as being quite fearless in matters of war; however, because of his courage or strength, he often waged or suffered serious wars with others. Because of these conflicts, he was accustomed to ride to locations convenient for him not always by day, but during the night.

Therefore, one night, having taken his servants with him, he wished to ride through the forest near the Rhine, and he entered its edge. But before they reached the end of the woods, beyond which lay a wide field, he sent a servant ahead—as is the custom of those who fear ambushes—to see if there were any traps in the field. Since the moon was shining and the stars were bright, these things could be seen. When the servant explored his assignment through the branches of the trees, he saw a quite marvelous army approaching on horses across the length of the field.

Having seen this, he reported what he had observed to the soldier, who said: "Let us stand still for a little while, because it is likely that others will follow as a rear guard for this army. We will hurry toward them, and we shall discover whether those who went before are enemies or friends; nor shall we fear a few."

Then, after a short delay had passed, the soldier left the forest with his men and came into the field; he saw no one except a certain rider sitting on a horse, leading another horse by hand and following his companions at a distance. # CHAPTER I.

<margin>Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas (c. 1225–1274), the most influential medieval theologian.</note> in his commentary on the 4th book of the Sentences, distinction 45, question 1, article 1, Chapter 16.</margin>
...his words, because they are heavy with meaning. "According to the disposition of divine providence," he says, "sometimes <term>separated souls</term> <note>original: *animæ separatæ*; souls that have left the body after death</note> emerge from their hidden dwellings and present themselves to the sight of men, just as Augustine proves in his book *On Care to be Taken for the Dead*, and he provides examples of the good, such as the saints in heaven. And it can also be believed that this sometimes happens with the damned; that they are permitted to appear to the living for the instruction and terror of men, or even to seek <term>suffrages</term> <note>original: *suffragia*; prayers, masses, or alms offered by the living to shorten a soul's time in purgatory</note> regarding those who are held in purgatory. This is clear through many examples in the fourth book of the *Dialogues* of Blessed Gregory <note>Pope Gregory the Great (d. 604), whose "Dialogues" contain many famous ghost stories used to teach moral lessons.</note>. For the glorified saints can appear to us when they wish, but others only when God permits. This is because the latter are so weighed down by their punishments that they grieve more for their own misery than they care to appear to the living. And although sometimes the souls of the saints or the damned are truly present where they appear, it is not to be believed that this always happens. Sometimes apparitions of this kind occur—either while sleeping or while awake—through the operation of good or evil spirits for the instruction or the deception of the living. Just as living men also sometimes appear to others and say many things to them in their dreams, even though it is certain those men are not actually present, as Augustine proves through many examples in his book *On Care to be Taken for the Dead*." Thus far from Thomas. <margin>chapter 11.</margin>

Ants that build their homes outside the wilderness near humans or beasts often suffer devastations. For sometimes by human curiosity, sometimes by the trampling of cattle, now by the investigation of dogs, now even by the eating of birds, and by other various disturbances in the world—or those nesting near the world—they are troubled. It happens to them just like that grain which fell by the wayside, and the birds came and ate it (Matthew 13). "For the evil one comes"—that is, the devil, the <term>gloss</term> <note>original: *glossa*; a standard medieval commentary on the Bible often written in the margins or between lines of text.</note> says—"and snatches away what was sown in his heart." This is the field that was sown by the wayside; so Truth itself, Christ, explains it. We must remember in this context the allegorical saying of Blessed Gregory in the 31st book of his *Moralia* (cited above in Book IV, Chapter 5), where he says regarding this: "The ostrich forgets that the foot may crush the eggs, or the beast of the field may break them" <note>This refers to Job 39:15, where the ostrich is described as a negligent parent.</note>. What, he asks, is meant by the "foot," if not the passage of human activity? What is the "field," if not a sign for this world? Of which the Lord says in the Gospel: "The field is the world." What is meant by the "beast," if not the ancient enemy <note>original: *antiquus hostis*; a common title for the devil.</note>? Who, lying in wait for the spoils of this world, is daily satisfied by human death.

<margin>
How everyone should fortify themselves against the snares of the devil.
</margin>
Through these ants who foolishly place their home near enemies, those people can be understood who do not diligently fortify their own home and dwelling against the snares of the devil with ecclesiastical ceremonies. For <term>holy water</term> <note>original: *aqua benedicta*</note> ought to be sprinkled in the dwellings of the faithful every Sunday (as the <term>exorcism</term> <note>Here referring to the formal prayer used to bless the water and salt, which commands evil spirits to depart.</note> itself notes), and <term>exorcised salt</term> <note>original: *sal exorcizatum*; salt blessed to act as a spiritual preservative and deterrent against evil.</note> should be faithfully taken then; and each of the faithful should mark themselves and their belongings with the sign of the cross in the morning and often, and keep themselves free from sins, especially grave ones, and often invoke their own <term>guardian angel</term> <note>original: *angelum proprium*</note> for protection with divine help.

In this aforementioned work, although the malice of the demon gained something (for some said: "Behold, when we walked the wide and old path <note>a biblical metaphor for a worldly or less disciplined life</note>, these things never happened to us"), nevertheless, by the grace of God, the devil lost more in this "game" than he gained. At this, the brother began to shout, "Thieves, thieves, help me, everyone!" The bell-ringer <note>original: *campanarius*</note>, who was sleeping in the same house, heard this and understood the situation; he lit a light and went to the one shouting, finding him in a state of shock. He saw the clothes with which the brother had been covered scattered <note>original: *distincta*; the marginal note suggests the intended meaning was *distracta* or *dispersa*</note> through the room by the spirit. However, they could not find the brother’s scapular <note>a part of the monastic habit consisting of a long piece of cloth worn over the shoulders</note> anywhere, until they finally spotted a very small hole in the wall. Into that hole, the spirit had hidden the scapular, which was rolled and balled up very tightly. After one year, or thereabouts, that phantom went away.

<margin>An illicit way of identifying a spell.</margin>
Someone who has been harmed in their person or property comes to a sorceress, seeking to know who did the deed. Then the sorceress would repeatedly pour molten lead into water until, by the work of a demon, some image appeared in the lead. Once the image was seen, the sorceress asked the inquirer: "In what part do you wish your sorcerer to be harmed, so that you may recognize him by that same wound?" When the seeker chose a location, the sorceress immediately inflicted a stab or wound with a knife into that part of the image reflecting in the lead. She indicated the place where the guilty party could be found, though she never revealed the name; yet experience testifies that the sorcerer was found injured in every way, just as his leaden image had been.

# CHAPTER IV.

Now it is clear that the mercy and wisdom of Almighty God—which <margin>Wisdom 8:1</margin> reaches mightily from one end to the other and disposes all things sweetly <note>original: "sapientia, quæ attingit à fine vsque ad finem fortiter, disponit... suauiter"; this is a direct quote from the biblical Book of Wisdom, emphasizing that God uses even evil for a good purpose.</note>—arranges even the sorceries <term>maleficia</term> <note>Harmful magic or "evil-doing" intended to injure others through supernatural means.</note> of these most wicked men and demons so graciously that, while they seek to diminish and weaken the kingdom and faith of Christ through their treachery, they actually strengthen and root that faith more firmly in the hearts of many. ### CHAPTER IV.

...[concupiscence]. We have heard in our own times of men being so inflamed through sorcerers <note>original: "maleficos"; individuals believed to use supernatural means to cause harm or manipulate others.</note> toward the love of other men's wives, and women toward men not their own, that they could be forced to stop by no amount of shame, beatings, words, or deeds. Conversely, we have sometimes experienced such hatreds being stirred up between the two sexes joined by the sacrament of marriage through sorceries <note>original: "maleficia"</note>, and similarly chillings <note>original: "infrigidationes"; a medieval term for magical impotence or the "cooling" of sexual desire.</note> of the reproductive power <note>original: "potentiae generatiuae"</note>, so that they were able to have no place for either the rendering or the demanding of the marital debt <note>The "marital debt" is the theological concept that spouses owe one another sexual intimacy as a duty of the marriage contract.</note> for the sake of offspring. Since, therefore, love and hatred exist in the soul—and according to all the authorities of your profession, a demon cannot enter the soul—it is useful to know what here is truth or falsehood. For the mind is ensnared by womanly love, as if by birdlime <note>original: "visco"; a sticky substance spread on branches to trap birds, used here as a metaphor for the trap of obsession.</note>, and when hatred is rooted, like a most rigid storm, a person grows cold toward the favor of their neighbor, and thus reason cannot proceed toward meritorious labor.

*THEOLOGIAN.* Although according to the harmonious doctrine of our teachers, a demon cannot act immediately upon the intellect or the will of a human being, nevertheless, according to these same teachers, he is able to act upon the body and upon the powers tied to the body, by God's permission, whether they be internal or external senses. Hence in Job 2, God says to the demon: "Behold, he is in your hand"—that is, Job is in your power, namely as far as the body is concerned—"but preserve his soul." You touch upon three difficulties in your question: namely, how <term>philocaptio: a magical ensnarement of love or erotic obsession</term>, and hatred in the will, and sorcery in the reproductive power are caused.

<margin>Carnal love arises from three causes, and examples of each.</margin>
Regarding love-binding, therefore, or the inordinate love of one sex for the other, you should know that it can arise from a threefold cause. Sometimes from the mere carelessness of the eyes; sometimes from the temptation of demons alone; and sometimes indeed from the sorcery of necromancers <note>original: "necromanticorum"</note> and demons together. # CHAPTER IV.

...we have heard in our own times of men being so inflamed by **sorcerers** <note>original: "maleficos"; practitioners of harmful magic</note> with love for women other than their own wives, and likewise women for men who were not their husbands, that they could not be forced to stop by any amount of shame, beatings, words, or deeds. On the other hand, we have sometimes seen such hatreds stirred up between those joined by the sacrament of marriage through sorcery, and likewise **chillings of the generative power** <note>original: "infrigidationes generatiuae potentiae"; a legal and theological term for magically induced impotence or the inability to consummate a marriage</note>, such that they could neither fulfill nor demand the "marital debt" <note>A medieval term for the obligation of spouses to engage in sexual intercourse for the purpose of procreation or to avoid sin</note> for the sake of children. Since, therefore, love and hatred exist in the soul, and according to all those of your profession, a demon is unable to enter the soul, I wish to know what is true or false here. For the mind is ensnared by womanly love as if by **birdlime** <note>original: "visco"; as previously defined, a sticky glue used to trap birds</note>, and when hatred takes root, like a most rigid storm, a person grows cold toward the favor of their neighbor, and thus reason is unable to move forward toward any meritorious work.

**THEOLOGIAN:** Although according to the unanimous doctrine of our teachers, a demon cannot act directly upon the intellect or the will of a human, they nevertheless—by God's permission—can act upon the body and the powers tied to the body, whether these are internal or external senses. Hence, in **Job 2** <note>Job 2:6</note>, God says to the demon: "Behold, he is in your hand"—that is, Job is in your power—"specifically regarding his body; however, preserve his soul." In your question, you touch upon three difficulties: namely, how **love-capture** <term>philocaptio: a magical "trapping" of someone's affections</term>, hatred in the will, and sorcery in the generative power are caused.

<margin>Carnal love arises from three causes, with examples of each.</margin>

Concerning "love-capture," therefore, or the disordered love of one sex for the other, you should know that it can arise from a threefold cause. Sometimes it comes from the mere **carelessness of the eyes**; sometimes from the temptation of demons alone; and sometimes truly from the sorcery of **necromancers** <note>original: "necromanticorum"; here used generally for practitioners of black magic or those who summon the dead</note> combined with the work of demons. Regarding the first cause, it says in the first chapter of James: "Each one is tempted by his own concupiscence..." <note>original: "concupiscen-"; the catchword from the bottom of the page completing the word concupiscentia (desire/lust)</note>

<summary>This page explores how sorcery and demons can influence human emotions like love and hatred, specifically within and outside of marriage. The Theologian explains that while demons cannot enter the soul directly, they can manipulate the body and senses to cause "love-capture" or impotence.</summary>

### CHAPTER V.

That this may come from the sorceries <note>original: "maleficijs"; referring here to harmful magic or "malefice"</note> of demons and idolaters is shown in Ezekiel 23, under the metaphor of a woman representing Israel, whose people were then following the idols and sorceries of the Assyrians. "She doted," it says, "upon her lovers, upon the Assyrians who were near to her, clothed in violet-blue <note>original: "hiacyntho"; a precious stone or dye, usually blue or purple</note>, princes and magistrates, all of them young men of desire, horsemen riding upon horses." It is established that all these men possessed sorcerers or were idolaters.

<margin>Pierre de la Palu <note>A 14th-century French theologian and jurist</note> in Book 4, Distinction 34, Question 2, Article 3.</margin>
<margin>Five ways in which a demon can act upon the generative and imaginative power.</margin>

In what manner, however, a demon is able to act upon the imaginative power, the phantasy, and the generative <note>the reproductive or sexual</note> power, is shown by Pierre de la Palu in his fourth book, distinction 34, in five ways. 

First, from the fact that it is a spirit, it has power over corporeal creatures regarding **local motion** <note>the ability to move from place to place</note>, either by preventing it or causing it. Therefore, it can hinder bodies so that they do not approach one another, either directly or indirectly, by interposing itself in an assumed body. This happened to a certain bridegroom who had betrothed himself to an idol <note>likely referring to a legend where a man placed a ring on a statue</note>, and yet had contracted a marriage with a young girl; despite this, he was unable to know her carnally because of the demon. 

Second, the demon can inflame a man toward that act, or cool him from it, by secretly applying the powers of natural things <note>such as herbs or minerals</note> which it knows best to be effective for this. 

Third, by disturbing the judgment <note>original: "æstimationem"</note> and the imagination, through which it renders a woman hateful, because it can impress such images into the imagination. 

Fourth, by directly suppressing 
<margin>He is also able to affect the stiffness <note>referring to the physical state of the male organ</note>.</margin>
the vigor of the member suited for fruitfulness, just as it can affect the local motion of any organ whatsoever. 

Fifth, by preventing the movement of the "spirits" <note>in medieval medicine, these were vital fluids that triggered bodily functions</note> to the members in which the motive power resides, as if by blocking the paths of the seed <note>semen</note>, so that it does not descend to the vessels of generation, or does not leave them, or is not aroused, or is not emitted, or in many other ways. 

When women perform sorceries with beans and the testicles of roosters, it is not to be believed that a man is rendered impotent by the inherent power of those things, but rather by the hidden power of demons mocking <note>original: "illudente"</note>...

Whence Cassian in the same place tells of two pagan philosophers and sorcerers <note>original: "maleficis"; those who practice harmful magic</note> who, through three different degrees of malice, successively sent demons by their sorceries to the cell of the blessed Anthony. They did this so that they might drive him away with temptations, being infected with hatred for the holy man because a multitude of people came to him daily. These demons (as the philosophers later confessed after being converted to the faith) struck the blessed Anthony with the bitterest stings of thought; however, he repelled them by the sign of the cross pressed upon his chest and forehead, and by persisting in the vigils of prayer.

<margin>Vincent, *Historical Mirror*, Book 15, Chapter 79. Example.</margin>
In Basil's time, a certain rich man had an only daughter, whom he intended to consecrate to the Lord. A servant of the rich man, unable to have her in marriage, went to a sorcerer and invoked a demon. He handed over to the demon a scroll renouncing his faith and obtained in return a demon of fornication <margin>carnal</margin> to be sent to the daughter. This demon inflamed her to such an extent that, rolling on the ground, she cried out that she was being tortured by love for the servant, and that for her deliverance, her father should give her to the servant in marriage. This was eventually done by the father with a most sorrowful heart. At last, however, the young servant was freed through the intercession of the blessed Basil.

# CHAPTER VI.

<margin>The intoxicated. Pleasures intoxicate the mind, and therefore they make people mindless.</margin>
Those who do not guard themselves from wine, or from a wine-sop <note>original: "vippa"; bread dipped in wine</note>, suddenly fall into drunkenness and walk staggeringly and heavily as if they were out of their minds. This I have seen through experience. For they greedily follow sweet things, and if these are sprinkled with bread dipped in wine, they become intoxicated by such food. By such "foolish ants" intoxicated with wine, we can understand those who, drunk on the pleasures of this world, pursue carnal things through false madness, like those who are out of their minds and lacking reason. To these people, God speaks through the person of Isaiah in chapter 51:
> Listen to this, you poor little one, drunk but not with wine; thus says the Lord your Ruler, and your God. Behold, I have taken from your hand the cup of stupor; I shall not add the dregs of the cup of my indignation for you to drink any further.

Furthermore, Solomon teaches in Proverbs 20 that lust <note>original: "luxuriam"; in this context, it refers to excess or debauchery</note> should be understood through wine, when he says:
> Wine is a luxurious thing, and drunkenness is riotous; whoever delights in these will not be wise.

And in chapter 21 of the same book:
> He who loves feasts shall be in poverty; he who loves wine and fat things shall not be enriched.

And in Psalm 106, it is said again of those who are intoxicated, though not by wine:
> Their soul withered away in evils. They were troubled and moved like a drunken man, and all their wisdom was swallowed up.

Because of this, the Apostle says in the fifth chapter of Ephesians:
> Do not be drunk with wine, in which is debauchery <note>original: "luxuria"</note>, but be filled

<header>THE ANT-HILL, BOOK V.</header>

<margin>Three principal doubts are treated in this chapter.</margin>
...[filled with the] Holy Spirit, speaking to yourselves in psalms and hymns, and spiritual songs, singing and making melody in your hearts to the Lord, giving thanks. <note>This is a continuation of Ephesians 5:18–20, contrasting the "drunkenness" of the Spirit with that of wine.</note> **THE SLUGGARD.** From the previous discussions, I now see clearly that one who is captured by love <term>philocaptum: from the Greek "philos" (love) and Latin "captus" (captured); a person suffering from an obsessive, often magically induced, infatuation</term> suffers from no less madness or "drunkenness" than one seen soaked in wine. Therefore, I now desire to be taught regarding three matters: first, what remedies ought to be applied to such people so they may be healed—not only they themselves, but also those whose generative power <note>In medieval theology, this refers to the ability to procreate or consummate a marriage, which was believed to be a frequent target of sorcery</note> has been hindered by harmful magic <note>original: "maleficiati"</note>. Second, how those may be healed who are captured by love *without* the use of harmful magic. Finally, whether a good spirit can confer as much benefit to chastity as a malignant spirit is accustomed to cause harm through its wicked spells.

<margin>Five remedies against harmful magic.</margin>
**THE THEOLOGIAN.** To answer the first question, you must know that there are five remedies that can be lawfully applied to such people: namely, a pilgrimage to the shrines of certain saints; the frequent use of the sign of the cross and devout prayer; true confession of one's sins or contrition; lawful exorcism through sober words; and the careful removal of the object used in the spell <note>original: "maleficij ablatio"; this refers to finding and destroying physical charms (like hidden dolls or knots) used to cast a spell</note>. Concerning the first remedy, you had an example above in Book One, Chapter Four. The same applies to fasts, abstinences, and other reverent offerings made to specific saints. Concerning the second, you heard in the preceding chapter how the blessed Anthony defended himself against the Tempter with such things. Regarding the third, you have also considered the counsel of Peter of Palude <note>A 14th-century Dominican theologian and Bishop</note>, which Saint Thomas and other doctors recommended before him. Concerning the last remedy, it was discussed recently in the third chapter. And in the second to last chapter, concerning exorcisms, almost everyone speaking on this matter admits that they can be performed in a Catholic manner.

<margin>Thomas Aquinas, in Book 4, Distinction 6, Question 2, Article 3. 2 Corinthians 6.</margin>
Hence, in the fourth book of his *Sentences*, Saint Thomas says: "Because of man's sin, the devil receives power over man and over all things that man uses, to his own harm. And because there is no agreement of Christ with Belial <note>original: "belial"; a biblical name for the devil, meaning "without a yoke" or "worthless"</note>, therefore whenever anything is sanctified..."

### CHAPTER VI.

<margin>

...that which is to be built for divine worship is first exorcised so that, once liberated from the power of the devil—by which he was able to seize that thing for the harm of man—it may be consecrated to God. And this is evident in the blessing of water, in the consecration of a temple, and in all such things. Whence, since the first consecration, by which a human being is consecrated to God, occurs in Baptism, it is necessary that the person also be exorcised first, for a much stronger reason than other things; for in the human being himself there is a cause why the devil receives power over him, and over other things which exist for the sake of man: namely, original or actual sin. And this is signified by those things said in exorcisms, when it is said: > **"Depart from him, Satan."**
Thus says Thomas <note>referring to St. Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the influential Dominican friar and theologian</note>.

However, notwithstanding the application of all the aforementioned remedies, sometimes the victim of harmful magic <note>original: "maleficiatus"</note> is still not released from the penalty, even if he is absolved from the guilt or the sin through which he incurred the magic.

# THE ANT-HEAP, BOOK V.

<margin>
The remedies of sorcerers make things worse, as shown by an example.
</margin>
<margin>
Matthew 12.
</margin>
<margin>
Gregory, *Dialogues*, Book I, Chapter 10.
</margin>
...of the Church, do not always have the power to suppress demons regarding all bodily troubles, as God’s judgment requires this; however, they always have power against those demonic infestations for which they were primarily established. Thus says Thomas <note>St. Thomas Aquinas, the influential 13th-century theologian</note>. But great care must be taken by those who prefer human health to the commands of God and the Church, lest they call upon sorcerers <note>original: *maleficos*</note> for remedies. Through such an invocation, the final state sometimes becomes worse than the first, as Gregory illustrates in an example in the first book of his *Dialogues*. He tells of a woman possessed by one demon; while it was being attempted to free her through the help of sorcerers, a whole legion immediately entered her through the works of those sorcerers.

<margin>
Three doubts concerning exorcism.
</margin>
PIGER <note>The "Sluggard," a character in this dialogue who asks questions of the Theologian</note>: I still have three doubts concerning exorcism. First, whether one who does not hold the formal order of Exorcist <term>Exorcistatus: one of the "minor orders" of the medieval clergy, specifically tasked with performing certain spiritual deliverances</term> may lawfully exorcise demons. Second, what is the difference between the effect of holy water and that of exorcism, since both are ordained against the trouble caused by the demon? Third, whether exorcism merely signifies something symbolically, or if it actually effects a change.

<margin>
Response to the first: Thomas in the *Sentences*, Book 4, Distinction 24, Question 2, Article 2, Reply 9.
</margin>
THEOLOGIAN: The Holy Doctor <note>Aquinas</note> responds to the first and the others. To the first question, in the twenty-fourth distinction of the fourth book, he says: In the order of the exorcist—and in all other minor orders—when they are conferred, a power is received so that a person may do this or that as an official duty, such as exorcising. However, the same thing can be lawfully done by those not holding the order, though not as an official duty, even if they do not hold this by office. Just as Mass can be said in an unconsecrated house—even though the consecration of a church is specifically ordained so that Mass may be said within it—this then pertains more to "grace freely given" <term>gratia gratis data: a spiritual gift granted by God for the benefit of others, independent of the personal holiness or official rank of the person using it</term> than to the "grace of the sacrament."

<margin>
To the second: Thomas in the *Sentences*, Book 4, Distinction 6, Question 2, Article 3. The same is found in the *Summa*, Part 3, Question 71, Article 2, Reply 4.
</margin>
To the second question, he responds in the sixth distinction, saying: The devil attacks us from the outside and from the inside. Therefore, holy water is ordained against the attack of the devil that comes from the outside, but exorcism is ordained against the attack of the devil that comes from the inside. Hence, those against whom it is given are called "energumen" <term>energumeni: from the Greek for "those worked upon," referring to people whose bodies are internally manipulated by a demonic presence</term>, which is to say, "inside..."

### CHAPTER VI.

...suffering either because of the infection of the "fomes" <term>fomes: literally 'tinder,' a theological term for the lingering inclination toward sin or the 'kindling' of lust that remains even after baptism</term> or because of physical possession by a demon. <margin>To the 3rd [doubt]</margin> He [Thomas] <margin>Thomas, in the same place</margin> responds in that same place that it also produces an effect. This is clear, first, because exorcisms are spoken in the manner of a command and not merely as a prayer—for example: "Go out, accursed devil!" <note>original: "Exi maledicte diabole"</note>. Second, it is clear because the blessed Gregory says in his commentary on Ezekiel: <margin>Found in Homily 29 on the Gospels</margin> "When the priest, through the grace of exorcism, lays his hands on the faithful and forbids the wicked spirits to dwell in their minds, what else is he doing but casting out demons?"

Nor is it inappropriate to say that even when an exorcism—previously neglected—is performed on someone who is already baptized, it still achieves something by restraining the attacks of the devil; for even after baptism, some power of the demon can be suppressed through holy water. Indeed, if a child is exorcised and dies before baptism, the ritual was of such value to them during their life that the power of the demon over them was and remains weakened. Therefore, exorcisms do not merely signify something, but they also effect a change, not only in the body but also in the soul, because the infection of the "fomes" <note>the 'tinder' of sin</note> exists in both. This effect is the weakening of the demon's power, so that it cannot hold as much sway over a person as it did before baptism, and so that it does not hinder other good things within them. These are all the words of Thomas.

# CHAPTER VII.

<margin>Ordinary Gloss <note>The *Glossa Ordinaria* was the standard medieval collection of biblical commentaries, often placed in the margins of Bibles.</note> according to the sense. Ordinary Gloss.</margin>

And although he suspected sorcerers—whom he desired to root out from the land with all his might—he did not know who was specifically guilty of this crime inflicted upon him.

# CHAPTER VIII.

She said to Peter <note>Peter of Bern, the judge mentioned in the previous chapter.</note>: "I saw that my husband summoned an old woman, who predicted that I was to be set free. I know that she is lying; because tomorrow, under your judgment, I will be burned to ashes." When the judge later told this to the husband, they waited with laughter to see which of the witches had spoken the truth. But on the following day, the burning of the unfrightened <note>original: *inturritæ*, likely a variant of *interritæ*, meaning fearless or unshaken.</note> woman took place through public justice, which made clear the truth of the witch who had a husband. 

However, Peter, you should not believe—as was held in the first example—that he was literally thrown down the stairs by the hands of the sorcerers who were not physically present in the castle. Rather, it was demons, drawn by the sacrifices or ceremonies of the sorcerers, who were present and caused that fall of Peter; and so that they might deceive the minds of the sorcerers, they acted upon the imagination of those superstitious men to make it seem to them that they were actually present. So too, in the second and third examples, it was caused by the demon's impression upon the imaginative power of the sorcerers, so that things absent were perceived as if they were present, just as you heard above in Chapter 1 and also Chapter 5 of this present book from the words of the Holy Doctor <note>A reference to Thomas Aquinas, often called the "Angelic Doctor" or "Holy Doctor" in medieval theological texts.</note>.

# THE BOOK OF THE ANTS, BOOK V.

<margin>
From Chrysostom in the *Imperfect Work*.
A description of a woman.

Concerning the wickedness of women, it is said in **Ecclesiasticus 25**: <note>original: *Ecclesiast. 25*; also known as the Book of Sirach, a book of wisdom in the Catholic Bible</note> "There is no head more wicked than the head of a serpent, and there is no wrath above the wrath of a woman. And among many things that follow and precede in the same place concerning the wicked woman, he concludes: "All malice is brief compared to the malice of a woman." Hence **Chrysostom** <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407), an influential Archbishop of Constantinople known for his eloquent preaching</note> says regarding that passage in **Matthew 19**, *It is not expedient to marry*: <note>original: *Non expedit nubere*</note> "What else is a woman but an enemy of friendship, an inescapable punishment, a necessary evil, a natural temptation, a desirable calamity, a domestic danger, a delightful detriment, a nature of evil painted with the color of good? One day, he replied to her as she was quarreling with him: "You are a woman, and you have not been corrected by my words. I do not wish to become a soldier against you through heavy beatings, nor do I desire to see you lying in bed crippled <note>original: *contractam*; implying physically incapacitated or shriveled from injury</note> by my blows. But I tell you, unless you improve yourself, I will one day set forth a complaint against you, unrestrained as you are, to my little friends." To which she replied: "In this," she said, "your effeminate spirit and ignoble lineage are clear, for you threaten me with friends of such low status; for you do not threaten a woman with commoners." But he replied: "This time only I will spare you, and on this day, but in truth, if you do not improve, I will complain to my little friends." 

And when the wretched woman did not become better, but rather grew worse, the discreet and prudent man took care to fulfill the truth of his threats on the following day. For then, just as before, she began to attack the man with many insulting words. To which the husband said: "Now the time is here to match my words with deeds." 

Therefore, he seized his own wife, stripped her of all her clothes except for her shift <note>original: *camisiam*; a simple linen undergarment</note>, bound the shifty woman <note>original: *versipellem*; literally "skin-changer," a term for someone deceitful or cunning</note> by her hands and feet, and on his own shoulders carried her, crying and cursing, and threw her into a mound of ants near his garden. There, after being sprayed for a little while with the usual fluid of the ants <note>original: *humore solito*; a reference to formic acid, which Nider previously compared to "mild" discipline</note> and corrected, she began to turn her mind toward better things. For the little creatures, in their usual manner, tormented her severely in her ears and nostrils, in her mouth, and in the woman’s other limbs. Then, with a great wailing, she promised with oaths and solemn vows that she would henceforth obey her husband's every whim, if only she might escape the torment of his "little friends." 

After this, the woman was freed by the man and was improved in a wondrous way and made happy; thereafter her own dangers made her more cautious. Therefore, this method of correction was sufficiently discreet and tempered. But those who correct indiscreetly because of injuries are [like] angry bees...

Why demons make themselves into incubi or succubi.

Now, the reason why demons make themselves into **incubi** or **succubi** <note>demons taking female form to engage in sexual acts with men</note> seems to be this: that through the vice of lust they might harm both parts of a human's nature—namely, the body and the soul—in which injury they seem to take particular delight. ### CHAPTER X.

Ants stain the hands of those who touch them frequently, or rather, those who handle them carelessly stain or defile themselves. # BOOK 5 OF THE ANT-HILL

...of corporeity. The higher man, who is called the spiritual man and the inner man; and there is the sensual man who is, as it were, the middle, and he is called the animal man <note>original: *animalis homo* — in medieval theology, this refers to the "natural" or "soulish" man who is governed by the soul's lower instincts rather than the divine spirit</note>. Each of these, because they possess their own root, branches, and trunk, is likened to a tree. 

<margin>Man as an inverted tree.</margin>
For the shape of the first [physical] man presents the likeness of a tree, but one that is inverted according to the philosophers. This is because the hair on the head is likened to roots, the chest and the parts adjacent to it are called the trunk, while the remaining limbs are seen to take the place of branches; the actions of such things are the bodily fruits. Hence, in Mark chapter 8, we read of the blind man whom the Lord healed little by little according to the growth of his faith; at first, He touched his eyes with spit and asked if he saw anything. To which the man responded: "I see," he said, "men like trees, walking." The Lord teaches that we should not be concerned with this tree of the body, saying in Matthew chapter 6: "Which of you by worrying can add a single cubit to his stature?" "All the hairs of your head," He says in Matthew chapter 10, "are numbered. Therefore, do not be afraid." 

But there is another, the animal man, of whom it is said in 1 Corinthians chapter 2: "The animal man does not perceive those things which are of the Spirit of God; for they are foolishness to him, and he cannot understand them." 

<margin>The Ordinary Gloss <note>The *Glossa Ordinaria* was the standard medieval commentary on the Bible, found in the margins of most scholarly manuscripts.</note></margin>

<margin>There are five causes for which some are possessed, and an example of each.</margin>

Second, they are effective for the guarding of virtue. Regarding this, he says that protection is withdrawn—not that such people are entirely excluded from God's providence, but they lose that specific protection which guards the children of the Church in a more special way. 

Third, they are effective for defending against the Enemy [the Devil]. Regarding this, he says that the devil is given greater power to rage against the person, both physically and spiritually. By the same reasoning, a physical thing can cause a disposition in the human body through which the body becomes unfit to receive the demon’s action. ### CHAPTER XII.

[...they are possessed in the body,] yet they are possessed even more destructively in the soul; for they are entangled by their own vices and pleasures. For according to the 
<margin>2 Peter 2</margin>
sentence of the Apostle: *For by whom a man is overcome, of the same is he brought in bondage* <note>original: "A quo quis superatur, eius seruus efficitur"; a quote from 2 Peter 2:19. The author argues that habitual sin is a more dangerous form of "possession" than physical affliction.</note>, except that these people are more desperately sick in this regard: because they are the slaves of their vices, they do not even realize they are being attacked by them, nor do they recognize that they are enduring their mastery.

The third way of possession is not true or literal, but rather "putative" <note>Putative here means "imagined" or "believed to be true but actually false."</note>, in which certain people think themselves to be possessed, either due to a mere temptation from a demon or from a defect in their bodily complexion <note>original: "vitio corporeę complexionis." In medieval medicine, the "complexion" was the specific balance of the four humors (blood, phlegm, black bile, and yellow bile) in an individual. An imbalance could cause mental distress or hallucinations.</note>. 
<margin>Example of a certain lady who thought she was possessed.</margin>
I knew in the city of Nuremberg a certain young and honorable lady from among the wealthier and more prominent citizens, who was established in the law of matrimony under a husband. For about four years, with only herself and a certain devoted servant of hers being aware, she thought she was entirely possessed by a demon. And because she feared being noticed—and feared for the children she had, should her condition be found out—she began to waste away in her body so severely that neither her beautiful children, nor the presence of her quite upright husband, nor her friends, nor the delights of any feasts were able to cheer her.

I came to the location of the aforementioned city, and because she knew of me, she began to consult me at the gate of the convent concerning the salvation of her soul and other matters. And when, during my words, I happened to name the demon—I know not by what chance—the woman began to turn her head away from me cautiously, so as to spit in a discreet manner <note>original: "faceto more saliuam eijceret"; literally "to cast out saliva in a polite way." Spitting was often a reflex or a ritualistic way to ward off the mention of evil.</note>. For from her past fantasies, whenever she heard the name of the demon mentioned, her soul shuddered from the habit she had contracted. 

Therefore, after we had spoken for a while, when I recognized in the woman's gestures the fear she had been hiding, I said to her: "Lady, if you are willing to confess the truth to me, I will reveal the secret temptation that you are hiding."

She responded in wonder, "I will do so, if you speak the truth."

Then I said: "You believe that you are possessed." 

At this she was astonished and replied: "It is the truth, and..."

Upon hearing this, she began to rejoice and felt better day by day; for a long time afterward, she lived cheerfully and uprightly.

<margin>Example of a man who believed himself to be dead and therefore refused to eat or drink.</margin>
During the time I stayed at the University of Vienna <note>original: "Vviennensi... studio." The University of Vienna was a major center for theological and medical study where Nider spent significant time.</note>, there was a certain married citizen there from one of the better families of the city, known to me and many others. This man, in the course of a certain secular legal proceeding, produced a written legal document. Unbeknownst to him—as it seemed to many—the document, when held up to the rays of the sun, appeared to have been falsified by <term>erasure</term> <note>original: "rasuram." Forgers would often scrape away the top layer of parchment to change names or dates; this was easily detected by holding the document to the light.</note>. Having been privately warned about this later in the presence of his friends, and because he had always been an honorable and trustworthy man, he was deeply ashamed. He believed day and night that he had brought a permanent stain of infamy upon himself, and he would accept no consolation from anyone.

He was therefore brought for examination by those skilled in medicine, and they saw that the young man was suffering from an illness—namely, mania. Consequently, after many remedies had been applied to him without helping at all, the doctors very prudently and in a Christian manner advised that he make a sacramental confession, receive the Sacrament of the Eucharist, and prepare himself in all things as if he were about to die. They did this lest, as his mania progressed and he became impossible to persuade, he might die without such rites and be thought to be possessed by a demon. And so it was done.

For shortly afterward, the idea struck him that he was already dead. And because the dead neither drink, nor eat, nor do other things common to the living, he refused to do any of these things, no matter how much he was urged. As a result, he finally died of pure hunger. Not even the remedy helped by which someone else, by pretending to be dead and eating, had reportedly once cured a similar <term>maniac</term> <note>Nider refers to a well-known medieval medical anecdote where a physician "cured" a man who thought he was dead by having another person pretend to be a corpse who still ate and drank, thus convincing the patient that the dead could eat.</note>. I saw another man, not of the lowest rank, in the city of

### CHAPTER XII.

<margin>Concerning another man who believed he was two people.</margin>
In Cologne, there was a learned and wealthy man, highly honored, from whose own mouth I heard that at one time he was dangerously ill. While he was lying in bed, wherever he looked at himself, it appeared to him that he was two different men. Stunned by this, he began to wonder whether he was dreaming or had gone mad. Then, concluding that this was impossible, and lest he be seen by others as having lost his reason, he secretly called for a physician of the body. The doctor, seeing that <term>mania</term> <note>As noted previously, Nider uses "mania" as a medical diagnosis for what we might call clinical delusions or psychosis today.</note> was present, comforted the sick man with good hope and gave him the spirit to recover, provided that he receive the divine Sacraments. Once this was done, the sick man recovered day by day; as the illness receded through the giving of thanks, that maniacal suffering <margin>maniacal</margin> also departed. He later concealed the fact that he had suffered this from almost everyone, until he heard from me in person that this infirmity was of a natural cause.

<margin>Concerning another very wealthy man who, out of mania, feared he would be forced to beg.</margin>
In another city, I had knowledge of another great, wealthy, and upright man who, although he was extremely rich and endowed with many permanent estates and rents, and was a man of great counsel, at last began to fear that he would eventually be forced to beg for his bread. This was despite the fact that, in everyone's judgment, he was a man of such great wealth and provided with such income that he had enough silver to eat, if he so wished <note>original: "ad comedendum argentum satis haberet." A common medieval expression for someone so wealthy they could theoretically consume their own assets without running out.</note>. Terrified by the aforementioned mania, he was burdened beyond measure, nor could these thoughts be removed from his head by any persuasion; and thus, having lived as a Catholic—though not without this [mental] mark—he finally passed away.

<margin>Concerning his son, who suffered from the same vice.</margin>
He had at that time an adult son, recently married, who was likewise troubled by a similar mania; it is said he suffered from it even more severely in the same matter than his father <margin>father</margin> had.

<margin>Concerning another man who despaired due to mania.</margin>
In the diocese of Bamberg, I was once called to the home of a certain craftsman who was quite ill. He spoke with total despair regarding the salvation of his soul and had frequently and anxiously sought out weapons so that he might kill himself. I urged the aforementioned craftsman—who was, clearly, a <term>maniac</term> <note>Nider continues to use "mania" as a medical category for what we would recognize as psychosis or severe clinical depression.</note>—with as many passages from Holy Scripture as occurred to me, so that, truly grieving for his sins, he might firmly hope to obtain full pardon from God. But I achieved nothing. He alleged that he had committed a certain quite moderate sin, and even repeated it, and for that reason he believed and stated that he could not be saved. I pressed him more sharply, replying that even greater sinners had obtained grace. Nevertheless, he rejected my words, saying, "Lord, I believe my experience; for I actually see the pits of hell, and from there I behold flames terrifyingly flying toward me." Then I urged that a physician be called, and that remedies for sleeping, or other necessary things according to the physician’s advice, be applied; and I left. I returned the following day and, as before, tried to persuade him regarding the hope of pardon. But he said, "Do you think I can obtain pardon for my sins?" I replied happily that he could. For he had slept, and through medical treatments his <term>melancholy</term> <note>In medieval medicine, "melancholy" was one of the four humors. An excess was thought to cause deep depression and hallucinations.</note> had cooled. Thus, because he now felt a sense of doubt and had become more composed in spirit, he seemed easily led back to the hope of pardon.

*PIG.* <note>The "Piger" or "Lazy One," a student character who asks questions of the Teacher.</note> Perhaps those who are sometimes found to be stubborn against the articles of faith by the <term>inquisitors of heretical depravity</term> <note>The official title for Church officials tasked with investigating heresy.</note> are suffering from such a maniacal passion; and those who are ignorant of these things immediately hand such people over to the <term>secular arm</term> <note>original: "brachium seculare." The "secular arm" refers to the civil authorities who carried out physical punishments, such as execution, which the Church itself was forbidden from performing.</note>, where they are burned with far too much haste.

*THEOL.* <note>The "Theologus" or "Theologian," representing Nider’s own voice.</note> It is possible that this happens through careless inquisitors, just as you suggest. Perhaps it would have happened this way with that Hungarian priest, whom I told you about above in Book III, Chapter 10, had he not been a man of great learn—

### CHAPTER XII.

<margin>1 John 4</margin>
...if prudence had prevented this. For this reason, one must test the spirits to see whether they are from God <note>original: "probandi sunt spiritus an ex Deo sint." A reference to 1 John 4:1, a key verse for the medieval practice of "Discretio spirituum" or the discernment of spirits.</note>, or if they arise from physical weakness, or from the malice of a demon, or from the stubbornness of one's own will. In these matters, those who have the duty to care for such people must provide time, the right setting, wholesome persuasions, and prudent considerations, so that nothing essential is omitted; for this concerns not only the health of bodies, but the perpetual danger to souls.

<margin>Concerning another man who wished to kill himself with his own knife.</margin>
Furthermore, I knew a certain most excellent professor of the liberal arts and of the Sacred Scriptures who began to be oppressed by a most heavy imagination and a <term>mania</term> <note>In this context, mania refers to a clinical mental disturbance rather than just "excitement."</note> regarding killing himself with his own knife. He was deeply ashamed to reveal this, yet he could not dispel the <term>phantasy</term> <note>Latin: *phantasia*. In medieval psychology, this refers to a persistent mental image or intrusive thought that takes hold of the mind's eye.</note>. At last, he came to me in secret, wept copiously, and asked for a remedy. For certain reasons, I first persuaded him to attempt a cleansing of his conscience through sacramental confession, which he did. However, he was not set free, because in the judgment of a physician of the body, he was suffering from a physical mania. 

Thus, at one point, this same sufferer—who in all other matters possessed great prudence—said to me while weeping: "It is a strange business," he said, "I experience myself using reason, and I know that I am, by all logic, free; yet I am not able to cast off this phantasy of killing myself, even with my full freedom of soul." For such people, there is often far more need for a physician of the body than for a physician of the soul.

# Front Cover of the Manuscript

This volume is encased in an ornate, <term>blind-tooled</term> <note>A decorative technique where patterns are impressed into leather using heated metal tools without the application of gold leaf or ink, resulting in a dark, recessed design.</note> leather binding. The craftsmanship reflects the era's dedication to preserving sacred and academic texts. 

The central panel displays a complex, symmetrical <term>arabesque</term> <note>A style of decoration characterized by intertwining fluid lines and scrolling foliage, often creating a sense of infinite patterns.</note> pattern, featuring interlaced scrollwork that radiates from a central floral element. This centerpiece is framed by several concentric borders:

*   A narrow inner frame that provides structure to the central design.
*   A wider primary border decorated with a repeating vine motif of flowers and leaves.
*   An outer border defined by simple, crisp ruled lines.

Small, six-petaled rosettes are stamped into the corners of the inner rectangular fields, adding a delicate detail to the geometric layout. 

The leather itself is a light brown hue, bearing the characteristic marks of age, including some staining and a small patch of surface wear in the upper right corner. Along the left edge, two dark metal hinges remain attached, once used to secure the book's clasps to keep the heavy parchment or paper leaves flat and protected from moisture.

<summary>This page illustrates the manuscript's exterior, a 16th or 17th-century style blind-tooled leather binding with intricate arabesque and floral motifs. The physical condition and metal hardware highlight the book's history as a durable, protected scholarly object.</summary>
